papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost of video-generative world models and the feature-space disconnect in existing latent policies.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers that couples the VLM with foresight and continuous action experts.
Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.
Trained on human videos and robot trajectories, it reports 81.9% success on SIMPLE and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk.
Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Unifies vision-language-action control with latent world modeling for robot foundation models.
papers.title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
papers.tldr: Z-sight unifies vision-language-action control with latent future prediction by jointly generating visual tokens and actions without pixel reconstruction or external encoders.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.
authors: Yupeng Zheng, Chaoyue Li, Linbo Wang, Xiang Li, Yuhang Zheng, Xiaotong Su, Songen Gu, Yichen Zhang, Zebin Xing, Shuai Tian, Jingxiang Guo, Jing Li, Zhiyong Zhao, Zhongpu Xia, Qichao Zhang, Haoran Li, Shuicheng Yan, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the gap between reconstruction-focused visual representations and the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation.
Uses dual-teacher distillation to enrich DINOv3 features with geometric and spatiotemporal knowledge, then CS-VAE to compress them into generative scene latents.
Jointly predicts scene-structure latents, appearance latents, and robot actions to model scene evolution and action generation.
Pretrained with approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot-manipulation data; achieves strong results across simulated and real-robot, single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous benchmarks.
Shows robustness to perturbations, improved scaling with more data than a video-VAE-only baseline, cross-embodiment transfer, and effective few-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Robot reward modeling faces two challenges: generalizing across tasks and accurately tracking progress in long-horizon manipulation. General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored. Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions. We train a language-conditioned model to estimate progress in short-horizon tasks and individual subtasks of long-horizon tasks. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask's predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress. General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores. Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.
authors: Zi-ang Cao, Kaiyuan Zheng, Yinzhen Xu, Haonan Duan, Jiasheng Gu, Fengyuan Hu, Nan Zhu, Kun Lei, Kevin Lin, Ruijie Zheng, Shenyuan Gao, Fangqi Zhu, Zhe Zhang, Radha Poovendran, Linxi Fan, Guanzhi Wang, Yuke Zhu
bullets: Addresses poor transfer from short-task reward models and limited reuse of task-specific long-horizon progress models.
Identifies unfinished subtasks and predicts their continuous progress from language-conditioned visual inputs.
Composes current subtask progress with credit for completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress.
Introduces dense progress supervision derived from sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations, accounting for failures and uneven subtask durations.
Pretraining on 200 diverse manipulation tasks supports zero-shot unseen-task reward prediction, improves adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, and boosts downstream policy performance.

papers.abstract: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.
authors: Yash Jangir, Karan Mirakhor, Renos Zabounidis, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, Yonatan Bisk, Homanga Bharadhwaj
bullets: Problem: Action-only world models must learn both known body motion and harder-to-predict environmental changes, limiting transfer across embodiments.
Method: Condition video prediction on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories.
Training: Jointly learns one backbone and conditioning adapter from about 600 hours across eight robot and human embodiments, without embodiment labels.
Results: Improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out robot-arm trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation.
Scope: Cross-embodiment training improves robot predictions on four of six evaluation sets, while requiring camera-pose recovery when extrinsics are unavailable.

papers.abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.
authors: Hengguang Zhou, I-Hung Hsu, Li Chen, Priyanshi Shrivastava, Anastasios Angelopoulos, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ion Stoica, Cho-Jui Hsieh
bullets: Prior evaluation methods detected only 5–6 of 10 deliberately induced failures, and combined scores could favor simulators that accepted broken work.
The study perturbs simulated replays with altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and other failures to meta-evaluate metrics.
The proposed suite combines utility for evaluating agents with population-level and trace-level fidelity to real users.
It detected all 10 tested perturbations under the study’s criterion.
Across 351 real multi-turn sessions involving 348 users, 23 languages, and six simulators, population-level measures sometimes missed wrong goals, ignored constraints, and out-of-character behavior.

papers.abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan, Bob Kamma, Michael Ge, John Xin Zhou, Andrea Olgiati
bullets: Addresses stale fixed dispatch rates caused by changing fleet capacity and unpredictable output lengths.
Uses fail-fast capacity checks, durable priority queues, and a stateful controller that probes upward and backs off based only on refusals.
Production A/B testing served a classifier with 43% fewer H100s, though lower-priority work waited longer during backfill peaks.
In replay, it achieved within 1% of tuned fixed-rate goodput with about one-quarter the refusal share.
Deployed at Meta for post and live-video understanding, processing over 300 million requests and hundreds of terabytes of media daily.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The traffic shaper implements CAP-AND-TRACK. (a) One enqueue interface feeds online and batch queues. TRACK runs in the online workers and dispatches each queue through the gateway at its learned rate. A refusal from any of the four kinds of CAP (model-server cap, provider admission, per-caller quota, or engine queue-depth aware router) returns as HTTP 429. Other failures stay outside the feedback loop. (b) Each worker paces each queue at the rate the leader pushes. A 429 returns the request to the front of its ready queue with media staged. Up to 3N media items are in flight, but only N download and N upload at once. The rest wait between the two stages to keep each worker container’s network bandwidth saturated.

Figure 2. Controlled replay at about twice a replica’s capacity, median of three runs per arm. Without the cap, goodput (successes per minute) falls to zero and stays there once requests queued inside the model server outlive the timeout. With the cap, goodput holds steady.

Figure 3. Classifier replay at a cap of 40 with only dispatch varied. One of two replicas was removed for minutes 15–25 (shaded) and then restored. Goodput per host (top) and refusal share (bottom) are in 15-second bins. Dashed lines mark measured full and cut capacity. During the cut TRACK’s refusals fell as it descended toward the new ceiling. The 100 and 120% rates drew 49% and 58% refusals over the cut. TRACK regained full capacity within about 5 minutes of the restore. Every arm tested at both caps had cap-64 goodput within about 0.8% of its cap-40 goodput in every phase (Table C1). Median of three runs per arm; bands span the runs.

Figure 4. On-demand workload over the three loss days, hourly from the start of the first. Completions are multiples of the median on the day before the first loss (log scale). The queue is in hours of median completions. Each morning the pool lost capacity and the queue held the excess. Each afternoon TRACK followed the pool’s 429s back up and drained the queue.

papers.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
authors: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses rule-state persistence across saving and loading and rule-to-visual realization, including unseen affected objects.
Represents rules, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph linked to video generation and perceptual feedback.
Uses dynamic object binding, state-constrained generation, attribute state replacement, and counterfactual reconstruction training.
Introduces RuleVerse, a rule-driven interaction dataset built from GTA-V and Habitat with detailed state and event annotations.
Experiments show improved consistency of saved/restored rules and accurate realization of rule outcomes on specified objects and attributes.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of WorldRuler. papers.abstract: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.
authors: Chenjie Zhao, Zhiliang Zhu, Quan Chen, Yuquan Xue, Xingxue Shi, Puyue Wang, Zhiqiang Zhao, Kangye Zheng, Boyang Xu, Mingwei Lin, Dejun Li

Reaches 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials without real-test-environment fine-tuning, versus 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
bullets: Addresses the underexplored challenge of effectively combining atomic, capability-specific reasoning skills.

Distills prototype preferences into a lightweight router that selects a problem-specific skill composition at inference time.
On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, improves average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2.
Raises average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8% on AtomicMath.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Atomic MathReasoner (AMR) framework. Top (Stage 1): Prototype Construction. We first decouple mathematical reasoning into atomic capabilities and train corresponding LoRA modules. A gradientfree optimization algorithm is then applied to the validation set to search for localized capability compositions, constructing a Compositional Prototype Set. Bottom (Stage 2): Route Selection Mechanism. We generate pseudo-labels via token-level NLL and apply a margin-based filtering strategy to obtain a noise-removed training set. Finally, a lightweight router utilizing TF-IDF feature extraction is trained to dynamically predict a suitable combination for unseen problems.

Figure 1: Conventional LLMs treat mathematical reasoning as a monolithic capability, often failing across diverse mathematical problems. In contrast, AMR dynamically composes atomic reasoning experts for each input through instance-level routing, enabling problem-adaptive capability synergy and more accurate mathematical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.
authors: Haozhe Wu, Zhonghang Li, Chao Huang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining reliable state as prices, news, portfolios, capital, and execution contexts change.

papers.abstract: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
authors: Mark Marosi, Peter Antal
bullets: Withholding skill-specific training signals delays, but does not prevent, capability acquisition.
The delay for larger models can be predicted from results on smaller models.
A chess model trained without explicit check responses ranked legal responses nearly as well as one trained with them.
Models regained withheld skills using only a small fraction of the data required from initialization, with the fraction shrinking as training progressed.
The findings span chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, web text, and a withheld programming language.

papers.selection_reason: Provides transferable insights into how general LM progress substitutes for withheld training data, relevant to language foundation model training and data filtering.
papers.title: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
papers.tldr: General model improvement can largely compensate for withheld training data, making hidden capabilities easier and faster to learn later.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: The study evaluates whether semantic forecasts change appropriately when the ego action is altered.
It compares feature-wise and input-level action conditioning with an otherwise identical model without action input.
Test-time action interventions are assessed using standard segmentation metrics in a synthetic environment, Cityscapes, and BDD100K.
Correct actions improve mid-term mIoU by up to 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K; incorrect actions reduce it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, respectively.
On real data, feature-wise conditioning is 1.6× more action-dependent than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy.

A U-Net maps the four context segmentations to logits, which are added to the scaled last context map and normalised by a softmax; the prediction is fed back for the next step. At test time, the future action is replaced to measure action dependence (bottom right). The thumbnails show a Cityscapes validation scene in which the vehicle turns left (v̄ = 4.6m/s, ω̄ = 0.36 rad/s) and the mid-term predictions of a trained FiLM model; the shuffled action (6.5m/s, 0.00 rad/s) and the training-mean action (6.3m/s, 0.00 rad/s) both correspond to straight driving.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies action-conditioned semantic forecasting as a driving world model, fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: Action-conditioned semantic forecasters may appear accurate without meaningfully using the ego action, so action-intervention tests are needed to measure true action dependence.

papers.abstract: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by $+2.42$ points on RULER, $+1.08$ on LongBench, and $+0.76$ on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only $0.72$--$3.57$ GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.
authors: Disen Lan, Xuanda Wang, Jianbin Zheng, Huafeng Kuang, Wei Tang, Yu Cheng
bullets: Hybrid attention models need to choose which layers retain full attention under a compute budget.
FlashMorph2 evaluates discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, avoiding off-policy selection errors.
It jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights to reflect performance after recovery.
Across Qwen3 scales and linear-attention variants, it improves over FlashMorph by 2.42 RULER points, 1.08 LongBench points, and 0.76 points on recall-intensive tasks.
Layer selection takes 0.72–3.57 GPU hours for 0.6B–8B models, indicating efficient scaling.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of FlashMorph2. Following layerwise alignment, FlashMorph2 constructs a hybrid attention model through on-policy layer selection, jointly optimizing layer scores and model weights over sampled discrete hybrid architectures. The resulting hybrid attention model is further trained using logits distillation and long-context finetuning to recover model quality.
Figure 3. Layer-selection Efficiency across Model Scales. Comparison of (a) FLOPs and (b) GPU hours required for layer selection across Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B parameters.
Figure 4. RULER Performance across Hybrid Ratios. Average RULER scores on the Qwen3-1.7B backbone across varying hybrid ratios for (a) GLA and (b) GDN variants.
Table 5. Training Configurations across the Four-Stage Transformer-to-hybrid Conversion Pipeline.
Table 4. Hybrid Attention Model Configurations across Different Scales.

papers.selection_reason: On-policy layer selection for hybrid full/linear attention Transformers; directly targets efficient attention with quality-efficiency trade-offs.
papers.title: On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models
papers.tldr: FlashMorph2 selects full-attention layers on-policy and jointly adapts weights, improving hybrid Transformer quality efficiently across model scales.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. This stems from the fact that existing MLLMs are trained on images with limited diverse camera-object relations and corresponding textual descriptions. To address this, we propose a synthetic generation pipeline to create large-scale 3D visual instruction datasets. Our framework takes 3D assets as input and uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation models to create photorealistic images preserving precise camera-object relations. Additionally, large language models (LLMs) are used to generate text prompts for guiding visual instruction tuning and controlling image generation. We create Ultimate3D, a large-scale 3D-grounded 2D visual instruction dataset. Ultimate3D consists of 240K VQAs with precise camera-object annotations, and corresponding benchmark. MLLMs fine-tuned on our proposed dataset outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks. Our code, dataset, and benchmark will contribute to broad MLLM applications.
authors: Liu He, Yizhi Song, Ruiqi Xu, Baris Sarper Tezcan, Xiao Zeng, Albert Y. C. Chen, Lu Xia, Shashwat Verma, Sankalp Dayal, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Daniel Aliaga
bullets: Targets weaknesses in recognizing object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots.
Uses 3D assets, rendering, diffusion-based image generation, and LLM-generated prompts to produce photorealistic training images with precise relations.
Provides 240K visual question-answer pairs with camera-object annotations and a corresponding benchmark.
MLLMs fine-tuned on Ultimate3D achieve a reported 29.7% average accuracy improvement over commercial models on camera-object relation tasks.
Scope is focused on 3D-grounded camera-object relation recognition.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Generating Synthetic Visual Instruction Dataset. Our framework uses open-sourced 3D assets to generate photo-realistic images with precisely controlled camera-object relation. Corresponding text instructions are also generated by Large Language Model (LLM). The generated Ultimate3D dataset (240K) and benchmark (8K) advance baseline MLLM models (Gemma-4, Qwen3-VL, etc.) to outperform commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5, etc.) on camera-object relation recognition tasks. The left panel illustrates representative MLLM failures, while the right panel provides a direct same-image comparison between base and Ultimate3D-fine-tuned models.

Fig. 5: Ablations on Image Generation Pipeline. Our framework shows superior performance by using multi-ControlNet with SDXL backbones, and introducing both Canny edges and depth maps as visual priors. It consistently delivers better robustness and quality compared to text-only SDXL and [80]. When these visual priors are removed (top-right: removing all visual priors; bottom-right: removing depth prior), the generator often fails to produce good results and brings lower generation success rate (see Sec 4.6, [80] only achieves 55.11% success rate v.s. ours 93.07%)

Fig. 2: Our Framework. Each shade box corresponds to a section in Sec. 3. Given open-sourced 3D assets, our approach leverages a 3D Renderer to generate 3D visual priors (Iβ) preserving ground truth camera-object relation (β). Meanwhile, LLMs take 3D asset category to generate diverse image descriptions (Timg) as conditional guidance. Both the 3D visual priors and diverse text prompts are used to generate synthetic images (Isyn) by multiple ControlNet-based networks. Corresponding text QA instructions (Tqa) are generated by LLMs given the ground truth camera-object relation. Our Ultimate3D dataset and benchmark (i.e. pairs of Tqa and Isyn) contribute to fine-tuning and evaluation of MLLMs.

Fig. 3: 3D Visual Prior Rendering. With a general camera model, our method utilizes a 3D Renderer (e.g., Blender) to render multiple 3D visual priors given arbitrary camera-object relations. O: camera center; A: object center; D: camera-object distance.

Fig. 4: Qualitative Results. We show responses by GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking, Gemma-4-31B-it, and finetuned Gemma-4-31B-it on the Ultimate3D benchmark. Each model is asked questions (in gray boxes) regarding object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot type, together with the input images on the left. The model responses illustrate that the Gemma-4-31B-it model finetuned on Ultimate3D can precisely recognize camera-object relations on synthetic images. GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.5-Flash with high thinking sometimes provide correct answers, but also exhibit inconsistent predictions across relation types. The original Gemma-4-31B-it frequently fails to produce the correct camera-object relation labels, while the finetuned model provides substantially more accurate and taskrelevant answers.

Table 1: Quantitative Comparisons. We evaluate open-source and closed-source MLLMs on the Ultimate3D and MMVP benchmarks. LLaVA and Llama models are fine-tuned using their original full fine-tuning recipes, while Gemma-4 and Qwen models are fine-tuned with LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning (for Qwen, the vision-language merger is also fully trained). Results report MLLM response accuracy (%) for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera-shot recognition. Superscripts indicate the fine-tuning setup: F full fine-tuning and L LoRA fine-tuning.

Table 2: Generalization. We finetune LLaVA1.6-13B model using a mixture of both general VQA and camera-object relation VQA datasets. Without degradation on general VQA tasks, finetuned model improves its ability on camera-object relation recognition and beats SOTA (i.e. GPT4o) by 28.42% accuracy on Ultimate3D benchmark. ∗ denotes the average accuracy (%) across all 3 types of camera-object relation VQAs in Tab. 1.

papers.selection_reason: Large-scale instruction data teaching MLLMs 3D camera-object spatial relations, fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Ultimate3D: Teaching Multimodal LLMs 3D Camera-Object Relations by Large-Scale Visual Instruction Data
papers.tldr: Ultimate3D improves MLLMs’ understanding of 3D camera-object relations through large-scale synthetic visual instruction data.

papers.abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.
authors: Tobias Braun, Marcus Rohrbach, Lorenzo Cavallaro
bullets: Unified models can expose intermediate reasoning concepts through their text-conditioned image-generation pathways.
V-lens visualizes a selected token’s hidden state without training a separate decoder.
Across six models, visualizations reveal implicit concepts linking questions to answers.
Concepts vary with context, token position, and network depth.
Lens tuning raises correct pronoun-referent visualizations from 2–11% to 86–94% and improves text answers indirectly.

Below, one word appears twice in a sentence with two meanings, and each occurrence is visualized separately.

Each column pair shows the V-LENS pictures of the boxed it after one kind of training, with correct pictures framed. Only lens tuning makes both pictures correct in all three models. The best later token is the best token after the description’s last word through the first answer token, including the instruction and chat-format tokens. The dotted lines mark each model’s insertion layer.

The resulting state replaces thing in the drawing request as it enters the insertion layer R. HunyuanImage-3.0 and Show-o2 process text and image with one shared transformer. Liquid and Janus-Pro write the image one token at a time after attending prior text and image tokens.

Figure 8. Training the pictured state changes the answer in Showo2 and HunyuanImage-3.0. The V-LENS visualizes the subject of supervised stories before and after lens tuning. Below each picture is the model’s text answer with its corresponding probability.

Figure 5. The model is asked to think about an object while copying an unrelated sentence. The V-LENS can reveal this object visually from a token of the copied sentence at layer 25. Each thinkinstruction is shown above and the copied sentence below.

Figure 6. The V-LENS reads contextual concepts through the purely autoregressive unified models Liquid [44] and JanusPro [8]. Each pair shows the highlighted word drawn on its own (left picture of each pair) beside the visualization of its hidden state in the question through the V-LENS (right picture of each pair).

Table 5. Ablations of Eq. (1). Each column changes one part: using no coordinate scaling (D=I), no centering on the source mean µℓ, no insertion-layer mean µR, or spreads from only one layer. We count the visualized unnamed concepts as in Tab. 1.

papers.selection_reason: Interpretability method for unified multimodal models via hidden-state visualization and lens tuning.
papers.title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
papers.tldr: V-lens visualizes hidden concepts in unified multimodal models and uses image-based supervision to improve both visualizations and text answers.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked several questions about the same image in a single prompt (co-asking), yet existing evaluations report conflicting accuracy gains and hallucinations at the prompt level without tracking how individual answers change. By pairing each question's single-question and co-asked answers across 22 open-weight VLMs (1B-35B), we find that erratic net shifts reflect two opposing effects: on Densely Captioned Images (DCI), every model repairs 15.4%-29.8% of its single-question errors under co-asking, while the share of correct answers turned wrong falls from 30.8% on weaker models to 4.7% on stronger ones. Across all 14 models supporting custom attention masks, we show through attention readouts and layer-window interventions that earlier same-image questions read visual information into their question tokens in the early-to-middle layers during prefill, helping later questions concentrate image attention onto their queried targets. This visual help accumulates across the scene even across non-overlapping regions, whereas blocking earlier questions from attending to the image lowers both target localization and accuracy in all 14 models. While cross-question help is established during shared question reading, part of the co-asking damage enters later during answer decoding when the decoder attends to other question stems. We therefore introduce Read Together, Answer Apart, a training-free decoding mask that keeps shared prefill intact and isolates each answer from other stems, improving co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI (up to +4.71 percentage points, closing 70% of the pooled gap to asking alone) and on 10, 8, and 5 of the 14 models on WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA (up to +11.4, +5.3, and +1.1 points).
authors: Xinyi Guo, Kaile Huang, Xitong Ling, Mingyi He, Chende Zheng, Jianyu Xu, Chao He, Dongqing Song
bullets: Co-asking produces mixed effects because it both repairs single-question errors and creates new errors.
On densely captioned images, all 22 models recover 15.4%–29.8% of prior errors, while stronger models make fewer correct-to-wrong flips.
Earlier questions transfer visual information across the image during early-to-middle prefill layers, improving later-question target localization.
Some damage arises during answer decoding when answers attend to other question stems.
The training-free Read Together, Answer Apart mask improves accuracy on most tested models across DCI, WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and improves VLM multi-question inference via attention masking, relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Read Together, Answer Apart: How Earlier Questions Help Vision-Language Models Look
papers.tldr: Earlier questions help VLMs inspect an image during shared prompt processing, but can hurt answer decoding; isolating answers from other question stems improves multi-question accuracy.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. Structural probes suggest that this advantage is associated with greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger dependence on temporal context. These results indicate that predictive and reconstructive objectives induce distinct representations of dynamics, trading state fidelity for properties that may benefit long-horizon prediction.
authors: Ron Kosova, Francesco Croce
bullets: Studies reconstruction versus latent-prediction objectives using capacity-matched video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck.
Introduces asymmetric discretization to apply the same discrete bottleneck to the predictive V-JEPA model.
Autoencoding retains substantially more physical state information and performs slightly better on one-step latent prediction.
Predictive representations accumulate less error during autoregressive rollout, with benefits linked to robustness to visual perturbations and stronger temporal-context dependence.
The objectives create a trade-off between state fidelity and properties useful for long-horizon dynamics prediction.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how reconstruction vs prediction pretraining shapes video representations for downstream dynamics, relevant to video representation learning and predictive video world models.
papers.title: Reconstruction vs. Prediction Pre-Training of Discrete Video Representations for Continuous Control
papers.tldr: Reconstruction pre-training preserves physical state information better, while prediction pre-training produces representations that are more robust and accumulate less error over long rollouts.

papers.abstract: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.
authors: Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun, Kerda Varaku
bullets: Factual transitions alone cannot identify what would have happened under another action when disturbances are hidden.
For smooth systems with separable action and disturbance forces, the counterfactual is approximated by the observed outcome plus the model’s alternative-versus-factual prediction difference.
The method requires no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining, with an $O(h^2)$ error bound and matching minimax lower bound.
Across rendered simulators, counterfactual $R^2$ improves from 38–46% to 86–96%; an underwater-vehicle task reaches 90–94%.

The approach improves hindsight planning, finding goal-reaching actions in 35–69% of events versus 14–23% for the comparison planner, but can fail at discontinuities, coordinate folds, or disturbance-scaled commands.

papers.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
papers.tldr: A simple physics-based correction lets JEPA world models answer counterfactual action questions from factual data alone, substantially improving prediction and hindsight planning.

papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.
authors: Austin C Baker, Raiyaan Abdullah, Daniel Zeev Yoffe, Shruti Vyas, Yogesh S Rawat
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for compositional reasoning about aggressive actions and participant roles.
Tests joint recognition of actions, role identification, and action–participant binding under distractors.
Evaluation of 17 multimodal models finds performance declines as reasoning complexity increases.
Models often confuse aggressors with victims or bystanders, despite recognizing coarse aggression.
Role-graph prompting improves compositional reasoning, while scaling and generic reasoning provide limited gains.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
authors: Zhaolu Wang, Jiacheng Xu, Lihong Wang, Shuqing Wang, Jianjie Fang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Rongze Tang, Yiding Ma, Xin Zhang, Jiawei Chen, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Evaluates human, simulated dexterous, and real dexterous hand models across six dimensions, including hand fidelity, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence.

Uses 500 manually selected clips spanning seven task families under a unified evaluation protocol.

papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/
authors: Emad Aghajanzadeh, Bethany Anne Wong, Leonhard Kunze, Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: Integrates a compact (<150M-parameter) language model for visual question answering, scene description, and action commentary.
Projects intermediate driving representations into language-embedding space to support effective reasoning with a lightweight LM.
Distills LM reasoning into surrogate features so planning can operate with either the LM or without it during deployment.
Uses an adjustable reasoning rate to balance computational cost and language-assisted planning.
Reports strong Bench2Drive performance and competitive NAVSIM and AlpaSim results at lower computational cost than VLM-based approaches.

papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.
authors: Zihe Huang, Sirui Zhou, Haozhi Han, Ruge Zhang, Teng Ma, Tao Ma, Zheng Liu, Ce Zhang, Ting Cao, Yunxin Liu, Yunquan Zhang, Yifeng Chen, Kun Li
bullets: Existing retrieved rollouts can harm performance, even on previously solved tasks.
Form compresses both successful and failed rollouts into short, verified operation records.
Fit teaches the policy to interpret records and predict when they will help.
Fusion adds records’ images, text, and actions as a prefix and action prior.
Trained on 200 examples, F³ achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab, including gains over native Cosmos 3 Nano and 57% fewer regressions.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.
authors: Zijie Xin, Tianyi Wang, Daoze Zhang, Jie Yang, Changli Tang, Qijie Wei, Fengyun Rao, Xirong Li
bullets: Tests complete videos with native speech, requiring a text reply or [SILENCE] when no response is needed.
Includes 1,000 Chinese and English samples across five categories and 16 subcategories, with contrastive scene-based pairs.
Uses separate rubric scores for language, intent recognition, and content fulfillment, verified against each video.
Across 30 model configurations, the best overall score was 59.6; intent recognition outperformed content fulfillment.
Models often respond to peer conversations and struggle when a reply must satisfy multiple people.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Qu\'ebec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Qu\'ebec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.
authors: Eeham Khan, Richard Khoury, Leila Kosseim
bullets: Studies CPT across nine LLMs using a budget-matched 30M-token protocol.
CPT benefits models with weaker existing competence in Quebec French, but is not uniformly useful.
Literary text drives most gains, while corpus register determines which regional expressions are learned.
Improvements mainly affect expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence.
CPT can reduce reading comprehension, effects that aggregate scores may hide.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

Uses paired advantages to distinguish reaching more solvable states from completing tasks afterward.
Expands capability backward along successful trajectories, then outward through on-policy exploration.

papers.abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.
authors: Eerik Alamikkotervo, Risto Ojala
bullets: Vision foundation models struggle with semantic prediction in natural, unstructured offroad scenes.
The method fits a sphericity–elevation distribution for each semantic class using only high-confidence vision predictions.
These class-specific geometric priors are fused with vision foundation model outputs to produce the final 3D semantic map.
The approach improves the SAM3 baseline on RELLIS-3D by 6.3 mIoU points and 8.9 accuracy points, and on WildScenes by 1.7 and 2.1 points, respectively.
The work focuses on offroad semantic mapping and plans to release its source code upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of general capabilities caused by model adaptation.
Uses local preservation-loss geometry to define a nearly invariant, low-curvature update space.
Scales the approach with K-FAC curvature approximations and a factorized projection; CurvLoRA provides a more efficient low-rank variant.
Across math reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning, achieves competitive task performance while better balancing acquisition and retention than baselines.
On TOFU and MUSE, improves the trade-off between targeted forgetting and retained knowledge, approaching from-scratch retraining retention.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Targets appearance and geometric defects in unseen categories without target-specific training data.
Uses Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation to refine 3D point features with density-adaptive neighborhoods.
Uses Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation to smooth multi-scale CLIP patch embeddings with a trainable adapter.
Introduces Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive loss to align normality and abnormality concepts across modalities.
Reports state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies, with up to 2.9% higher pixel-level AUPRO than competing methods.

(b) The proposed AggCLIP framework effectively addresses these gaps. It refines noisy back-projected point features via the Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module, suppresses 2D spatial noise using Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) paired with a learnable Adapter, and directly enforces deep cross-modal semantic interaction via the Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
bullets: MatterChat uses a large bridge and separate contrastive alignment; this work instead learns representation selection jointly on downstream tasks.
Different target properties benefit from representations at different depths of Zatom-1, while CHGNet and Zatom-1 provide complementary information.
Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, including up to 47.8% lower RMSE, with fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.
Adding UMA-S shows flexibility across encoder combinations; the three-encoder setup reaches 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our proposed Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) methodology. (a) Frozen domain encoders (Zatom-1 and CHGNet) extract complementary atom-level representations from a crystal structure. Here, features from all 16 Zatom-1 layers are retained, and CHGNet features are projected from 64 to 512 dimensions. (b) The property requested by the prompt selects a learned task residual, which is added to 32 latent queries. Two Perceiver blocks apply cross-attention to the structural features, followed by latent self-attention and a feed-forward network. These taskconditioned queries allow the bridge to weight encoder sources and layer depths differently for each property. (c) The fused latents are projected into the language-model embedding space and combined with prompt embeddings. A frozen language model then generates the response. The trainable components are optimized jointly using a downstream language-modeling objective.
