papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
authors: Guilherme Guedes, Marco Apolinario Lainez, Charlotte Frenkel
bullets: Addresses online, one-sample-at-a-time adaptation and limited edge-device resources.
Uses a dual-phase wake/sleep design inspired by brain learning cycles.
Wake phase: RISC-V MCU performs efficient inference and gradient-free prototype updates.
Sleep phase: a smart charger uses available energy and memory for rehearsal-based gradient updates.
On CORe50 NICv2-391, it reports 78.6%–81.6% accuracy, 7.79–10.54 s latency per sample, and lower learning cost than quantized latent replay.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) Performance/availability view of continual adaptation at the edge. Middle: fully on-device learning keeps the device available with online adaptation, at the cost of increased catastrophic forgetting. Bottom: proposed hybrid scheme, lightweight on-device learning during daily use (wake) with consolidation on the smart charger (sleep), combining the availability of online methods with offline-like accuracy. (b) Proposed device–charger system realizing hybrid adaptation, combining (i) a low-footprint edge device for online adaptation with (ii) a smart charger augmented with additional compute and memory budgets for offline consolidation.

papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
authors: DiffuSpace Technical Team
bullets: Uses Gated Delta Networks adapted to block diffusion, combining historical recurrent memory with current-block bidirectional softmax attention.

Leads the report’s seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
Reports 680 tokens/s on one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 and batch size one for internal agent workloads.
A decision-model variant improves joint question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on 500 internal groups.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.
authors: Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Jinhao Deng, Dongbin Zhang, Chaoda Zheng, Shijia Chen, Yuqi Zhang, Choo Sin Wai, Boyi Sun, Puyi Wang, Yu Zhang, Xianming Liu, Boyang Wang
bullets: Addresses target retention, superficial edits, and unintended changes to surrounding content.

Adds frozen HPSv3 perceptual feedback for synthesized content.
Optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen and keeps evaluation regions fixed across candidates.
Achieves substantial reconstruction gains over the original H3, with better removal and background preservation qualitatively.

papers.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Sangwon Yu, Sangkwon Park, Hye Youn Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Reasoning-trained models retain broadly similar global gradient organization but develop localized changes within a contiguous layer span.
Diffusion-map embeddings were applied to matched base and reasoning-trained models across three model families.
Transplanting weights from the span into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, especially when donor and host regions overlapped.
The span emerged gradually during early performance gains; intermediate-training grafts also helped and often preserved more previously solved problems than other graft locations.
A similar transferable span was found in a medical model, though the analysis supports a reasoning-related region rather than a universal mechanism across all models.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
authors: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David
bullets: Targets the accuracy–interpretability–compute trade-off in activation-based LLM monitoring.
Represents each probe as explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features under a gate budget.
GateWatchServe computes only selected features, streams binary values across layers, and evaluates probes via lookup tables.
Across 24 Gemma-2-9B tasks, it averages 80.49% accuracy using 3.8 features and 3.5 gates per probe, 1.17 points below full SAE probes.
Reduces probe memory by 99.98%; high-concurrency serving retains 97–98% baseline throughput and 99.8% KV-cache capacity.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces GateWatch, a low-overhead monitoring method for LLMs using Boolean circuits and sparse autoencoders, contributing to interpretability and efficiency in LLM architectures.
papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.tldr: GateWatch enables highly compact, interpretable LLM monitoring by classifying behavior with Boolean circuits over a few binarized SAE features, with minimal accuracy and serving overhead.

papers.abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.
authors: Chunggi Lee, Hanspeter Pfister
bullets: Uniformly sampled frames often miss the short moments needed to answer egocentric-video questions.
The method reads the VLM’s output distribution when it chooses among labeled candidate frames, rather than asking for a written timestamp.
EgoJev revisits the selected temporal windows and places a small number of answer frames at distribution quantiles.
With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, accuracy on QAEgo4D improves from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%.
The approach is training-free, runs with one frozen VLM, and has a single-level version for Mac and iPhone deployment.

papers.title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
papers.tldr: EgoJev uses a frozen VLM’s labeled-frame choices to locate brief evidence in long egocentric videos, improving question-answering accuracy without training or a second model.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.
authors: Houman Mehrafarin, Ioannis Konstas
bullets: CoT hidden states are labeled as recovering or failed based on whether patching them into a direct prompt produces the correct answer.
A linear probe distinguishes these two hidden-state classes.
For each question, a direction derived from recovering and failed states is used to rotate the direct prompt’s final hidden state before generation.
Across 25 tasks, accuracy rises from 46% to 85% on LLaMA 3.1 8B and from 52% to 86% on Qwen 2.5 7B, exceeding CoT accuracy with roughly one-tenth as many tokens.
The approach requires question-specific directions and is presented as a basis for future state-alignment training.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our analysis on one Multistep Arithmetic question. The means of the question’s recovering and failed states, c+ and c−, give the task-solving direction d ∝ c+− 0.5 c−. Before generation, we rotate z onto the direction of d, keeping its norm; the direct prompt then writes four short lines and answers 48 instead of −40, even though the CoT itself answers 80.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
papers.tldr: Question-specific hidden-state directions can steer direct-answer prompting to substantially higher accuracy than CoT while using far fewer tokens.

papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
authors: Rong Zou, Haiqing Hao, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses feature staleness when visual content changes between image observations.
Uses events to incrementally transport and correct multi-layer DINOv3 features from an anchor image.
Trains a lightweight updater end-to-end on synthetic data without downstream-task supervision and transfers to real event streams without adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task settings, it outperforms evaluated event-based methods for detection, segmentation, and depth estimation.
On DSEC with a 200 ms-old anchor, it improves anchor predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency 2.5× versus image re-encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ALIVE. (a) Training uses synthetic RGB–event sequences. A frozen DINOv3 encodes every RGB frame: F0 initializes the feature state (with memory h0 = 0), and later frames provide teacher features Ft. For each event packet E(t−,t], the ALIVE updater Uθ predicts a displacement dt that transports both the features and the memory, a residual correction ∆t that yields Ut, and a signed, zero-sum 3× 3 kernel kt per token that refines Ut into F̂t. The ConvGRU memory ht conditions the residual and the refinement. All modules are trained jointly with feature-level losses only, without task labels or task heads. (b) The trained updater is applied without adaptation to real event streams. Moment matching aligns the per-channel statistics of F̂t with the anchor moments to produce the updated features F̄t, and frozen task heads trained on DINOv3 features of real RGB images read F̄t directly. Predictions are shown 200 ms after the anchor on DSEC, and detections are drawn on the RGB frame at that time for visualization only (C: car, P: person).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an event-based method to incrementally update foundation model features (DINOv3) at inference time, addressing feature staleness and efficiency.
papers.title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
papers.tldr: ALIVE efficiently keeps frozen visual foundation-model features current between image frames by using event streams, improving downstream vision tasks while avoiding repeated image encoding.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.

ReKey regresses these signals into a few key-value neurons per block while measuring edit site and strength from the model’s own responses.
The model performs all recursive roles using forward passes, and edits from different sites compose within one checkpoint.
Across ten visual reasoning benchmarks, BaseRSI improves the base model both in-distribution and on held-out benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free mechanism for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) in Vision-Language Models, allowing the model to internalize its own harness improvements into its weights.
papers.title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
papers.tldr: BaseRSI enables a vision-language model to recursively internalize harness-based improvements into its own weights through training-free, self-directed edits.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
authors: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
bullets: Problem: Standard early exit leaves past-token key-value caches incomplete, while full recurrence increases sequential decoding latency.
Method: New tokens enter directly into the final K recurrent steps; Wake verification checks projected states using a logit-margin tolerance τ within a static CUDA graph.
Modes: τ=0 provides greedy-exact decoding, τ>0 enables margin-gated verification, and τ=∞ gives non-rollback lossy late entry.
Results: On Ouro-2.6B, K=2 achieved 5.2× exact and 6.8× lossy speedups; scaling recurrence on Huginn-3.5B reached up to 8.4× exact and 12.5× lossy speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for looped LLMs that reduces latency and cache-related overhead; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Late entry accelerates looped language-model decoding by letting new tokens skip early recurrent passes while preserving configurable exactness or accepting controlled approximation.

papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. Prior work trains all streams toward a shared objective. We instead study whether assigning distinct learning objectives to different streams can improve task performance and induce objective-specific specialization. Using complementary lexical (sparse) and semantic (dense) retrieval objectives as a test case, we find that objective-specialized mHC consistently outperforms a non-specialized mHC model across the full sparse--dense fusion range, for both two- and four-stream models and at two model scales. We then examine how specialization changes the model internally using probes of stream representations, residual mixing, objective-specific gradient flow, and read/write gates. The specialized and non-specialized models behave similarly through most of the network but diverge in the final layers: the specialized model develops increasingly objective-specific gradient flow, distinct read/write routing patterns, and reduced cross-stream mixing, and streams assigned to different objectives become increasingly dissimilar while those trained toward the same objective remain highly similar. Fixing the residual mixing to the identity leaves the specialization benefit intact, indicating that the benefit stems from objective-specific read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing. These results show that assigning distinct objectives to mHC streams can improve multi-objective retrieval while inducing structured, depth-dependent specialization in the residual computation.
authors: Shantanu Agarwal, Ruchita V. Maitri, Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel

Streams trained on the same objective remain similar, while streams trained on different objectives become increasingly dissimilar.

In all three, streams propagate through the full encoder stack and the retrieval heads read only the final-layer (l = L) stream representations. (left) Single-stream: the standard ModernBERT encoder, with a single residual stream read by both the sparse and dense retrieval heads. (middle) Non-specialized mHC: the residual stream is expanded into n parallel streams with learned cross-stream routing. (right) Objective-specialized mHC: the sparse and dense heads instead read disjoint sets of final-layer streams, so each objective selectively trains its assigned stream(s). papers.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.
authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limits of appearance-only guidance for diagnosing geometry, material, and illumination errors.
Combines geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues during iterative scene refinement.
Uses Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, evidence, and revision history, including partially visible or unseen sources.
Requires no additional training or differentiable rendering.
Reports improved reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, with benefits for editing, object insertion, and relighting.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for MKGR. NaviGATE first aligns graph-derived structural representations with textual semantics, then performs structure-aware internal knowledge activation by fine-tuning the multimodal language model with multimodal entity summaries and injected structural tokens. In the noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning stage, NaviGATE jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views: reliable retrieved candidates are reinforced through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. In inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts generation to valid entities in the target knowledge graph. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that NaviGATE consistently outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generation-based baselines, and remains robust under noisy retrieval scenarios.
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha, Cui Miao, Xiaodong Wang
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed multimodal embeddings and noisy, invalid outputs from generative MKGR methods.

Outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generative baselines and remains robust under noisy retrieval.

papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Qiyu Chen, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Addresses weaknesses of intra-modal reconstruction and cross-modal reconstruction, including missed complementary information, projection bias, and ambiguous mappings.
Uses bidirectional cross-modal attention with channel alignment and dynamic spatial priors to combine image and point-cloud features.

Uses dual-path collaborative reconstruction with cross-modal consistency constraints to recover the original modalities.
Reports 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% on Eyecandies, improvements of 2.9 and 4.1 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art methods, respectively.

papers.abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
authors: Biswa Sengupta
bullets: Compares five architectural and optimization changes under the same data and training budget.
Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimization, and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid yield the largest gains; extra normalization also helps.

Most improvements combine effectively, but small interactions recur across repeated random seeds.

papers.abstract: Generalizable AI-generated video detection remains challenging because natural motion and content variations can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable indicators of authenticity. To address this challenge, we propose Spatial and Contextual Reference-informed Detection (SCRiD), a framework that interprets video variations through complementary spatial and contextual references. Specifically, we introduce Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling conditions. We further develop Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA), which learns a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos and probes its responses across multiple noise scales and quality views to guide feature adaptation. To integrate these complementary sources of evidence, we design Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) to enable information exchange through reversible symplectic updates. We train SCRiD using synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluate it across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks. Our method achieves average ACC and AP of 72.72% and 74.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage points.Ablation and robustness experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and the stability of SCRiD under common post-processing operations.
authors: Hao Tan, Zekai Zuo, Boyang Chen, Jinghui Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of distinguishing synthesis artifacts from natural motion and content variation.
Uses Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to model temporal residuals under aligned motion and coordinate references.
Uses Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA) to derive denoising references from authentic videos across noise scales and quality views.
Combines evidence through Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) with reversible symplectic updates.
Trained on videos from 4 generators and evaluated across 88 subsets and 6 benchmarks, achieving 72.72% average ACC and 74.23% AP; robustness tests support stability under common post-processing.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.
authors: Jie Peng, Yongxue Shan, Yongfu Zha, Xiaodong Wang
bullets: Addresses element dominance caused by coupled interactions and coarse multimodal aggregation.

papers.abstract: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.
authors: Claudia Cuttano, Tamy Boubekeur, Elena Garces, Giuseppe Vecchio
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed disentanglement of appearance factors from a single RGB image.
Trains a shared decoder to reconstruct intrinsic maps from DINOv3 features, separating reconstruction from decomposition without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision.
Uses lightweight, modality-specific projections to predict teacher representations from RGB and support partially annotated data.
Predicts all intrinsic properties in one forward pass with a compact 165M-parameter model, reported as 100× faster than diffusion-based methods.
Achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, improved resolution robustness, and interpretable modality-specific feature spaces.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RAID overview. (a) We first learn an X → X reconstruction autoencoder across RGB and intrinsic signals, i.e. albedo, irradiance, normals, roughness, and metallicity. A frozen DINOv3 backbone with trainable AdaptFormer modules encodes each modality into a shared, decodable feature space; one DC-AE decoder reconstructs the input modality from that space. (b) We then freeze the reconstruction model and learn to infer its features from RGB. A student encoder and modality-specific projections predict the features that the teacher extracts from the corresponding GT maps. Feature alignment guides these predictions, while supervision on the decoded maps enforces pixel alignment. At inference, the teacher is removed: the student, projections, and same shared decoder produce all five maps.

Figure 6. Qualitative robustness to input resolution. We compare RGB↔X, MVInverse, and RAID with and without multi-resolution training at input resolutions from 256×256 to 2048×2048. At each resolution, we show the predicted albedo and surface normal maps. RGB↔X exhibits artifacts at both extremes, whereas MVInverse degrades at high resolution. The single-resolution variant of RAID produces more consistent predictions than either baseline, suggesting that our adaptation to intrinsic decomposition preserves the resolution robustness of the pretrained DINOv3 representation. Multi-resolution training further improves prediction consistency.

Figure 5. Feature-space selection. Given an image and a query patch +, we compute cosine similarity between the query and patch features in each modality-projected feature space (red: high, blue: low). The resulting maps show that albedo, normal, irradiance, and metallicity projections induce different selection axes, grouping regions according to the corresponding physical property.

Our model is more stable across resolutions; multi-resolution supervision further improves highresolution accuracy while keeping peak memory below 3GB.

The autoencoder preserves the spatial structure and modality-specific details of the input maps. papers.title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition

papers.abstract: LLM-based artificial societies exhibit rich behavior but often lack scientific grounding: personas and environments are assumed, interaction networks are synthetic, and simulators are generated as free-form code, making results difficult to tie to real populations and sensitive to the backbone model. We argue that simulated worlds should be sampled from observed data, while simulation logic should be implemented by composing operations from a shared, task-independent vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce ABSClaw, a zero-code agent that compiles natural-language requests into executable, reality-grounded social simulations. ABSClaw grounds who acts, where they act, and with whom they interact in survey and census data, geospatial sources, and real networks. It expresses state transitions through 26 atomic operations. To support an open and extensible ecosystem, ABSClaw further allows capabilities to be added as lifecycle-scoped skills without modifying its core. Furthermore, we propose ABSBench, a benchmark of 193 real-world social-simulation tasks. On ABSBench, ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated social simulators. Three real-world case studies show that grounding personas, environments, and interaction networks each improves agreement with observed outcomes. With one runtime skill, ABSClaw executes 13 population-scale simulations, collectively involving 25 million agents. Together, these results demonstrate ABSClaw's real-world fidelity, extensibility, and scalability.
authors: Shaobin He, Yan Gao, Quan Zheng, Zhenyang Lin, Zhen Liu, Jiyan He, Shuxin Zheng
bullets: Addresses the weak scientific grounding and backbone-model sensitivity of many LLM-based artificial societies.
Uses 26 atomic operations to express simulation state transitions instead of generating free-form simulator code.
Supports extensibility through lifecycle-scoped runtime skills without modifying the core system.
Introduces ABSBench, comprising 193 real-world social-simulation tasks; ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among evaluated simulators.
Case studies link grounding to improved agreement with observed outcomes, while one skill enables 13 simulations involving 25 million agents.

papers.abstract: Video world models are used as simulators, so when a first frame leaves several physical outcomes open, repeated generations should produce each outcome as often as it occurs in the data. Physics post-training scores every generation against the single recorded future of its history, which makes single videos more faithful, but the expected score is linear in the model distribution and is maximized by always producing the most likely outcome. The log-likelihood of the recorded outcome is maximized by the data distribution, and its gradient weights agreement with the record by the inverse of how often the model produces the generated outcome, a frequency that other generations of the same history with independent noise, its siblings, can estimate. To train with this weight from a finite group, we propose SibPO, which performs Sibling-paired Policy Optimization: siblings estimate a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the record, and a second term subtracts the same weight times the agreement with the siblings, which makes the expected objective a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size. On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and it lowers the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.
authors: Xin Li, Yiwen Chen
bullets: Single-future scoring can favor always generating the most likely outcome rather than matching the full data distribution.
SibPO estimates inverse outcome frequencies from sibling generations and uses them in a sibling-paired optimization objective.
Its expected objective is a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells for any finite group size.
On PisaBench, it reduced landing-time KS distance by 9.1–10.2% on three of four models and reduced robot-policy success-rate estimation error by 13%, without harming single-video quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SibPO on one training group. All G = 8 generations xg share the history h and draw their own noise εg (shared noise is only a comparison setting in Section 6.3). A frozen readout maps each video to a two-cell outcome vector, contact (orange) or no contact (teal). The matrix pairs the eight generations, grouped by outcome, with each other and with the record (left column): a cell takes the outcome color when the two agree (κ = 1) and stays white when they differ. The reward rg of Eq. (4) weights agreement with the record by ωg , which grows with the white cells of row g, and subtracts the sibling term ρg . The baseline bg recomputes the rewards without xg .

Figure 4. Rewards against the recorded future collapse an ambiguous landing, and SibPO keeps its minority outcome. Five generations per method on Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B at frame 12 of one PisaBench input, where the simulator places 70% of objects on the ground.

Figure 1. What each generation is compared with decides the outcome frequencies after post-training. The frame leaves open whether the red cloth will touch the yellow object, and 60% of such futures show contact. Each block is the readout of one generated video, and five samples per method are only illustrative. Flow-GRPO compares each generation only with the recorded future, so the no-contact outcome loses on average and disappears. SibPO also compares each generation with its siblings, the other generations of the same input. Its reward, in the simplest form, subtracts the mismatch with the record (−) and adds the mismatch with the siblings (+), so the rare outcome is kept.

papers.abstract: Robot learning systems require synchronized, high-quality demonstrations that combine visual, proprioceptive, and action data. However, collecting such datasets with mobile manipulators is often slowed down by fragmented teleoperation interfaces and manual post-processing workflows. This paper presents an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection on a Clearpath Dingo-O mobile base equipped with a Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator and an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera. The framework combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for data capture, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to machine-learning-ready Zarr datasets. We validate the system on a pick-and-place mobile-manipulation task in which the robot transports a bottle between two surfaces. The results show that the unified controller supports complete task execution and recording without external commands, while the data pipeline produces synchronized datasets for short demonstrations and identifies corrupted visual frames. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for producing structured demonstrations for robot-learning research.

papers.abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.
authors: Oana Balmau, Saurav Banka, Jiaxuan Chen, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Ramya Narasimha Prabhu, Rafael Pires, Mathis Randl, Martijn de Vos

Compiler passes automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM without requiring model-specific training-engine ports.
Across three MoE models on four A100 GPUs, BubbleTea achieves 1.9–6.2× higher fine-tuning throughput than LLMStation.
It keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads and performs strongly on bursty production traces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.
authors: Jiayou Zhu, Peng Guo, Litian Zhang, Xinze Shi, Yuting Zhang, Zelong Yu, Yize Tian, Jirong Liu, Zifeng Kang
bullets: Targets adversarial patches that corrupt vision-language-action policies and subsequent observations.
Uses attention changes from local visual edits to guide patch localization and select local purification treatments.
Revalidates and updates defenses as embodied actions change the observed scene.

Succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of evaluated tasks, improving LIBERO-Object success from 0% to 70.0%, with 548.9 ms mean decision time per control step.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.
authors: Donghyeon Ki, Xiaoyu Chen, Jun Ho Seo, Hayeong Lee, Kyungyoon Kim, Byung-Jun Lee, Li Zhao
bullets: Latent Action Models usually use behavioral cloning, lacking an explicit policy-improvement objective.
Naive offline RL can propose unrealizable latent actions or merge physical controls with different rewards.
The paper derives conditions for policy improvement and optimality to transfer from latent actions to physical execution.
LAPIS uses observed state–latent transitions, value-based improvement, and a conditional flow policy for multimodal latent actions.
It outperforms baselines on most tasks, especially visual manipulation, and remains effective with only 1% action labels.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
authors: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Clustering queries and keys together limits sparse-attention accuracy because queries in a cluster share key selections.
PQRS clusters only keys, performs per-query key-cluster selection, and approximates unselected keys with cluster centroids.
It efficiently executes per-query routing by grouping queries with identical selections and merging results with a carried softmax offset.
Evaluated on four Wan and HunyuanVideo text-to-video and image-to-video models, it achieves 1.66–2.10× end-to-end speedup.
It reports 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo, while remaining closest to dense attention among evaluated sparse methods.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficiency in video diffusion transformers via a novel sparse attention mechanism (PQRS). Highly relevant to video generation and efficient AI.
papers.title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention

papers.abstract: Planning with a visual world model requires deciding both which actions to execute and how long to search for them. We introduce Selective CEM Refinement (SCR), a learned rule for deciding whether to continue cross-entropy method (CEM) search with a frozen LeWorldModel. After five it- erations, the gate measures how far the mean first action chunk has moved, how much the mean terminal cost of elite plans has fallen, and how widely their first chunks vary. It returns the current plan for execution or continues the same search for ten more iterations. The gate requires no addi- tional world-model rollout. On 16 PushT scenes evaluated with two planning seeds, SCR succeeded in 25 of 32 trials, compared with 28 of 32 for fixed 15-iteration search (Fixed-15). All 25 SCR suc- cesses occurred in trials that Fixed-15 also solved, yield- ing 89.29% paired success retention. Across complete episodes, including replanning, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time per eight-environment batch by 17.22%. Its observed suc- cess rate was 5.36 percentage points above an analytic mix- ture of the two fixed-depth controllers at the same expected candidate workload, although the difference changed sign across planning seeds. Compared with gating only at the initial solve under the same random-draw padding proto- col, gating again at replanning produced nine additional early exits. This reduced total candidate evaluations by 15.79%, while successes fell from 27 to 25.
authors: Jingni Huang
bullets: SCR decides after five CEM iterations whether to execute the current plan or search for ten more.
Its gate uses first-action movement, elite-plan terminal-cost reduction, and first-chunk diversity, requiring no extra world-model rollout.
On 32 PushT trials, SCR solved 25 versus 28 for fixed 15-iteration search, retaining 89.29% of paired successes.
Across episodes, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time by 17.22% per eight-environment batch.
Replanning-time gating produced more early exits and 15.79% fewer evaluations, but reduced successes from 27 to 25.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models struggle to forecast moving objects due to motion uncertainty and shape distortion. A single trajectory can average plausible futures into an implausible path, and repeated re-voxelization can erode or inflate object shape even under correct motion. We introduce ShoWorld to address these challenges through separate motion and shape representations. The motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents and the future ego trajectory. Each hypothesis is rendered into occupancy and fused according to its probability to retain alternative futures. The shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and offsets from local geometry. These points move rigidly with the object, and voxel occupancy follows the probability that at least one occupied point falls within it. This representation reduces shape distortion under motion. ShoWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on Occ3D-nuScenes. With ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, it improves mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points overall and by 6.06 and 5.53 points on dynamic classes.
authors: Zhiqiang Yan, Guangfa Wang, Yuan Wu, Jian Yang, Gim Hee Lee
bullets: Addresses motion uncertainty and shape distortion in occupancy world models.
Predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene context, nearby agents, and future ego motion.
Renders and probability-fuses multiple trajectory hypotheses instead of averaging them into one path.
Models shape with moving sub-voxel points, occupancy probabilities, and geometry offsets to reduce voxelization distortion.
On Occ3D-nuScenes with ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, improves overall mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points, respectively; dynamic-class gains are 6.06 and 5.53 points.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies implicitly assume that third-person cameras remain fixed at their data-collection poses; once a camera is bumped, remounted, or swapped at deployment, task success degrades precipitously even though the underlying task and robot remain unchanged. We present Homeward, a training-free, plug-and-play observation adapter that canonicalizes observations from an uncalibrated deployment camera back into the training view for frozen VLA policies. Our design stems from a closed-loop diagnostic paradox in simulation: while re-rendering perturbed views into the training camera with oracle geometry recovers much of the lost performance, substituting an off-the-shelf feed-forward 3D foundation model can leave the policy worse off than applying no correction at all. This degradation concentrates on the thin, articulated robot arm, which feed-forward depth prediction tears and scatters - yet the arm's exact 3D state is already known from robot kinematics. Homeward exploits this asymmetry: it estimates what is unknown - camera parameters and static scene depth - from the live RGB frame and a single training-view reference, and renders what is known - the moving robot links - directly from the kinematic model. Evaluated across $\sim$300,000 closed-loop episodes spanning four frozen VLAs, Homeward boosts success across all 1,599 camera variants of LIBERO-Plus from 62.5%, 76.5%, 68.0%, and 3.6% to 77.6%, 95.1%, 91.2%, and 26.4% for OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_{0.5}$, $\pi_0$, and OpenVLA, respectively. Without any scene fine-tuning or deployment camera calibration, Homeward extends to 6-DoF random placements, focal-length changes, and, with per-step pose estimation, continuous intra-episode camera drift, while matching or surpassing a calibrated, scene-trained view-synthesis baseline on three of four policies on LIBERO-Plus.
authors: Mingyang Lyu (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Yinqian Sun (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Gongce Cao (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Guobin Shen (ByteDance, China), Yuhao Zhang (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA), Lu Jia (University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China), Chenfei Yan (Beihang University, Beijing, China), Qian Zhang (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Pin Lyu (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China), Chen Gao (Tsinghua University, Beijing, China), Bo Wang (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China)
bullets: Addresses severe VLA degradation when third-person cameras are bumped, remounted, swapped, or drift during deployment.
Uses a training-free observation adapter that estimates camera parameters and static-scene depth from RGB plus a training-view reference.
Renders the robot arm from known kinematics, avoiding artifacts from inaccurate feed-forward depth models on articulated links.
Across ~300,000 episodes and 1,599 LIBERO-Plus camera variants, it improves all four evaluated frozen VLAs, with gains varying by policy.
Supports 6-DoF camera placement changes, focal-length changes, and continuous camera drift; scope includes reliance on pose estimation for drift.

papers.abstract: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning (EFCIL) requires models to learn new classes sequentially without retaining training samples from previous tasks. Continual concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make their predictions interpretable by identifying visual concepts in an image and using them to score each class. However, these methods typically focus on preserving learned concepts or approximating past classes with generated features, which can leave new concepts underused in old-class predictions. We propose RetroCBM, which retains a small set of vocabulary-independent statistics relating frozen visual features to the embedding space of a pretrained vision-language model. Even after earlier training images have been discarded, we can use these statistics to supervise new concepts. To do so, we develop a retroactive regression rule that yields the same predictor for each new concept as class-balanced ridge regression on all images seen so far. We then reproject the stored statistics to recover the full-history squared classification loss and thus learn how much each new concept should contribute to old-class predictions. Since the classifier may use systematic concept errors to distinguish nearby classes, we further introduce a graph-weighted penalty on the margin shifts caused by those errors. Across six datasets, RetroCBM outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable methods in all class-incremental settings, with an 18.1\% relative gain in mean average incremental accuracy over the strongest exemplar-free baseline.
authors: Yang Ji, Ying Sun, Yuanxin Zhuang, Yuting Zhang
bullets: Addresses EFCIL, where models must learn sequentially without retaining past training images.
Stores vocabulary-independent statistics linking frozen visual features to a pretrained vision-language embedding space.
Uses retroactive regression to reproduce the new-concept predictor from class-balanced ridge regression over all previously seen data.
Reconstructs historical classification loss and applies a graph-weighted penalty to control margin shifts from systematic concept errors.
Across six datasets, it achieves an 18.1% relative mean average incremental accuracy gain over the strongest exemplar-free baseline among interpretable methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Model architecture. At inference (bottom), the sparse classifier scores all seen classes from the concept responses predicted for each image. During training (top), retroactive regression updates all current concept predictors using stored statistics from all seen classes. We then reproject these statistics to update the classifier and penalize error-induced margin shifts between neighboring classes.

Figure 5. Tracing a Late-Arriving Concept on CUB. Rows show selected concept responses across phases, with dashes before each concept is introduced. papers.abstract: Text prompted 3D computed tomography (CT) segmentation requires both full slice context and fine boundary precision across volumes where over $80\%$ of organ prompted slices lack the queried target. Existing medical vision language models (VLMs) are largely non native segmenters: they delegate pixel delineation outside the VLM by compressing reasoning into a 1D [SEG] vector for an external Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder, quantizing masks into lossy discrete codebooks, or issuing box prompts to stateless external SAM tools without empty slice screening or spatial state memory. We introduce NativeSeg, a native vision language segmentation framework on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapted Qwen3.8-27B that performs dense mask decoding, volumetric triage, spatial error self diagnosis, and multiround local zoom directly over the VLM's 2D spatial visual tokens without external SAM decoders. NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five slice U-Net pathway, halts at zero zooms on $>91\%$ of standalone evaluations via a native presence gate ( ), localizes uncertain boundaries via a 20 cell multiscale error gate ( ), and accepts zoomed updates only when predicted error decreases. Trained solely on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round $0$ DSC by $+19.81$ and $+7.04$ points over discrete codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts on the identical backbone, reaches $86.81\%$ adult and $87.04\%$ zero shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines 2D nnU-Net ($89.52\%$ adult; $86.86\%$ pediatric), 3D SegVol ($86.81\%$), and 3D VoxTell ($89.85\%$).
authors: Chengqian Ma, Gaole Dai, Zijie Meng, Weixuan Jin, Yijie Du, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses missing-target slices and boundary imprecision in text-prompted 3D CT segmentation.

Performs volumetric triage, spatial error diagnosis, and multiround zooming, accepting refinements only when predicted error decreases.
On adult CT, achieves 86.81% DSC and 87.04% zero-shot pediatric DSC; it also safely refines several existing segmentation systems.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.
authors: Xiaolin Lin, Kai-Chiang Wu, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Targets the high first-token latency caused by prefill on roughly 100K-token interleaved image-text inputs.
Uses an early attention head in a small hybrid model, with images at half resolution, to rank whole input units.
Keeps the top 10% of tokens/units and feeds them to the target VLM as a shorter ordinary prompt.
A single untrained selector transfers across different target model families.
On MMLongBench at 128K tokens, it maintains average accuracy while reporting 3.7×, 11.6×, and 8.2× prefill speedups for three target models.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets inefficient perception of long interaction histories in LLM-based agents.
Renders past interactions as images and allocates resolution according to relevance to the next decision.

Scope: focuses on adaptive perceptual granularity rather than deciding what memories to retain or retrieve.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.
authors: Yuhan Li, Shuran Zhang, Haixin Tian, Baonuo Rao, Weipeng Li, Yujia Hou, Zhenyu Wang, Zijun Wang, Luoyang Lin, Lijing Luo, Jiehui Huang, Kaiyuan Yang, Jingbin Tan, Panwen Hu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Measures physical responsiveness through simulator inversion of gravity, friction, and initial speed, plus event outcomes near critical transitions.

Shows that responsiveness failures are complementary to visual-quality errors, which metrics such as PSNR can miss.
Provides 72,000 simulated videos across 20 multi-object interaction types as training data; fine-tuning improves held-out interactions and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark.

papers.abstract: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.
authors: Seungyub Han, Taehyun Cho, Dohyeong Kim, Kyungjae Lee, Jungwoo Lee
bullets: Addresses the variance–long-horizon trade-off caused by products of per-step trace coefficients and sensitive trace-length tuning.
Uses a binary meeting-time stopping indicator that remains active until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet.
Provides a model-free surrogate based on one sampled action, requiring neither a transition model nor a mixing-time estimate.
Derives contraction conditions for both the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation.
