papers.title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
papers.tldr: MINT adaptively truncates multi-step off-policy backups when behavior and target trajectories meet, aiming to reduce variance without sacrificing long-horizon learning signals.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.
authors: Xinyu Deng, Bohao Lan, Kunpeng Li, Mingkai Yuan, Weihang Pan, Binbin Lin
bullets: Addresses forbidden-zone traversal and collision sliding in visual world-model planning when explicit dynamics or collision geometry are unavailable.
Unrolls future latent action prefixes in a frozen JEPA world model and trains a lightweight risk head using process-violation supervision.
Uses predicted prefix risk for both search triggering and feasibility gating; risky plans invoke local CEM search, while safe plans execute unchanged.
Introduces an amplitude-preserving deviation metric to retain tangential progress instead of collapsing obstacle-directed actions into stalling.
Across five tasks, improves Safe Arrival Rate by 2.08–41.67 percentage points, matches every-step search action-for-action, and reduces controller time by 17.71%–70.41%.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.

papers.abstract: Efficient and accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view images remains a fundamental challenge in Gaussian splatting. Many existing methods rely on sparse geometric initialization and iterative densification, resulting in substantial optimization overhead and difficulties in balancing rendering quality and geometric accuracy, particularly in reflective and weakly textured regions. To address these limitations, we propose RAPID, a geometry-first framework that uses multiview polarization cues to recover dense surface priors. We integrate surface normals into depth maps using sparse geometric anchors. These depth maps are then fused across views. Curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization then support efficient optimization. Experiments on the PISR dataset demonstrate an approximately \(5\times\) speedup over PhyGaP, which is a state-of-the-art Gaussian-based reconstruction method. RAPID reduces the average optimization time from approximately 21 minutes (PhyGaP) to 4 minutes while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of RAPID in accelerating Gaussian optimization from polarimetric multi-view inputs.
authors: Daisong Ouyang, Linlin Xia, Liangkun Yan, Song Gu, Shedong Zhao, Xin Dai, Yi Zheng
bullets: Addresses optimization overhead and geometric inaccuracies in reflective and weakly textured regions.
Recovers dense surface priors by integrating polarization-derived normals with sparse geometric anchors, then fuses depth across views.
Uses curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization for efficient optimization.
On the PISR dataset, achieves approximately 5× faster optimization than PhyGaP while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis and mesh reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $\mu$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $\mu$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $\mu$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGPT2 including an optimised CUDA-graph baseline), at a cost of 8.5 (DistilGPT2) and 8.6 (BERT) points of gold accuracy for the synthesised seed-0 circuits.
authors: Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Xintong Li, Nguyen H. Tran, Ken-Tye Yong
bullets: Extracts 0/1 token predicates and minimised truth-table or implication-rule mappings from the entire trained network, including attention.
Uses iterative Ship-of-Theseus block replacement, allowing the remaining soft network to adapt after each circuit component is frozen.
Fits attention selection using either integer-score ordering or learned rules, trained only on teacher-correct examples.
On TweetEval-emotion, circuits achieve 57.4–70.0% test accuracy versus 74.7–77.8% for the teacher, depending on model and selection method.

The synthesized hardware uses no multipliers or weight traffic and is estimated to run 2–3 orders of magnitude faster than batch-1 GPU inference, with an 8.5–8.6 point accuracy loss for seed-0 circuits.

papers.selection_reason: Converts attention networks into hard-logic circuits achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
papers.tldr: The work replaces attention networks with interpretable hard-logic predicate circuits, achieving much faster low-power inference while sacrificing some accuracy.

papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
authors: Vedant Navale
bullets: Splits history into blocks and uses a fast yes/no selector to reveal relevant blocks while masking others in one key-value cache.
On a synthetic lookup task with Qwen3-1.7B, selective context improved accuracy from 93/120 to 119/120; masking was comparable to deletion.
Context selection is the main weakness: a supervised linear probe reached 110/120, while keyword search achieved perfect task performance.
The probe did not transfer to a second task, limiting evidence for general-purpose selection.
Block switching also supports undoing failed attempts and running subagents without creating a new context.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have been shown to suffer from shortcut learning and causal confusion, limiting their ability to generalize robustly under distribution shift. To mitigate these limitations, recent works based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored incorporating linguistic reasoning capabilities into driving decision-making, reporting improvements in driving performance. In particular, counterfactual (CF) reasoning has been proposed to enable self-reflective, high-level causal understanding. However, it remains unclear whether the language-based reasoning mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual representations to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. Moreover, existing approaches often conflate intervention-based reasoning with CF reasoning, leaving the effects of genuine CF reasoning unexplored. In this work, we examine what CF reasoning actually induces in VLM-based autonomous driving and observe that it shifts the action distribution toward more conservative behaviors while increasing uncertainty in reasoning and decision-making. This effect persists under reinforcement fine-tuning, suggesting that it is not merely a transient artifact. Furthermore, visual attention analysis shows that CF reasoning does not alter visual grounding, while causal intervention experiments reveal that masking causally relevant and non-causal factors in accident scenarios results in comparable decision change rates. Overall, these results suggest that CF reasoning does not induce genuine causal reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Instead, it acts as a linguistic shortcut that reshapes the action distribution, teaching models what to say but not how to reason, highlighting a gap between language-based reasoning and causal understanding in autonomous driving.
authors: Hayeon Oh, Donghwan Lee
bullets: VLM-based driving systems may shift shortcut learning from visual features to linguistic reasoning patterns.
CF reasoning makes actions more conservative and increases reasoning and decision-making uncertainty.
The effect persists after reinforcement fine-tuning, indicating it is not merely transient.
Visual attention is largely unchanged, and masking causal versus non-causal factors produces comparable decision changes.
The study highlights a gap between language-based reasoning and true causal understanding in driving.

papers.abstract: Object search in unknown environments requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles and accounting for limited sensor visibility. We present SearchDiffusion, a diffusion-based planner that generates position and heading trajectories using a learned dense utility map. The map represents geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress. It conditions trajectory generation and provides an objective for sampling guidance. Sampled map hypotheses provide additional geometric context, while geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection support execution. Across 90 simulated tasks on 24 map layouts, SearchDiffusion achieved 95.6\% target detection at greater computational cost. Ablations show complementary benefits from utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime map hypotheses. In ten physical quadruped trials using OneMap relevance maps, eight were successful under operator assessment, without fine-tuning on real-robot data. These results support combining learned spatial utility with guided trajectory generation for object search under partial observability.

Achieved 95.6% target detection across 90 simulated tasks on 24 layouts, at greater computational cost.
Succeeded in 8 of 10 physical quadruped trials using OneMap maps without real-robot fine-tuning.
Ablations found complementary benefits from utility and guidance, while runtime map hypotheses added limited detection benefit.

papers.abstract: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.

Existing compression criteria may discard earlier views that remain useful for future exploration, especially when crops replace only local evidence.
CanopyKV uses parent–child crop relationships and tool metadata to retain complementary history, stabilize retained tokens, and protect ongoing reasoning state.
It avoids additional attention-based scoring and reduces subsequent attention costs through compact KV storage.

Across four evaluated benchmarks, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the compared KV-compression methods; on MME-Lite, it retains about one-quarter of Dense’s KV, improves accuracy by 10.5 percentage points, and speeds reasoning by 1.64×.

papers.abstract: Reliable tissue detection is essential for whole-slide image analysis, yet high average segmentation accuracy can conceal failures involving pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining. Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations, but exhaustive inference is computationally demanding and may introduce false-positive tissue predictions. We propose SCOUT (Selective Correction of Uncertain Tissue), a risk-guided cascade that selectively refines an initial thumbnail-based tissue mask. A lightweight audit network estimates the spatial distribution of segmentation errors and prioritizes candidate regions for processing by a frozen pathology foundation model. An asymmetric consensus rule integrates the resulting predictions with the initial mask to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives. A calibrated slide-level review score additionally controls the marginal rate of unflagged case-group failures under the calibration assumptions. Evaluation on a public multi-source, multi-stain benchmark shows that SCOUT reduces the proportion of case groups requiring mask correction from 38.1% for the best released detector to 18.6%, with particularly pronounced improvements in immunohistochemistry. Source-held-out experiments demonstrate better generalization than a segmentation network trained on the same annotations, while selective inference achieves an observed failure rate no higher than processing all candidate regions. Downstream, lymph-node classification with SCOUT masks is non-inferior to that obtained with two of the three released detectors evaluated. A variant built on an openly licensed foundation model is publicly released as an installable Python package with trained weights. These results support risk-guided foundation-model inference as an effective approach to tissue detection across heterogeneous histopathology data.
authors: Cristian Tommasino, Antonio M. Rinaldi
bullets: Targets failures hidden by average accuracy, including pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining.
Uses a lightweight audit network to identify likely mask errors and prioritize regions for foundation-model refinement.
Combines initial and refined masks with an asymmetric consensus rule to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives.
On a multi-source, multi-stain benchmark, reduced case groups needing correction from 38.1% to 18.6%, with strong gains in immunohistochemistry.
Source-held-out results showed better generalization than a similarly annotated segmentation network; an openly licensed implementation was released.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.
authors: Wenhao Li, Zhongyi Han, Yuhao Wei, Liang Han, Yilong Yin, Liqiang Nie
bullets: Problem: Standard few-shot VLA policies memorize camera-to-robot geometry and fail after camera bumps or robot re-docking.
Method: Uses the robot arm via forward kinematics as a metric calibration target and static scene geometry as a world anchor.
Canonicalization: Corrects the image, robot state, actions, and start pose to the original calibration frame without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data.
Evaluation: Introduces LIBERO-PoseShift and evaluates simulation plus four real-world UR5e tasks under camera, base, and compound shifts.
Results: Improves shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and 36.7 points on the real robot, without perturbed training data or test-time calibration.

papers.abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.
authors: Guolong Zheng, Chen Hou, Xu Yang, Jianshan Zhang, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses growing full-history prompts that increase inference cost and can obscure relevant information.

In a 150-task SWE-bench study, Pass@1 increased from 80.0% to 86.9% at essentially unchanged token use and execution time.
The complete system used 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest task-performance baseline.

papers.abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Jiajun Zha, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Huihao Jing, Kexu Cheng, Shipeng Luo, JinYang Huang, Shing-Chi Cheung, Changsheng Lu, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
bullets: The study evaluates six multimodal models reviewing 31 full scientific manuscripts with hidden, reviewer-documented inconsistencies.

Naming the figure increases accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while consistency instructions and coarse visual cues provide little benefit.
Contradictions visible only in rendered figures receive no accepted diagnoses from text-only review, versus 15.8% when the figure is named and pages are rendered.
A centrality-based figure-selection baseline reaches only 4.8%, highlighting the difficulty of autonomously selecting evidence to verify.

papers.abstract: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/
authors: Aditya Gandhamal, Aniruddh Sikdar, Arya Kishor, Suresh Sundaram
bullets: Targets robust perception for embodied AI in unseen objects, adverse weather, cross-domain settings, and changing viewpoints.
Evaluates multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary semantic segmentation from aerial and ground perspectives.
Covers varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensor modalities, including infrared.
Introduces Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ) to model aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty jointly.
Provides a robustness-focused foundation for evaluating and improving open-world embodied-AI perception.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.
authors: Boxi Zhou, German Sviridov, Dmitrii Ustiugov, Haris Javaid
bullets: Recent small open-weight models perform well on easy and medium software-engineering tasks, with most of the accuracy gap concentrated on hard tasks.
The study evaluates 36 large and small models released since 2024 on SWE-bench Verified.
A hybrid strategy starts with a small model and escalates to a large model when needed.
The cascade reduces GPU-hour costs by up to 33% overall and 16.4% across all tasks without sacrificing accuracy.
It nearly matches an oracle-style task router while requiring minimal engineering complexity.

papers.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.
authors: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi, Jingwei Li, Shipeng Cen, Pengcheng Luo, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets lifelong learning beyond fixed tasks, curricula, and objectives.
Uses a two-layer representation: situated memories plus transferable experiences and skills with applicability conditions.
Consolidates textual experience into an evolving shared knowledge graph and shares executable skills directly.
In Minecraft, agent groups sustain exploration and achieve advanced technological milestones.
Knowledge transferred to a new group using a different backbone improves survival and exploration progress.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.
authors: Zizhuo Fu, Haochen Huang, Shengxuan Qiu, Linye Wei, Ziyu Tang, Runsheng Wang, Meng Li
bullets: Existing wave-style methods waste computation by drafting at fixed loops and following stale predictions.
They can also amplify memory traffic by loading KV caches from multiple loops per decoding step.
LoopCache uses confidence-guided draft updates across intermediate loops to improve speculative trajectories.
A cyclic loop KV-cache strategy limits each step to one loop’s KV traffic while enabling lossless verification; selective shallow-layer caches further improve acceptance.
It reports average speedups of 10.25× over WFD and 14.56× over LoopSpec.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.
authors: Kotaro Horikawa, Keisuke Toida, Junya Komori, Kazuhiro Hotta
bullets: Motivation: Bilinear or bicubic interpolation already captures smooth feature content, leaving learned upsamplers to mainly recover edges and fine details.
Method: Interpolate the coarse features, predict a residual correction with a small guidance network, and blend them using one learnable scalar gate.
Contribution: A parameter-efficient upsampler with 167,425 parameters and 64% of NAF’s latency.
Results: Trained only on DINOv3 with one training stage, AnchorUp matches two-stage NAF on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes across six held-out backbones.
On DAVIS-2017, it surpasses NAF on every backbone, with larger gains in contour accuracy F.

Figure 2. AnchorUp. (a) The low-resolution feature map is upsampled in two ways: by a classical upsampler with no parameters, which gives the anchor, and by a NAF-style upsampler, a guidance network followed by neighborhood cross-attention. papers.tldr: AnchorUp makes feature upsampling smaller and faster by using classical interpolation as an anchor and learning only edge- and detail-focused corrections.

papers.abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.
authors: Haoran Luo, Jiapu Wang, Linhao Luo, Luu Anh Tuan
bullets: Existing knowledge-engineering systems typically support at most two of omnimodality, closed-loop updating, and multi-granular use.

KnowledgeClaw constructs an omnimodal typed hypergraph, maintains it through a closed-loop lifecycle agent, and routes queries to the needed granularity.
It ranks first among 30 baselines across all six tasks, achieving an overall OKE score of 55.9, 14.6 points above the strongest baseline.
The benchmark and system are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. However, existing prompt-learning methods are not well suited for ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones or pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment. We propose CROMPT, a prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation. CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA), combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting (HTP) to jointly adapt visual and textual representations. We further propose CROMA-VL, which leverages vision-language models to generate domain-conditioned prompts, and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy for improved domain invariance. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods, achieving 1.63-2.63% mIoU gains while maintaining inference-time complexity. These results establish CROMPT as an effective and efficient framework for zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=FxqFsIL685
authors: Aniruddh Sikdar, Arya Kishor, Snehashis Dhibar, Suresh Sundaram
bullets: Addresses zero-shot domain adaptation when target-domain images are unavailable during training.
Introduces CROMA, combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting for cross-modal feature adaptation.
Adds CROMA-VL for vision-language-model-generated, domain-conditioned prompts and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy.

papers.abstract: Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels. Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets. A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to improve policy performance.
authors: Zhaoting Li, Cosimo Della Santina, Jens Kober
bullets: Interactive imitation learning produces abundant autonomous experience but sparse human action labels.
SeRA uses later policy checkpoints to relabel autonomous rollouts and filters labels where checkpoints agree.
It represents accepted relabels as desired action sets rather than assuming exact correctness.
An action-chunking diffusion policy is trained with a step-masked denoising loss over relabels and human corrections.
Across simulated manipulation tasks and a real tomato-picking task, SeRA improves performance, reaching 80% success versus 40% for SDP on the real robot.

papers.abstract: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.
authors: Pengyu Li, Zhitao Gao, Lingling Zhang, Wenxuan Huang, YiCheng Xiao, Chen Zheng, Jun Liu
bullets: Maintains a clean short-term frame window to preserve current-scene perception and reduce hallucinations.
Chooses among direct answering, high-resolution inspection, historical recall, and waiting for future frames.
Uses an isolated verification sub-agent and stream-decoupled attention to integrate recalled evidence without disrupting present visual tokens.
Trains tool-use decisions with counterfactual information gain to encourage evidence-gathering only when useful.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B accuracy on OVO-Bench from 47.6% to 65.9% and doubles zero-shot accuracy on Video-Holmes with minimal added visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.
authors: Pengyu Li, Zhitao Gao, Lingling Zhang, Heng Wang, Chengqian Ma, WenHao Wang, Wenxuan Huang, Chen Zheng, Jun Liu
bullets: Long-video dependence is concentrated early in the response, so continued video access is often unnecessary.

On Qwen3.6-27B, notes preserve accuracy better than unrestricted reasoning at the same withdrawal point; substituted notes hurt, while retaining the video adds no significant benefit.
Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy at 0.12–0.13× the modeled decode cost.
With fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model withdraws after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound-guided needle interventions have primarily focused on target localization and accurate needle placement, while the subsequent acquisition of diagnostic material remains comparatively underexplored. Moreover, pleural fluid aspiration and tissue biopsy are typically addressed as separate procedures, despite sharing common requirements for ultrasound guidance, safe access, and sample transport. This work presents a unified robotic framework for ultrasound-guided fluid and tissue extraction using a single vacuum-assisted end effector. The proposed system combines force controlled ultrasound scanning, semantic target identification, automated needle deployment, and procedure specific material acquisition. A coaxial needle assembly and shared pump assisted pathway enable direct pleural fluid aspiration, while controlled cannula actuation provides the additional cutting action required for solid-tissue acquisition. End-to-end evaluation using a Franka Emika Panda robot over 50 phantom trials achieved successful extraction in 23/25 pleural fluid aspiration trials (92\%) and 22/25 tissue acquisition trials (88\%). Following successful tissue-target access, acquisition and transport were completed in all 22 trials.

bullets: Addresses the underexplored step of acquiring diagnostic material after robotic needle placement.

Uses a shared pump-assisted pathway for fluid aspiration and controlled cannula actuation for tissue cutting.
In 50 phantom trials, fluid aspiration succeeded in 23/25 cases (92%) and tissue acquisition in 22/25 cases (88%).
After successful tissue-target access, tissue acquisition and transport succeeded in all 22 trials.

papers.abstract: Long video sequences make attention a substantial cost in video diffusion models. Block sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing selected blocks exactly while compressing the remaining blocks. However, fixed token grouping can place tokens with dissimilar attention preferences in the same group, while uniform key averaging can underestimate the attention mass of compressed blocks. We introduce Spark-Attn, a training-free BSA method comprising Spark-Reblock and Spark-Reweight. Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens by attention preference while preserving regular block shapes for efficient GPU execution. Spark-Reweight uses the global mean query as an anchor to construct attention-weighted key-value representations and logit biases for the compressed blocks, calibrating their attention mass. We instantiate Spark-Attn in MiniMax-H3 as Spark-H3. At 10% exact-block density, Spark-H3 delivers a 2.49$\times$ DiT speedup and reaches 24.81 dB PSNR against the corresponding dense outputs on MiniMax-H3 (20 denoising steps, 345 frames, 1344$\times$768). Increasing the density to 20% further improves PSNR to 26.76 dB while still achieving a 2.26$\times$ DiT speedup. These results demonstrate that Spark-H3 achieves a state-of-the-art quality-efficiency trade-off for training-free BSA on video diffusion models.
authors: Zecheng Tang, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Xinyao Rao, Liuxuan Sun, Jian Zhang, Yao Yao, Wei Li
bullets: Targets the high attention cost of long video sequences in diffusion models.
Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens with similar attention preferences while retaining GPU-friendly regular blocks.
Spark-Reweight uses a global-mean-query anchor to build weighted key-value summaries and calibrate compressed-block attention mass.
At 10% exact-block density, it achieves a 2.49× DiT speedup and 24.81 dB PSNR versus dense outputs.
At 20% density, PSNR rises to 26.76 dB with a 2.26× speedup; the method is training-free and instantiated in MiniMax-H3.

papers.abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

The teacher features are then mapped into the student feature space using the optimal orthogonal transformation matrices. Finally, the student model is trained by minimizing the distillation loss between the fused teacher features and student features, together with the supervised driving action loss.

papers.abstract: Filming a scene from an additional angle after production usually requires a costly reshoot. We present One Shot Any View, a system that takes a recorded clip and generates a reshot video of the same performance along a user-specified camera trajectory. As in recent geometry-grounded methods, the system conditions generation on the source video and an explicit 3D prior, namely a point video rendered along the requested trajectory from a feed-forward reconstruction of the source video. We target human-centric cinematic videos, which are often shot with long lenses, shallow depth of field, and low-key lighting, all of which degrade feed-forward reconstruction. Existing geometry-grounded methods tend to inherit the degraded point video, and their output quality drops visibly. Two designs make such point videos usable. First, in addition to rendered videos of 3D assets, we train on real-world multi-camera videos, whose point videos are produced by the same reconstruction pipeline as at inference. This training-inference consistency enables the generator to take only the composition of people and scene elements from the point video, and their appearance from the source video. Second, a geometry-anchored RoPE offset keeps the generated video temporally synchronized with the source while largely preventing the output from copying the degraded appearance of the point video. Meanwhile, since the generator is a pretrained reference-to-video (R2V) model, the system also accepts optional character and scene reference images, which supply the appearance of regions that the source never shows. In both objective and human evaluations, One Shot Any View outperforms existing reshooting methods.
authors: Kai Huang, Runze Xu, Hui Ren, Taiyi Wu, Xinyuan Li, Xun Gao, Quande Liu, Dong Tang, Tongtong Shen, Xuefeng Su, Alan Zhao
bullets: Addresses costly reshoots for human-centric cinematic footage captured with long lenses, shallow depth of field, and low-key lighting.
Uses a feed-forward 3D reconstruction to render a point video along the requested trajectory.
Trains on real multi-camera videos to handle degraded point-video geometry while preserving appearance from the source video.
Introduces a geometry-anchored RoPE offset to maintain temporal synchronization without copying degraded point-video appearance.
Supports optional character and scene reference images, and outperforms existing reshooting methods in objective and human evaluations.

papers.abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.
authors: Yiyang Zhu, Guangyuan Liu, Jingdi Lei, Li Wei, Chau Yuen
bullets: Static pooled embeddings can collapse distinct physical executions under identical conditions into the same representation.
Theoretical analysis shows that longer temporal pooling converges toward the stationary recording condition, making twin events indistinguishable from pooled features alone.
Physical events are identified by an “event gap”: instantaneous, synchronized changes across modalities that accumulate along unpooled trajectories.
CounterPoint removes each modality’s temporal mean and scores frame-level cross-modal agreement.
Integrated into four multimodal aligners, it consistently outperforms existing temporal alignment methods, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
authors: Haotian Xu, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Tuo Feng, Wenguan Wang, Quanjun Yin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting changing viewpoints with stable spatial evidence during long-range flight.
Builds a north-up navigation map from visual observations, geographic priors, and landmarks.
Uses instruction- and state-conditioned memory retrieval to predict map-frame targets, then converts them into body-frame commands.
Early goal commitment stabilizes long-horizon execution by fixing the target from the first K predictions.
On Test Unseen, it improves navigation error, success rate, and success-weighted path length, with efficient 0.68-second inference and 8.6 GB peak memory on one A100.

papers.abstract: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.
authors: Yuqi Ping, Tianhao Liang, Tingting Zhang
bullets: Targets safe, cellular-connected flight in dense urban canyons without prior 3D maps or channel knowledge.
Fuses multimodal histories with a categorical recurrent state-space model into a coordinate-invariant latent belief.
Trains an online policy through multi-step latent imagination rather than model-free trial and error.
In zero-shot unseen urban morphologies, it achieved 100% mission success with zero collisions and a median route SINR of 8.02 dB.
Reduced effective SINR outage by over 50% versus radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines; scope is evaluated in the AeroCity-RT ray-tracing simulator.

papers.abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.
authors: Kevin Zhai, Bian Sun, Zhenyi Wang, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding of autoregressive models and independent per-step prediction in discrete diffusion models.
Jointly models output embeddings with parallel token decoding using learned image guidance and prediction-aware decoding.
Uses a visually adapted teacher for image-guided denoising supervision and trains a decoder to convert continuous predictions into words.
The decoder can be adapted independently; for captioning, decoded text also provides feedback during late denoising.
Reports gains of up to 8.46 points on VQAv2, 4.50 points on GQA, and 16.25 CIDEr over masked diffusion on COCO Karpathy test.

papers.abstract: Visual planning with a frozen joint-embedding world model supports robotic reaching and object manipulation by evaluating candidate action sequences against an image goal before execution. Standard cross-entropy method (CEM) planners roll out every candidate independently through a billion-parameter predictor, even when nearby actions induce similar scene changes. This redundant computation grows with population size and search rounds, slowing closed-loop replanning. We observe that candidates within a planning step share an observation history and thus a common action-to-feature map. Based on this insight, we propose ProbeShare, which measures local responses with a few representative probes and reconstructs each candidate's feature grid through scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting. When promising candidates move beyond existing probe coverage, ProbeShare evaluates a new probe to rescore nearby candidates. Across four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.8--128.9 times over dense RoboJEPA and at least $14.2\times$ over competitive baselines, with greater mean goal progress in a matched-time comparison.
authors: Zejian Kang, Xiantao Lin, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Shengwen Zheng, Chengtai Guo, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Targets redundant computation in CEM planning with frozen, large joint-embedding world models.
Uses a few representative action probes, then reconstructs other candidates’ feature grids with scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting.
Adds new probes when promising actions fall outside existing coverage.
Across four RoboCasa tasks, achieves 43.8–128.9× faster episode planning than dense RoboJEPA and at least 14.2× faster than competitive baselines.
Provides greater mean goal progress than dense planning under matched time, with scope limited to the evaluated robotic reaching and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Intuitive robot programming approaches, such as Programming by Demonstration, enable non-experts to teach robots tasks through hand-guided demonstrations. However, for in-contact tasks requiring force control for parts of the motion, automated segmentation of motion types is crucial for improving usability. Considering the related work, this work proposes a neural network-based segmentation method categorizing motion into three fundamental types using input data of cartesian twists and wrenches at the end effector. We collect demonstration data using a 7-axis robot with a wrist-mounted force torque sensor and generate ground truth labeling by hand. While still in development, our research direction aims to enable non-experts to program in-contact tasks more intuitively.
authors: Johannes Hartwig, Marcello K\"ogler, Dominik Henrich
bullets: Targets Programming by Demonstration for non-expert robot users.
Addresses the need to distinguish motion types when force control is required.
Uses end-effector Cartesian twists and wrenches as neural-network inputs.
Considers three fundamental motion categories.
Demonstrations are collected with a 7-axis robot and wrist-mounted force-torque sensor, with labels assigned by hand.

papers.tldr: A neural-network method segments hand-guided robot demonstrations into motion types for more intuitive programming of in-contact tasks.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.
authors: Md Abtahi Majeed Chowdhury, Md Rifat Ur Rahman, Md Sakib Hossain Shovon, Jaesik Choi, Minhyuk Sung
bullets: Drifting world models reduce the cost of multi-step diffusion rollouts but can weaken action following.
Existing repulsive guidance remains active even when predictions match the recorded future, creating target bias.
MSA uses semi-relaxed optimal transport to subtract the correct future’s closed-form mass share, making guidance vanish at the target.
Theory shows the recorded future is the unique fixed point for collapsed predictions and that guidance decreases with prediction error.
On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines.

papers.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.
authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Wenyu Dai, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke K Nandi, Anthony Cohn
bullets: Targets the scalability costs of multi-agent red teaming, including redundant communication, inefficient routing, and weak feedback attribution.
Represents agent roles, dependencies, and input bindings as versioned executable graphs with records of information flow.
An LLM controller uses workflow records, target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain, refine, restructure, or freeze workflows.
Evaluated on HarmBench with multiple execution backbones and target models, including ablations, transfer, and evaluator checks.
Across six configurations, L2C raises ASR by 1.4–4.5 percentage points over EvoSynth while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6–37.3%.

papers.abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
authors: Philippe Forest, Giulia Lioi, Mai Pham Quyen, Alix Lamouroux, Javen Shi, Adrien Merlini
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong within-subject decoding and poor generalization to unseen individuals without collecting labeled calibration data.
Introduces incremental transductive calibration: each EEG query is decoded first, then accumulated unlabeled data and the known candidate gallery are used for calibration.
GALA aligns EEG embeddings with the gallery using shrinkage whitening, hubness correction, and Sinkhorn–Procrustes alignment with continually estimated query frequencies.
On THINGS-EEG-2 with 200 candidate images, accuracy for a new subject improves from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes.
Across 60 settings, GALA is the most accurate label-free method, averaging 6.6 percentage points above the strongest competitor at stream end.

papers.abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.
authors: Mohammad Ali Vahedifar, Behzad Bozorgtabar, Qi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between preserving existing knowledge and deleting selected knowledge.
Scores each weight for retention and deletion, dividing the network into four update zones.
Freezes retention-only weights, clears deletion-only weights, and orthogonally removes contested knowledge.
Uses remaining capacity with teacher-guided self-distillation to learn incoming tasks.
Matches or outperforms strong baselines across CL and MU settings, including image generation and dangerous-content removal; practicality is demonstrated on a PAI dataset.
