papers.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.
authors: Baiang Li, Enze Xie, Jincheng Yu, Jin Wang, Haozhe Liu, Yitong Li, Juanxi Tian, Felix Heide
bullets: Maintains world state outside the generator as a panorama with revision history, preventing revisit drift and preserving prior edits.
Uses MLLMs to translate requests into state operations, select edit regions, and validate generated candidates before updating the world.
Supports navigation, text- or box-based object edits, subject placement, and changes to lighting, weather, and season.
Reports the strongest results across stated environment-recovery and editing benchmarks, including consistent revisits and region-preserving edits.
Scope is single-image initialization with generated views serving presentation rather than state storage.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Each driving record pairs an executed ego trajectory with its observed future, providing a factual outcome for learning this connection. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision-language driving through auxiliary bird's-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Together, these objectives train the shared planner to generate driving waypoints. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and eight successful routes.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting future scene prediction with action planning in autonomous driving.

At inference, directly generates waypoints without running the auxiliary future-prediction branch.
On 220 Bench2Drive routes, achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, outperforming a schedule-matched planning-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.

Dynamic pricing improves large-budget performance across all eight domains, with 11 ms planning cost; reported gains reach 28.4 AP points on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS versus static priority.

papers.abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

papers.abstract: 3D affordance acts as a critical link between perception and action, providing priors for robotic manipulation. While existing approaches predominantly leverage human priors as direct references, they often overlook that affordance is not an object-intrinsic property but is inherently coupled with the agent's embodiment. Due to the structural and morphological disparities between human hands and robot end-effectors, directly applying human priors causes severe incompatibility for robotic execution. Motivated by this, we introduce a novel task setting, 3D Human-to-Robot Affordance Transfer, which addresses the affordance misalignment arising from distinct embodiment structures. To support this task, we construct the Human-Robot Paired Affordance Dataset (HPAD), the first large-scale 3D affordance benchmark in which every object is annotated with both human-prior and simulation-validated robot labels. HPAD covers 2,137 objects across 80 categories and 13 atomic action primitives, yielding over 27,000 object-action pairs. On top of HPAD, we propose the 3D Affordance tRansfer neTwork (ART). ART first filters geometric false positives in the human prior via a reliability gating stream, then reconstructs the prior into a robot-actionable distribution through hierarchical reconstruction and a graph-diffusion refinement that resolves the topological mismatch between human and robot affordances. Experiments on HPAD demonstrate the reliability of the proposed task and the superiority of ART. We further validate ART on a 6-DoF arm with a parallel-jaw gripper in a 2,400-execution benchmark across 12 objects and 4 action categories; ART attains the best success rate (86.5% over its 480 trials), confirming the practicality of the transfer paradigm. Project page: https://derek0907.github.io/ART/
authors: Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Xuji Zhang, Yang Cao, Yu Kang

papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.
authors: Idan Ben-Ami, Arnon Netzer, Sarah Keren, Idit Diamant
bullets: Targets the inference cost and mixed uncertainty signals of sampling-based Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC).
Uses a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation and Jacobian-vector products to derive action-level uncertainty.
Measures local uncertainty around the selected execution trajectory, unlike AAC’s global dispersion across alternative chunks.
Correlates strongly with AAC while being less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid strategies.

papers.abstract: World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution. However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory. We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components: (1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory; (2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors; and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification. The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online. On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher's PDMS gain over execution-aware selection. On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%). The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger. HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon visual agents must do more than inspect images: they must turn observations into evidence that remains usable as a task unfolds. Existing active-perception methods teach agents where and how to look, while a final-answer reward gives little structure for deciding which observations satisfy dependent subgoals or should be retained for later use. We present ViStep-RL (Visual Stepwise Reinforcement Learning), which models execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals. A verifier tracks which subgoals are supported by valid evidence, and changes in graph potential provide a net-progress learning signal; an active memory protocol preserves evidence across turns and links retrieval to downstream use. On ViInteract, ViStep-RL reaches 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, compared with 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning. Controlled studies show that incremental task-state rewards outperform cumulative rewards by 3.2 points, while active evidence writing improves strict completion by 7.75 points over automatic writing. Under a common interaction framework, the task-trained ViStep-RL policy achieves 59.5% answer accuracy, 24.0 points above the strongest of six general-purpose reference models. Held-out episodes confirm the gain at both Qwen scales, and gains extend to three external visual reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

papers.abstract: Robot navigation requires both an understanding of the scene and an efficient adaptation to new robots, yet current methods rely on expensive LiDAR sensors, long mapping and modular pipelines. We present BEV-Diffusion, a camera-only model that learns a bird's-eye view (BEV) traversability map, its uncertainty and the path in a single network. A frozen DINOv2 backbone encodes consecutive RGB frames, which inverse perspective mapping and Bayesian fusion lift into the BEV, and a ranking loss keeps outdoor traversability graded rather than binary, separating asphalt from grass (median 0.94 vs. 0.75). On this map, a transformer denoiser generates polar waypoints in a few DDIM steps, and uncertainty-aware guidance refines the path and ends it where the map is no longer reliable. At deployment, a metric BEV memory keeps obstacles after they leave the camera view and warm starts each sample from the previous, ego-motion compensated path. Because the planner jointly learns the path, the map, and its uncertainty, it selects routes through terrain it can confidently traverse. In an unseen courtyard, a wheeled-legged robot autonomously traveled 120 m, completing 96% of the route without intervention, compared with 75-88% for the baselines. Even under low-light conditions after sunset, the proposed model completed the route without requiring any intervention. Retraining only the BEV head, about 3% of the parameters, adapts the model to a small legged robot in 2.3 min. Indoors, the memory gets this robot out of maze-like traps: it retains 62-66% of the nearby out-of-view obstacles, against at most 3% for the baselines, and the robot achieves 67-100% task progress, compared with 20-40% for the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

papers.abstract: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or boundary-risk cases use conservative score-grounded propagation. Across eight standard OVSS benchmarks, SEER reaches 58.0 average mIoU without updating OVSS weights. Matched-input controls isolate the repair mechanism, while resource measurements report the cost of the complete frozen system.
authors: Junyang Chen, Xiao Li, Yiguo Qiao, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets local, structured OVSS errors that depend on the active label vocabulary.
Uses OVSS scores to propose candidate labels and a frozen vision-language model to verify regional semantic evidence.
An execution gate accepts only evidence that is both vocabulary-legal and actionable in the segmentation score field.
Applies broad propagation to coherent high-confidence regions and conservative score-grounded propagation near objects or boundaries.
Achieves 58.0 average mIoU across eight standard OVSS benchmarks without updating OVSS weights; controls and resource measurements assess the repair mechanism and full-system cost.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process visual information and textual instructions and, by using their ability to understand and reason about context, are well-suited for predicting robot failures before they occur. However, evidence supporting this remains limited. To address this, we present an empirical evaluation of VLMs for predicting robot failures. In particular, we experiment with Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies (HuRoN, Pal Robotics, and CrowdBot), analyzing both video and odometry data for early failure warning (i.e., before an unsafe situation occurs). Specifically, we evaluate their performance in classifying situations as safe, potentially unsafe, and unsafe, together with uncertainty quantified using various metrics, and study the relationship between uncertainty and performance. Our results showed that Qwen provides the strongest overall classification and prediction-reliability performance, while InternVL shows stronger early-warning capability in several configurations. The results further show that the effect of robot-state information and temporal history depends on the model and evaluation objective. Overall, our findings indicate that general-purpose VLMs can support early robot-safety monitoring, but the most suitable configuration depends on whether the priority is accurate assessment of safety-state, reliable confidence and uncertainty, or timely warning before unsafe events.
authors: Muhammad Farooq, Aitor Arrieta, Paolo Arcaini, Shaukat Ali, Thomas Peyrucain
bullets: Evaluates Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies using video and odometry.
Classifies situations as safe, potentially unsafe, or unsafe while assessing uncertainty and prediction reliability.
Qwen achieves the strongest overall classification and reliability, whereas InternVL offers stronger early-warning performance in some settings.
Robot-state information and temporal history affect models differently depending on the evaluation goal.
Results support VLMs for robot-safety monitoring, with configuration choices balancing accuracy, confidence, and warning timeliness.

papers.abstract: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each expert is initialized from its predecessor at no extra cost: the domains share their classes, so an image misrouted to a later expert loses less. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol, Lamarck is first on CDDB-Hard by 5.2 points, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.
authors: Gyutae Oh, Hyunmin Kong, Jitae Shin
bullets: Problem: Test images lack domain labels, so routing among domain-specific experts is difficult, while the experts themselves also limit accuracy.
Method: Add trainable adapters after each deep ViT block and use a training-free Mahalanobis router.
Method: Initialize each new domain expert from the previous expert, exploiting shared classes and reducing harm from later-expert misrouting.
Results: Adapters add 4.4 final-accuracy points on CDDB-Hard; Lamarck ranks first on CDDB-Hard, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.
Scope: Evaluated against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol.

papers.abstract: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

Uses object-relative constraints, contact-guided inverse kinematics, and object preservation during robot-data compositing.
Reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7% on HOT3D and realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts on EgoDex.

papers.abstract: Biological learning systems acquire knowledge incrementally through broad, reusable representations established early and kept largely stable, while integrating new experience with minimal interference with previously learned knowledge. Replay-based methods approximate this by storing samples or features from previous tasks and mixing them into the current task. However, memory buffers grow with the number of tasks and may retain task-specific noise that reduces generalization. To address these limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network), an unsupervised class-incremental learning method for image classification that continually updates feature representations using autoencoders. Since images share structural features such as edges, corners, and shapes, we first divide each image into patches and train independent autoencoders on external data to reconstruct each patch. The layers of all patch encoders are aggregated into global frozen layers that generalize across tasks and remain fixed throughout learning. Learnable adapters then build global image representations from these features to reconstruct the entire image. To prevent feature drift without storing data, we introduce the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a fixed-size running average of adapter outputs updated after each task to penalizes representation drift. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is applied to the learnable layers to preserve previously learned features by constraining important weights. Finally, a linear classifier is trained on the frozen latent representation and GFC for class-incremental evaluation. We evaluate PatchAdaNet in both CNN and Vision Transformer settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets, providing a comparative study of the two architectures under identical class-incremental settings. Code is available.
authors: Kamel Aouaidjia, Yanchao Duan, Zihui Zhen, Xin Li, Yongfei Lv, Chongsheng Zhang
bullets: Targets replay-based class-incremental learning, which can require growing memory and retain task-specific noise.
Trains independent patch autoencoders on external data, aggregates their encoders into frozen global layers, and uses learnable adapters to reconstruct full images.
Maintains a Global Feature Centroid (GFC) to penalize representation drift without storing prior data.
Uses Elastic Weight Consolidation on learnable layers and trains a linear classifier on frozen latent features plus the GFC.
Evaluated with CNNs and Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet, and 5-Datasets under matched class-incremental settings.

(b) ViT-based framework: frozen patch-level features are pretrained using a patch-level ViT autoencoder (ViT-PatchAE). In continual learning phase, frozen tokens are concatenated and combined with the previous depth’s adapted tokens, then refined through adapter Transformer blocks via image reconstruction (ViT-ImageAE).

papers.abstract: E-commerce visual effects (EVF) are dynamic, product-centered visual presentations in e-commerce videos, often accompanied by promotional text. They play an important role in attracting viewer attention and conveying product information. However, general measures of visual quality and text relevance alone do not establish whether generated videos preserve product appearance, maintain readable text, and produce coherent, contextually appropriate effects. To address this issue, we introduce EVF-Bench, a dedicated benchmark spanning six evaluation dimensions: visual quality and text relevance as general dimensions, and motion, product consistency, text stability, and creative rationality as EVF-specific dimensions. To complement the benchmark and support task-aligned research and model adaptation, we further construct EVF-32K, a dataset of over 32000 curated image-text-video triples tailored to e-commerce scenarios. Using this suite, we systematically evaluate representative video generation models and their domain-adapted variants. The results reveal complementary strengths, with no evaluated configuration leading all six dimensions. Together, EVF-Bench and EVF-32K provide a task-oriented evaluation framework and a supporting data resource for e-commerce video generation.

Evaluates six dimensions: visual quality, text relevance, motion, product consistency, text stability, and creative rationality.

Provides a task-oriented benchmark and data resource for evaluating and adapting e-commerce video generation models.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

bullets: Addresses redundant visual information and error accumulation in long-horizon world-model rollouts.

Experiments on Minecraft, Crafter, and web interaction demonstrate effective relational imagination; in Minecraft, it is the only evaluated method reported to obtain diamonds within the budget.

papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Jian Yang, Ge Sun, Junyu Luo, Wenkai Zhang, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Addresses step-level backdoor detection for open-weight GUI agents, which existing image- and CLIP-focused detectors do not cover.
Uses Intent Counterfactual Probing to measure instruction influence and Region Causal Audit to measure candidate-region influence.
A gated conformal score compares these effects with clean steps at comparable manifold distances, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families report consistent detection at controlled false-positive rates, trigger localization, and modest overhead.
Scope: detection is performed per step without trigger knowledge or attack data; the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Embodied robots increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to interpret user intent and coordinate with robot-specific action models for physical interaction. This multi-model pipeline creates a critical semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: semantic consistency may break between what the large model understands, how the small action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what physical actions the robot ultimately performs. As a security consequence, commercial robots may execute unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands. To measure this problem, we develop TARS, a black-box framework that explores the command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors. We evaluate TARS on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, conducting 133,400 executions. TARS uncovers widespread cross-model action misalignment and achieves up to 94% verified action coverage.

bullets: Identifies cross-model action misalignment as a security risk in multi-model robot pipelines.

papers.abstract: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.
authors: Ruisi Zhao, You Li, Sihan Chen, Aosong Cheng, Chixiang Ma, Sen Pei, Zhen Yang, Hehe Fan, Dongliang He, Yi Yang
bullets: Addresses the lack of comprehensive benchmarks and mature workflows for automatic video rough-cutting.

Includes 101 visual cases with 831 raw videos and 1,476 highlight annotations, alongside 84 transcript-based cases with annotated cleanup spans.
Compares generated cut plans with annotations and uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator for rendered visual cuts.
Introduces agentic workflows for producing structured cut plans; experiments find current LVLMs remain limited in expert alignment.

papers.abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.
authors: Kamel Aouaidjia, Yanchao Duan, Zihui Zhen, Xin Li, Yongfei Lv, Chongsheng Zhang
bullets: Targets knowledge loss in regularization-based continual learning as task sequences grow.
Uses independent autoencoders to decompose inputs into complementary, independently learned representations.
Applies weight regularization within representations, localizing updates and reducing interference across tasks.
Evaluates representations with a linear classifier on several sequential image-classification benchmarks.
Reports competitive performance against supervised and replay-based continual-learning methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overall illustration of the proposed continual learning framework using independent regularized representations (right), compared to existing methods with a single representation (left). Colored nodes represent neurons that are important for previous tasks.
Fig. 11 Activation maps preservation across tasks for 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet. Classes from task 3.
Fig. 3 Left: Independent hierarchical representations (LevelNets). Right: Independent parallel representations (SideNets).

Fig. 2 Geometric intuition for the theoretical analysis. (a) After learning task j, the weights θ(j) sit at a minimum of the loss. Learning a later task moves the weights away from it and increases the loss, which is forgetting. A small move along a stiff direction (high curvature) causes a large loss increase, while even a large move along a soft direction (low curvature) causes little. (b) For a single shared representation, the importance matrix F is dense: the off-diagonal entries are the hidden couplings that diagonal EWC ignores. (c) For independent representations, F is block-diagonal (F1, . . . , FR). The cross-block couplings are exactly zero, so forgetting separates into one term per representation and each block can be protected on its own.

papers.abstract: Efficient use of expert demonstrations is essential for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, directly imitating expert trajectories couples nominal intention, which specifies where the vehicle should go, with multimodal driving styles, which determine how that intention is executed. Different combinations of these factors can yield similar expert trajectories, obscuring their respective causal contributions and forcing the policy to learn both from a single entangled target. This ambiguity limits how effectively the policy can exploit expert demonstrations. We propose CausalDrive, a causal decomposition framework for data-efficient driving policy learning that separates deterministic nominal intention prediction from probabilistic driving style modeling. Specifically, we construct counterfactual nominal trajectories from navigation command, map topology, and ego state by removing style dependent effects, providing a Nominal Intention Planner with supervision independent of expert trajectories. Conditioned on the predicted nominal intention and surrounding agents, a diffusion-based Style Execution Policy models diverse driving styles as a multimodal distribution over residuals between nominal and expert trajectories. This causally structured supervision reduces redundant learning of shared nominal behavior in routine scenarios, directing expert supervision toward informative execution variations and improving data utilization. CausalDrive achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Further experiments demonstrate strong performance with limited expert data and clear advantages in challenging interactive scenarios.
authors: Xiaobao Wei, Jingxian Wu, Lirong Yang, Qing Han, Yuan Gao, Ziwei Yang, Shuai Yang, Weiwei Liu, Chang Huang
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of learning intention and execution style from entangled expert trajectories.
Builds counterfactual nominal trajectories from navigation commands, map topology, and ego state for independent intention supervision.
Uses a diffusion-based policy to model diverse style residuals conditioned on nominal intention and surrounding agents.
Achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong results under limited data and in interactive scenarios.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have significantly improved video understanding capabilities, yet processing long videos remains challenging due to the substantial computational cost of extensive visual inputs. Frame selection offers an efficient alternative, but many existing region-based methods rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions, which may result in suboptimal temporal regions, compromising subsequent budget allocation and frame selection. In this work, we propose Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (APS), a training-free framework that adapts temporal partitions to local variations in query-frame relevance. Specifically, APS formulates temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, jointly optimizing partition boundaries and local models through dynamic programming. The resulting adaptive temporal partitions guide frame budget allocation based on query relevance and temporal extent, enabling informative frame selection under limited visual budgets. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that APS consistently improves performance across diverse LVLM backbones, achieving the highest average gains over uniform sampling among competing methods. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of adaptive partitioning and demonstrate its generalizability across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.
authors: Junxiang Wen, Yinxi Zhao, Jiawei Chen, Jingying Hu, Lijun Wang, Zhen Qin, Shuiguang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of processing long videos with LVLMs.
Uses a training-free, complexity-regularized fitting objective with dynamic programming to jointly optimize temporal boundaries and local relevance models.
Allocates frame budgets according to local query relevance and temporal extent.
Improves performance over uniform sampling across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench and diverse LVLM backbones.
Generalizes across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.
authors: Shiwei Wu, Yuwen Pan, Zhi Li, Yaowen Li, Yan Zhou, Xuemiao Xu, Yu Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable human labels and reliable rule-based repairs for failures encountered during closed-loop UAV navigation.
Uses recursive self-improvement: the current policy anchors failures, proposes or samples repairs, evaluates them by flying onward, and distills verified repairs.
Renews supervision each round to uncover failures hidden behind earlier failures while preserving behavior elsewhere.
On TravelUAV, three rounds improve success from 46.4% to 67.5% and halve collisions, with no extra human labels or inference cost.
Scope: evaluated on a supervised 2B-parameter policy and the TravelUAV benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AERORSI. The top row shows the policy πk, of which only the visual merger and the LoRA are trained. In each round, (1) AFA samples anchors from probes before every failure of πk; (2) CVR restores each anchor, lets πk continue the executed action a−, its sampled actions, and rule-based proposals, and accepts as the repair c⋆ the first candidate that qualifies again in a re-flight; and (3) RRL distills the verified repairs into a student copy of πk, keeping the outputs of πk on states that need no repair, to obtain πk+1.

(b) Pass@k of newly sampled actions of each policy at the reproducible anchors of the first round, at all of them (solid) and at those that only a rule-based proposal repaired (dashed). (c) Test SR when a round learns from the rule-based proposals, the sampled actions, or both, each single-source round starting from the previous round with both sources. (d) At the anchors accepted in the first round, the verified repair and the action at which π0 failed, each continued by a later policy (π0 continues the repair again). (e) Distance between the failure points of two flights on the training routes on which both fail. (f) SR gain of π3 over π0 on 999 test routes with and without an altitude cap. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals, paired in (f).

Figure 5. Case study of AERORSI. From a state before π0 crashes, π0 flies on from each candidate action (top), and π1 flies after one round (bottom). (a) Flying toward the target looks best at first but crashes, whereas a turn that falls behind completes the flight, so a repair can be judged only by flying on. (b) The sampled actions nearly repeat the crashing action, so only a rule-based proposal repairs it, and π1 learns this repair. (c) The same action crashes when π0 flies on but not when π1 does, so every round must judge its repairs anew.
Figure 3. Failure types across rounds. Share of test routes that end in each type of failure for the policy of every round of AERORSI (SFT init.), with the total failure rate after each bar.

Table 4. Ablation study on all test routes. Variants in (a) and (c) are compared with the first round and those in (b) with the second. In (a), unverified variants label every anchor without flying the label, verified variants keep only the labels that the policy completes, and the two-action variant scores the candidates after two actions instead. papers.tldr: AeroRSI improves aerial vision-language navigation by having UAV policies iteratively discover, verify, and learn from repairs to their own flight failures.

papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.
authors: Ryoichi Kurihara, Kota Sunamoto
bullets: The study evaluates two LIBERO-Spatial tasks that differ only in the landmark word identifying one of two bowls.
Unseen synonyms often direct the policy to the named bowl, unlike made-up words, but one task’s closed-loop completion falls to 67.6% versus 100% for the original wording.
Token-pasting tests suggest landmark information affects object choice before the connector, while coordinated information from landmark, instruction, and image tokens affects behavior after it.
Diversified landmark-word finetuning—and even connector-only training—can repair synonym completion; original-instruction finetuning does not.
Closed-loop evaluation should separately measure object choice and completion, with interventions on both sides of the connector; open-loop starting-frame scores can miss part of the repair.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies VLA policy robustness to landmark synonyms in closed-loop robot manipulation, fitting vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
papers.tldr: In GR00T N1.7, landmark synonyms can guide the correct object choice but still reduce task completion, with vulnerabilities spanning both sides of the vision-language/action connector.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.
authors: Sachith Abeywickrama, Peiliang Gong, Emadeldeen Eldele, Min Wu, Chau Yuen
bullets: Operating-condition shifts affect only parts of the embedding space, making global adaptation prone to forgetting stable regions.
PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for affected regions.
An identity path and learned gate combine the original representation with accumulated condition-specific transports.
Using 5% labeled calibration data per condition, PACT achieves average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream.
Similar retention and adaptation behavior is observed on public benchmarks with homogeneous tasks and label spaces.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Proposed PACT architecture. Source embeddings define fixed nearest-centroid charts. At inference, the selected chart’s gate combines the identity branch and available transports, and the frozen head classifies the corrected embedding. The encoder and head remain unchanged throughout adaptation.

papers.title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models

papers.abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Bingqian Wu, Fan Zhou, Jianjie Zhang, Chentao Shen, Wentao Yang, Rui Qian, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language-conditioned reference motions and controller-executed motions under balance and contact constraints.
Uses a differentiable world model with a fixed tracking controller to predict execution segments and assess the complete resulting trajectory against the instruction.
Backpropagates semantic feedback through inserted predicted segments to adapt the motion generator.
Adds an anchoring loss to keep adapted references close to those from the initial generator.
On BONES-SEED, it largely preserves reference-to-execution instruction retrieval accuracy and achieves the highest executed-motion retrieval accuracy among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.
authors: Yi Lu, Qianshi Lin, Yumeng Yang, Hongxia Wang
bullets: Separates content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights for context billing.
Context ablations find relevance dominates position; distance-decay weighting does not beat a relevance-only baseline.
Serving measurements show cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute costs by over 100× at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends limit discounts.
Calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31–42%, but revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs produce similar reductions and increase median charges.
The work offers bounded per-token accounting and deployment constraints, not a validated utility estimator.

papers.abstract: Reliable lithology interpretation requires accurate geological recognition and reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Although Multimodal Large Language Models show promise in remote sensing, their reliability in geological interpretation remains unclear. We introduce HyGeoBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 10,000 questions based on hyperspectral imagery across three dimensions: reasoning reliability, prior_evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination. It covers ten task types, with both multiple-choice and open-ended response formats. Integrating hyperspectral satellite imagery with geological annotations and verified evidence, HyGeoBench examines reasoning errors, conflicts between geological priors and visual evidence, and cross-band inconsistencies. Evaluations reveal limitations in fine-grained recognition and evidence-grounded interpretation. To address these challenges, we propose HyGeoAgent, a tool-augmented framework integrating region observation, text knowledge retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis through adaptive tool use. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, improving geological image interpretation across diagnostic dimensions.
authors: Jun Wang, Fengpeng Li, Wei Han, Yuxuan Li, Tianjin Huang, Jining Yan, Sheng Wang, Kan Sun, Lizhe Wang
bullets: Introduces a 10,000-question hyperspectral benchmark spanning reasoning reliability, prior–evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination.
Covers ten task types with multiple-choice and open-ended formats, using geological annotations and verified evidence.
Finds limitations in fine-grained lithology recognition, evidence grounding, and consistency across spectral bands.
Proposes HyGeoAgent, combining region observation, text retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis.
Reports consistent improvements over corresponding base models across the benchmark’s diagnostic dimensions.

papers.title: Benchmarking Reasoning Reliability,Prior_Evidence Contrast,and Spectral Discrimination in Remote-Sensing Geological Image Interpretation
papers.tldr: HyGeoBench diagnoses reliability gaps in multimodal geological image interpretation, while HyGeoAgent improves evidence-grounded reasoning through adaptive tool use.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.
authors: Xianhao Pan, Chi Li, Hanchao Li, Yunxin Liu, Jiankai Sun, Luhui Hu
bullets: Addresses the conflict between language-conditioned control and instruction-independent world dynamics.
Uses dual latent representations: language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention predicts dynamics from observation history and actions.
On 40 trained LIBERO tasks, achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters.
Outperforms the authors’ task-ID-conditioned baseline, improving overall success from 76.0% to 84.9% and LIBERO-Goal success from 67.1% to 88.5%.
Instruction-switching tests show task and policy outputs change with language, while dynamics representations and predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and actions.

papers.abstract: High-resolution visual question answering (VQA) requires models to identify question-relevant small objects in high-resolution images and select the correct answer based on what they recognize, demanding fine-grained perception. Previous methods focus on obtaining better visual evidence (image crops), but obtaining it alone is insufficient, using it effectively is equally crucial. Visual evidence should therefore be utilized as effectively as possible throughout inference. We argue that small-target evidence is obscured by unconditional information that remains observable in subsequent processing even after the condition on which it should depend is removed. Such information hinders the effective use of small-target evidence. We propose R$^{3}$Sieve (Residual-Region-Response Sieve), a training-free framework. We divide inference into three stages---localization, cropping, and answering---and introduce distinct counterfactual references to suppress interference at each stage. During localization, the Shared-Subspace Canceller (SSC) uses a generic image description to construct a counterfactual reference and obtain question-relevant attention maps. During cropping, the Unique-Contribution Spotter (UCS) constructs counterfactual references from visual and non-visual features to identify distinctive, complementary crop regions. During answering, the Content-Aligned Voter (CAV) constructs an image-free branch to calibrate answer responses. Experiments on three high-resolution VQA benchmarks show that R$^{3}$Sieve achieves the highest overall accuracy among compared methods across diverse settings, improving base models by up to 21.5 percentage points.
authors: Yifan Cao, Yawen Zhang, Xiaocui Yang, Faxian Wan, Shi Feng, Daling Wang, Yifei Zhang, Shangshu Yu, Xianbing Zhao
bullets: Targets the problem that small-object evidence can be obscured by unconditional information during inference.
Uses counterfactual references across three stages: SSC for question-relevant localization, UCS for complementary crop selection, and CAV for answer calibration.
Evaluated on three high-resolution VQA benchmarks across diverse settings.
Reports the highest overall accuracy among compared methods, improving base models by up to 21.5 percentage points.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of R3Sieve. Each module removes the unconditional information of one stage with a counterfactual reference. SSC removes the attention that a generic prompt explains, UCS discounts responses that other locations repeat and selects complementary crops through GCS, and CAV pools answer scores over option orders by content and subtracts the image-free preference.

Figure 2. Comparison of high-resolution VQA approaches. (a) Training-based methods acquire visual evidence. (b) Search-based methods locate relevant regions iteratively. (c) Attention-based methods guide cropping with attention signals. (d) Our R3Sieve uses all-stage counterfactual filtering to suppress unconditional information during localization, cropping, and answering, improving evidence utilization.
Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of BVS and our contribution scoring. BVS often highlights irrelevant regions, while our method better focuses on the queried targets.

Figure 1. Unconditional information can disrupt high-resolution VQA. Here, raw attention to question-irrelevant sky impairs localization, causing errors. R3Sieve suppresses interference during localization (SSC), cropping (UCS), and answering (CAV), progressively reducing distractor responses and strengthening target responses (bottom), yielding the correct answer.

Figure 3. Unconditional information in localization and cropping. (a) Subspace Projection versus pointwise corrections on minimum target coverage and answer accuracy. (b) Contribution Scoring versus Pointwise Ratio under the same source-area budgets.
Figure 4. Unconditional information in answer generation. (a) Option-order sensitivity across three benchmarks. (b) Accuracy gains from Permutation Pooling and Calibrated Pooling on V∗Bench [33].

Table 1. Comparison on high-resolution fine-grained perception benchmarks (accuracy, %). Best/second-best results are bold/blue. TF: training-free. †: indicates results taken from the original papers due to unavailable model weights or excessive evaluation time.
Table 2. Component ablation on V∗Bench (%). Bold: best.

papers.title: R$^{3}$Sieve: Suppressing Unconditional Information from Attention to Answers for High-Resolution VQA
papers.tldr: R³Sieve is a training-free framework that improves high-resolution VQA by suppressing irrelevant information during localization, cropping, and answer selection.

papers.abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.
authors: Luca Lusvarghi, Javier Gozalvez
bullets: Compares attention-based object relevance estimates with counterfactual causal relevance.
Analyzes more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using the PlanT 2.0 planning model.
Finds that attention often misses relevant objects and falsely highlights objects with little driving impact.
Attention performs better in simple single-lane, straight-road scenes but degrades on multi-lane roads and intersections.
The results motivate relevance methods that distinguish causal influence from correlation.

papers.abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model families and language directions, with a single worst case of 2.19 chrF; (iii) on consumer GPUs, INT8 and INT4 quantisation provide substantial memory savings (49-61% at INT4) but do not reduce inference latency relative to FP16 - in fact, latency increases by 1.3x to 5.3x; (iv) a clear performance gradient tracking training-resource availability is visible across languages (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba). These findings motivate a research agenda focused on hardware-aware compression and error-type analysis beyond aggregate metrics for low-resource deployment.
authors: Abbas Sani
bullets: The study evaluates Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba translation across three model families and FP16, INT8, and INT4 precision settings.
The specialised NLLB-200 model substantially outperforms both tested LLMs, despite being much smaller than the 8B instruction-tuned model.
Quantisation changes aggregate quality by about 1 chrF or less in nearly all settings, with a worst case of 2.19 chrF.
INT4 cuts memory use by 49–61%, but INT8 and INT4 are slower than FP16, with latency increasing 1.3×–5.3×.
Performance follows apparent training-resource availability: Swahili performs best, followed by Hausa and Yoruba.

Dashes mark metrics not recorded by the Yoruba extension run.

papers.title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
papers.tldr: Post-training INT8/INT4 quantisation greatly reduces memory use while largely preserving translation quality, but does not improve latency for low-resource African-language MT on T4 GPUs.

papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of AI-generated videos (AIGVs) has raised critical concerns about content authenticity. Existing benchmarks suffer from a fundamental limitation: real and fake videos are often collected or generated from different semantic distributions. As a result, detectors may rely on spurious correlations involving objects, scenes, or actions rather than intrinsic artifacts introduced by generative models. To this end, we introduce SAVGE, a large-scale semantically aligned AIGV detection dataset comprising 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real videos and 1,945,707 generated videos. SAVGE organizes samples into real-fake semantic groups by using captions paired with real videos as prompts for text-to-video generation, thereby providing both group-level correspondence and textual semantic anchors. Based on SAVGE, we further propose Explicit Disentangling and Semantic-aware Contrasting (EDSC), a model-agnostic training framework for learning artifact-focused representations with reduced semantic interference. EDSC first extracts and aligns visual semantic features with textual representations, and then explicitly suppresses semantic information in the artifact branch while contrasting real and fake samples within each semantic group. By integrating caption-guided semantic supervision with intra-group contrastive learning in a two-phase optimization strategy, EDSC encourages detectors to capture generation-related cues under matched semantic conditions. Extensive experiments on SAVGE and GenVideo demonstrate that EDSC improves most evaluated backbone-metric combinations, enhances robustness under challenging evaluation settings, and strengthens cross-dataset generalization. These results highlight the importance of semantic alignment in AIGV detection and validate explicit semantic-artifact disentanglement as an effective strategy for robust detector learning.
authors: Jiaquan Yu, Jingyi Xie, Zeyu Zhang, Yunhang Qian, Xiaobin Hu, Jiawei Liu
bullets: SAVGE addresses benchmark bias by grouping real and generated videos with matched semantics and textual anchors.
The dataset contains 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real and 1,945,707 generated videos.
EDSC aligns visual semantic features with text, suppresses semantic information in an artifact branch, and applies within-group real–fake contrastive learning.
Experiments on SAVGE and GenVideo show improvements across most evaluated backbone–metric combinations, with stronger robustness and cross-dataset generalization.
The approach focuses on generation-related artifacts under semantically matched conditions, rather than object, scene, or action correlations.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The overall framework of our proposed EDSC approach. It consists of two alternating phases: (1) Semantic Extraction and Alignment (SEA) and (2) Semantic Suppression and Intra-Group Contrasting (SSGC). The frozen boxes indicate fixed parameters in the corresponding phase, not fixed output features.
Figure 3: Example video samples from the SAVGE dataset. Each fake video is generated using the caption of a real video as the prompt, and the resulting real–fake set is organized as a semantic group.
Figure 5: t-SNE visualization of the learned feature representations produced by BERT+TALL, XCLIP-B-FT, and DeMambaXCLIP-B-FT, together with their EDSC-enhanced counterparts, on the SAVGE test set.

Figure 2: “Fake Video–Caption” and “Fake Video–Real Video” similarity-score distributions before and after the filtering process. The distributions show that retained fake videos are more semantically aligned with their corresponding real videos or captions than videos in the unfiltered set, indicating that the filtering process reduces real–fake semantic mismatch.
