papers.abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.
authors: Yunhe Gao, Ashwin Kumar, Jiaming Liu, Chong Wang, Maya Varma, Fuying Wang, Stefania L. Moroianu, Louisa Fay, Sergios Gatidis, Akshay S. Chaudhari, Curtis Langlotz
bullets: The paired-identity contrastive target causes zero-shot performance to decline despite decreasing training loss and prevents effective learning from large batches.
A synthetic CLEVR-Radiology testbed shows that overlapping clinical facts alone reproduce both failures, indicating a structural rather than radiology-specific issue.
The authors explain the failures through a deterministic, batch-size-amplified gradient bias from target misspecification.
CorLIP treats reports whose clinical assertions agree with an image as positives without changing the model architecture.
CorLIP reduces post-peak degradation, enables stable large-batch training, improves data scaling, remains stable up to B=2048, and transfers from chest X-rays to 3D CT.

papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.
authors: Junlin Long, Xu Deng, Yiran Wang, Yue Yang, Yang Zhao, Zeyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses language-guided loco-manipulation for arm-free quadrupeds, including walking on three legs while using a front leg to manipulate.
Uses two stages: cross-morphology adaptation with on-policy self-distillation, followed by reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation.
The first student retains near-teacher performance (76.7% vs. 77.0%) while sampling 14× faster.
Task-specific RL and multi-teacher distillation improve performance to 85.0% on ten QLM-Bench simulated tasks.
The initial distilled student is also deployed on a real Unitree Go2 Air.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Wenqing Tian, Qiang Liu, Liang Wang
bullets: Addresses tool-augmented agents’ inconsistent object/reference-frame semantics and poor judgment of evidence sufficiency.

Uses a Control Agent to diagnose evidence-chain failures and revise tools, interfaces, skills, memory, and decision rules.
Across multiple benchmarks and four base models, it reports substantial accuracy gains on ViewSpatial and MMSI.
Provides a unified approach for deriving answers from spatial evidence rather than simply increasing tool calls.

papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Weiming Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Fixed latent horizons can hurt performance because later reasoning may reorganize candidates and weaken support for the correct answer.
Latent CoT progresses through stages: early steps form frontier reasoning states, while later steps may provide diminishing or negative benefits.
The work characterizes progress using realized constructive progress and remaining constructive progress.
A lightweight estimator adaptively adjusts the inference horizon without retraining the language model.
Across multiple arithmetic benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points and reduces latent computation by up to 29.0%.

papers.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Guoyao Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Role information may be internally represented without reliably constraining the model’s outputs.

Causal analysis links role-span contributions to response structure, content selection, and factual-value decisions.
Role-consistent outputs require adequate role-span support at key decisions; increasing this support can reverse failures.
The framework attributes ICL and OOC hallucination to how effectively functional-role contributions remain active across output decisions.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
papers.tldr: A unified mechanistic analysis explains why in-context learning can follow contextual rules while models still produce out-of-context hallucinations.

papers.abstract: People often understand the world by comparing different views of it. Vision-language models (VLMs), however, receive these views as separate images and still struggle to relate them. One problem is data. Training on these tasks requires groups of images with a known relationship: the same object from different viewpoints, or the same scene before and after a change. Such examples are hard to collect at scale from existing photo collections. We introduce ReSynth, which turns single-image perception and controllable image generation into cross-image relational supervision. Localized editing produces before-and-after pairs, viewpoint generation produces multiple views of the same instance, and verified scene contents support comparisons of counts and attributes. ReSynth combines Qwen3-VL-8B's captioning, grounding, and counting capabilities with Qwen-Image-2.1's generation and editing capabilities. It verifies single-image facts such as object counts and attributes, then combines these facts to construct multi-image QA. Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xin Yu, Xinyi Guo, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of scalable training data for cross-image relationships such as viewpoint changes and before/after differences.
Uses localized editing, viewpoint generation, and verified scene content to construct multi-image question-answer pairs.

papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

bullets: Targets the limitations of static RAN slicing for dynamic semantic representations in split neural networks.
Uses dynamic neural compression with adaptive “box” quantization to balance communication payload, computation, and robustness to transmission errors.
Formulates device-side accuracy optimization and edge-server max–min accuracy resource allocation under QoS, queue-stability, and capacity constraints.
Applies causal contextual multi-armed bandits with Lyapunov control at devices and block coordinate descent at edge servers.
Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, reduces QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while improving the accuracy–violation trade-off.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST1.0, a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST1.0 predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot-object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST1.0 revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation.
authors: Hao Chen, Xuheng Zhang, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Shaobo Zhang, Jialin Gao, Zhonghao Yan, Di Wu, Sixiang Chen, Peng Jia, Chi-Wing Fu, Shanghang Zhang, Pheng-Ann Heng

papers.abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

papers.abstract: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) grasp the overall content of an image but often miss the fine details a question hinges on, such as a small object in a large photo or a number in a dense infographic. Yet even when their answer is wrong, the region they point to often contains the evidence. We introduce Self-Elicited Evidence (SEE), a training-free method that lets a frozen VLM look again where it points. When the initial answer has low confidence, SEE prompts the model to propose regions where the details may appear, answers the question on these enlarged crops, and aggregates the answers with the original prediction through confidence-weighted voting. The model also answers with its own transcript, which helps on text-rich images. SEE needs no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones, SEE improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and outperforms five training-free baselines on small objects. With SEE, Qwen3.5-4B surpasses the direct answer of Qwen3.5-9B and matches the 6 times larger Qwen3.5-27B.
authors: Alin-Ionut Popa, Tuo Zhang, Dimitrios Dimitriadis
bullets: Addresses VLMs missing small objects, numbers, and other details despite often localizing relevant evidence.
Uses a training-free, detector- and OCR-free pipeline triggered by low-confidence answers.
The VLM proposes likely evidence regions, answers from enlarged crops and its own transcript, then performs confidence-weighted voting.
Improves small-object benchmarks by 2.3–13.1 points across five backbones and beats five training-free baselines.
Enables Qwen3.5-4B to surpass Qwen3.5-9B’s direct answers and match the 6× larger Qwen3.5-27B.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.
authors: Xin Zhang, Shiqi Zhang, Siyuan Cao, Juncheng Cai, Yedong Shen, Yuxuan Gao, Dianlong Wen, Kaixue Long, Lu Zhang, Yao Li, Jiajun Deng, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and visually ambiguous contact states that make local geometry and object relations difficult to infer from vision alone.
Builds a shared robot-base-frame visuo-tactile representation from RGB-D points, dense five-finger tactile measurements, taxel locations, and force vectors.
Adds hand-object and object-object relations from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces to guide contact adjustment and object alignment.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with a UR7e and XHand, improving average success by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and 20 points over the strongest alternative.
Ablations show complementary benefits from scene geometry, spatial tactile feedback, shared spatial grounding, and explicit geometric relations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of 3DTouch. Separate encoders produce scene tokens and finger-level tactile tokens. (b) Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) aligns reference object meshes using estimated poses and encodes relative displacements and distances between hand landmarks and nearby object surface points, and between representative regions of interacting objects, into hand–object (HO) and object–object (OO) tokens. The scene, tactile, and relation tokens jointly condition the action expert, while the original vision-language pathway and flow-matching objective are preserved.

Compared with the 2D-only VLA shown on the left, 3DTouch augments a pretrained vision-languageaction policy with scene geometry, spatially grounded tactile feedback, and explicit geometric relations. Scene points and tactile measurements are represented in a shared robot-base coordinate frame, while hand–object and object–object relations describe task-relevant geometric configurations. These complementary representations jointly condition action generation, with the bottom panels illustrating five real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and their success-rate comparisons against baselines.

Figure 4. Overview of five contact-rich manipulation tasks performed on the UR7e robot equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. Each column shows the start and end states of a task, with red dashed arrows indicating the intended manipulation motions.

papers.abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang

Designed as a simple baseline; it uses no parameter updates or auxiliary trigger modules.

papers.abstract: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing. In this work, we present MitoWorld, a stochastic world model that generates these future appearances as continuous evolution in a Gaussian reference latent, terminated by a division hazard and converted into images by a conditional diffusion renderer. The ordinary transition provably preserves its Gaussian reference, tying its noise to its dynamics; paired observations identify its discrete transition where stationary marginals cannot. The hazard turns division timing into a survival likelihood that can be tested against real cycle lengths. On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks spanning 17 knockdowns and a control, MitoWorld lowers FID by 34.6\% and the video metric JEDi by 45.6\% relative to the strongest baselines. Its latent-space prediction intervals achieve near-nominal 90\% coverage, are 35\% narrower than those of a model with freely fitted noise. The hazard also yields cell-cycle length distributions with KS distance close to the model-based finite-sample reference. Testable single-cell stochastic dynamics thus offer a generative tool for time-lapse perturbation screens.
authors: Ting Long, Xiaojing Sun, Cheng Han, Zhicheng Ji, Yingnian Wu, Jiebo Luo, Heng Fan, Dongfang Liu
bullets: Addresses the joint prediction of cell appearance trajectories and division timing after gene knockdown.
Uses Gaussian-reference latent dynamics, a division hazard for survival-based timing, and a conditional diffusion renderer for images.
Paired observations identify discrete transitions that stationary marginals cannot, while the hazard supports testing against real cycle lengths.
On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks across 17 knockdowns and a control, it improves FID by 34.6% and JEDi by 45.6% versus the strongest baselines.
Produces near-nominal 90% prediction-interval coverage, narrower intervals, and realistic cell-cycle length distributions.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The pipeline of MitoWorld. (a) trains the encoder to place cell states in a Gaussian reference space (§3.2). (b) freezes the encoder and moves each state with a reference-preserving transition whose operator splits into a contraction Sg and a rotation Kg (§3.3), and a diffusion renderer converts every state into an image (§3.5). (c) uses a division hazard h to determine the survival probability Sk and the division-time distribution. A hazard trigger initiates the terminal transitions, which end the cycle with a two-daughter composite (§3.4).

Figure 1. Cell-cycle prediction. (a) One-step endpoint predictors learn to map control populations to perturbed populations, while video world models synthesize population-level cell dynamics. Neither explicitly models how an individual cell grows or when it divides. (b) From one cell xt under knockdown g, MitoWorld rolls out stochastic latent trajectories, renders every step (faded box), and stops each at a division (red point) sampled from p(Tdiv).
Figure 4. Long-horizon latent dynamics.

papers.abstract: Diverse, semantically synchronized, and low-latency facial expressions are essential for human-robot interaction. While large language models (LLMs) have endowed anthropomorphic robots with fluent speech, facial expression still struggles to follow the conversation. Motivated by this gap, we present Emo-H2A (hidden-to-actuation), a paradigm that drives a facial robot directly from LLM hidden states during autoregressive decoding. Without a separate emotion label, expression stays continuous and context-sensitive, and the face moves with the unfolding reply. We instantiate this paradigm as EmoManifold, a training-free method that extracts a valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) coordinate from each hidden state, projects it, and drives the face at token granularity. The readout is checked on six language models, and the same projection drives our 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) facial robot. When driven by this projection, the face shifts its expression in the matching direction on 87.5% of within-reply valence transitions, whereas holding a single label for the whole reply leaves directional tracking near the 50% chance level, and first moves in 0.96s rather than waiting 10-26s for the reply to finish and a turn-level label to return.
authors: Yige Liu, Jingcheng Huang, Hao Sun, Min Li, Zhouping Yin
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fluent LLM speech and slow, poorly synchronized facial expression in human–robot interaction.
EmoManifold is training-free: it extracts valence-arousal-dominance coordinates from each hidden state and maps them to facial actions.
The same projection operates across six language models and controls a 29-DoF facial robot.
Expression changes follow within-reply valence transitions in 87.5% of cases, versus near-chance directional tracking with one label per reply.
The robot begins moving after 0.96s, avoiding the 10–26s delay of turn-level emotion labeling.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Emo-H2A. (a) Schematic of token-level expression. (b) Overview. Existing pipelines (above) pass the reply through a category label and an expression generator to play one preset [1], [2]. EmoManifold (below) drives the face directly from the token stream as the reply is generated.

Fig. 2. EmoManifold. Online expression driving (top): ht is projected onto VAD; its valence–arousal (VA) components are mapped by a Fuzzy Kohonen Clustering Network (FKCN) into seven-dimensional expression weights, fused with presets to drive the facial actuators. Offline calibration (right): NRC-VAD pole words and the unembedding matrix Wout construct the affective axes once, offline and training-free.

papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/
authors: Yuze Wu, Mo Zhu, Xingxing Li, Yuheng Du, Zhaoqi Wang, Yuxin Fan, Wenjun Li, Kenghou Hoi, Zhichao Han, Xin Zhou, Fei Gao
bullets: Separates multimodal reasoning from low-level control by predicting 3D poses and navigation intentions that are converted into dynamically feasible actions.
Uses an automated 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline to generate scalable, photorealistic UAV navigation data and address data scarcity and domain gaps.
Employs progressive three-stage training for improved grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation.
Adds a memory-aware cognitive agent for long-horizon task decomposition and onboard optimizations such as token sparsification and model lightweighting.
Reports 7.1×–9.4× speedups while maintaining high navigation performance, with improvements demonstrated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$\pi_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.
authors: Tianqi Gong, Haochen Niu, Yusheng Zhao, Lantao Zhang, Haoyu Liu, Rendong Ying, Peilin Liu

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.
authors: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo, Shuaike Shen, Ziwen Wang, Hui Ren, Xianrui Zhong, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the latency and cost of requiring a large model before every vision-language agent action.
A training-free judge scores candidate steps against the current screenshot in one forward pass; accepted drafts avoid invoking the large model.
A 2B draft with Vanguard matches or exceeds its 8B target on web, mobile, and embodied tasks, with especially strong gains on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED.
The large model generates only a minority of steps, enabling more completed closed-loop episodes and faster, more accurate operation with a 27B target.
The calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and Vanguard also composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery. We present ReLoco, a framework that uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn locomotion, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and command resumption within one proprioceptive policy. During training, robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs. Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery, while temporary assistance facilitates exploration. A simulation-based refinement stage supplies robot-executed motion references for this supervision. Ablations examine conditional supervision, output separation, and reference quality under matched settings. At a common training iteration, the full policy achieves $96.80\%$ independent get-up success and $96.96\%$ push-recovery success, including command resumption. Its torso planar velocity root-mean-square error is $0.1266$~m/s, $14.7\%$ lower than the conditional single-output variant, with similar joint-angle discrepancy measured by dynamic time warping. Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong~3.0 humanoid demonstrates walking, running, get-up, and locomotion resumption after falls using one proprioceptive actor, without controller switching or on-robot policy fine-tuning.
authors: Lequn Fu, Yufeng Hu, Yijun Zhong, Jie Zhang, Xiao Li, Lingxiang Ji, Zhiyuan Xu, Jian Tang, Shiqi Li

Robot posture selects the expert motion pool, while a shared discriminator uses separate behavior-specific outputs.
Task rewards, regularization, temporary assistance, and simulation-refined robot motion references support learning and exploration.
The full policy reports 96.80% independent get-up success and 96.96% push-recovery success, including command resumption.
Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong 3.0 demonstrates walking, running, fall recovery, and resumed locomotion.

papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.
authors: Haowei Chen, Yichen Wang, Congfu Xu
bullets: Uses learned nonlinear features and covariance-guided recursive ridge-regression updates to store associations.
Applies a content-dependent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition to control retention and restore uncertainty for future writes.
Has an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and an inference state whose size does not grow with context length.
Associative block maps and explicit adjoints enable parallel training while preserving the recursive update.
Controlled language-modeling experiments report better prediction quality than attention and recurrent baselines, plus stronger associative recall than evaluated recurrent models.

papers.abstract: Exocentric cameras, mounted on walls or ceilings in indoor environments, offer wider vantage points and are less easily occluded than robot-mounted cameras, making them an appealing alternative for perception in robot navigation algorithms. Previous methods that use such cameras, however, require their pose and intrinsics to be known before deployment, demanding calibration that is time-consuming, requires specialized personnel, and must be repeated whenever a camera moves or a new room is navigated. We propose Robot-centric Obstacle Maps from Unknown and uncalibrated eXocentric cameras (ROMUX), an agent that navigates a robot toward point goals while avoiding obstacles using exocentric cameras that are both uncalibrated, meaning the system does not require their pose or intrinsic information as input, and unknown, meaning it is not fit to a specific camera during training and does not require pre-deployment fine-tuning. We train a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images, without conditioning image tokens on camera information. A small policy trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) then navigates on the predicted maps toward a goal coordinate relative to the robot. We benchmark our agent in simulation with cameras randomized per episode, and it matches the success rates of a PPO policy that navigates from a robot-mounted camera. Further, ROMUX works with one camera or multiple cameras with partial views and has been transferred zero-shot to a real robot using a camera at varying positions and orientations across various room layouts.
authors: Raul Steinmetz, Raphael Druon, Yusuke Yoshiyasu, Akihisa Ohya, Ayanori Yorozu
bullets: Addresses the costly calibration and camera-specific adaptation required by prior exocentric-camera navigation methods.
Uses a cross-view transformer to estimate metric, robot-centric obstacle maps without camera pose or intrinsic information.
A PPO policy navigates toward robot-relative point goals using the predicted maps.
In simulation with randomized cameras, ROMUX matches the success rate of a robot-mounted-camera PPO policy.
Supports single or partially overlapping multiple cameras and transfers zero-shot to a real robot across camera placements and room layouts.

papers.abstract: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. GitHub: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sixthview_benchmark
authors: Pooya Khosravi, Jen-Feng Chang, Fnu Pramono
bullets: The task predicts a sixth view from five observed views plus component-shape information, requiring part-placement, occlusion, and coordinate reasoning.
It includes 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2–10 parts and evaluates dense part-label grids using exact-view and cell-level metrics.
The benchmark verifies that every legal assembly consistent with the inputs has the same hidden target view, removing inherent ambiguity.
Across three vision-language models, exact-grid accuracy ranges from 33.2% to 85.4% across evaluated conditions.
Adding exact text geometry substantially improves image-based performance, while adding images to exact text provides little benefit; separate image panels also outperform merged sheets.

papers.abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.
authors: Yu Yuan, Ruizhou Ding, Shaoheng Fang, Stanley H. Chan, Zhuo Chen
bullets: Addresses video evaluators’ difficulty detecting motion defects across physics, smoothness, and dynamics without a reliable verifier.
Uses controlled video edits to create supervision, with a small set of human-labeled videos anchoring judgments to human preferences.
Assigns each quality dimension an LLM agent, while a leader coordinates updates using Nash bargaining to balance competing improvements.
Human-designed curriculum stages guide exam construction, candidate review, and revisions.

Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, it improves motion evaluation, generalizes to unseen defects, and benefits motion generation and data selection; the abstract reports top dynamics scores among 21 tested models.

papers.abstract: Children's book illustrations carry developmental, pedagogical, and cultural responsibilities that are often formally codified in guidelines. As AI systems begin entering children's publishing pipelines, both as evaluators and as generators, a natural question arises: can they reliably meet the structural, safety, and cultural standards required? We investigate this across three criteria: guideline compliance, safety, and cultural alignment, using Indonesia's Book Leveling Guideline as a government-issued evaluation framework with explicit visual criteria for four reading levels. To understand how well VLMs can identify and apply these guideline criteria, we first evaluate them on real published children's book pages and compare their assessments against a human baseline. To then examine whether AI-generated illustrations meet the same standards, we apply the VLM judge to images produced by two generation models and cross-check them against a subset of human illustrator raters. We find that VLMs are reliable on explicit criteria such as compliance and safety, but fall short on cultural alignment, systematically missing content that human raters flag as culturally inappropriate. AI-generated illustrations show the same blind spot: they satisfy structural and safety criteria but fail to capture implicit cultural details that human raters consistently identify.
authors: Rian Adam Rajagede, Rochana Prih Hastuti, Fitri Hasanah Amhar
bullets: Evaluates AI understanding across guideline compliance, safety, and cultural alignment.
Uses Indonesia's Book Leveling Guideline across four reading levels as the evaluation framework.

papers.abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.
authors: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen, Huynh Thi Thanh Binh
bullets: The correctable error is the Bayes gap between the deployed prediction and the Bayes prediction given the modalities that remain; ambiguity itself cannot be removed.
When a more-complete model is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs can estimate the missing-modality Bayes target without retrieval labels.

GUARD leaves the deployed model unchanged, learns when candidate retrieval corrections are useful from deployment-matched labeled data, and calibrates an application threshold with conformal risk control.
Under exchangeability, the probability that an applied correction exceeds a specified loss-increase tolerance is bounded by a preset level.

Across nine frozen model–dataset pairs spanning six domains, correction gains track headroom rather than raw error, and GUARD retains most blanket-correction gains within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

papers.title: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities

papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.
authors: Zhang Ziyue, Juwei Jian, Baiyang Song, Yunshan Zhong, Jun Peng, Yiyi Zhou, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses evidence loss caused by selecting frames before pruning tokens in long videos.
Builds position-matched empirical-null distributions from irrelevant control queries and converts affinities into Monte Carlo p-values.
Combines calibrated screening with a high-recall semantic guard, deduplication, and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation.
Evaluated with frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on video benchmarks without subtitles or audio.
On Video-MME at 64 full-frame equivalents, achieves 65.81% and 68.85%, outperforming evaluated baselines for the respective backbones.

Figure 2. Query-dependent allocation for three questions from one preregistered long video (rows 2289–2291). (a) Deduplicated candidatetoken counts per sampled frame. papers.abstract: Reconstructing hand-object interactions is an important task, and achieving it with a single camera makes large-scale capture practical but challenging due to heavy occlusions. We introduce HOForce to track hands and objects, and further recover interaction forces from single-view RGB-D video and known object properties. For two-hand manipulation, we jointly model fingertip forces of both hands and the contact forces between objects when two objects are presented. The reconstructed forces also improve motion tracking by giving pose constraints in the occluded regions. HOForce recovers hand and object motion more accurately on DexYCB and TACO and produces less hand-object penetration than interaction baselines on DexYCB. On our dataset of fingertip forces recorded with tactile sensors, HOForce reduces normal-force MAE by 24.5% relative to the strongest baseline. The recovered forces reproduce object motion in MuJoCo and transfer to other engines after adaptation.
authors: Jiahui Wang, Wanqing Du, Yuanbin Zou, Zhefeng Xu, Feng Xu
bullets: Targets single-camera hand–object reconstruction, where severe occlusions make motion and force estimation difficult.
Models fingertip forces for both hands and contact forces between objects during two-hand manipulation.
Uses reconstructed forces as pose constraints in occluded regions, reducing hand–object penetration.
Improves motion accuracy on DexYCB and TACO and achieves lower penetration than interaction baselines on DexYCB.
Reduces normal-force MAE by 24.5% versus the strongest baseline on a tactile-sensor dataset; recovered forces reproduce object motion in MuJoCo and transfer to other engines after adaptation.

The remaining motion error guides adjustments to contact locations and hand poses, and the forces are then re-estimated at the updated contacts.

The entry-face normal guides the thumb back toward the side it entered from. (b) Only the middlefinger capsule crosses the wall. The object SDF gradient at b identifies the exit direction.

papers.selection_reason: HOForce reconstructs hand-object interaction forces from single-view RGB-D video. This advances embodied perception and manipulation by recovering physical properties (forces) from visual data.
papers.title: HOForce: Motion and Force Reconstruction of Hand-Object Interaction Using a Single-View RGB-D Video
papers.tldr: HOForce jointly reconstructs hand–object motion and interaction forces from a single-view RGB-D video, using force-based constraints to improve tracking under occlusion.

papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

papers.selection_reason: 3D vision-language grounding benchmark for chest CT; relevant to 3D perception and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Grounding Radiology Reports in 3D Chest CT: Results of the ReXGrounding Challenge
papers.tldr: The ReXGrounding Challenge substantially advanced 3D localization of radiology findings in chest CT, with top models reaching radiologist-level Dice overlap but still struggling with diffuse, multiple, and correctly located findings.

papers.abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. MobileWeave abstracts each app into a typed capability graph with semantic types shared across apps, composes atomic programs into single- and cross-app composite programs through explicit value and object dependencies, and verifies each program by native execution, deriving both its instruction and its completion check from the same program. Trained on teacher trajectories collected for these tasks and on recovery supervision at the policy's own stalls, MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld, with comparable gains at 4B. Beyond these gains, we find that composition is learnable from task structure: explicit dependencies between subgoals act as a training signal that teaches a policy to compose skills it already masters. We release data, model, and code at https://maxxnotmarx.github.io/MobileWeave/ .
authors: Ziyi He, Xian Wu, Qiyuan Chen, Haitao Li, Cehao Yang, Yinghao Zhu, Xichen Zhang, Xiao Chen, Yushi Feng, Lequan Yu
bullets: Targets a limitation of free-form task synthesis: implicit subgoal dependencies can cause agents to complete subtasks individually but fail to chain them.
Represents apps as typed capability graphs and composes atomic programs using explicit value and object dependencies across apps.
Verifies tasks through native execution, deriving both instructions and completion checks from the same executable program.
Training includes teacher trajectories and recovery supervision at policy stalls.
MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld; comparable gains occur at 4B.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MobileWeave. Left: a typed capability graph of entities, semantic types, and operators is extracted from app code and state and grounded in native functions. Middle: atomic programs are woven into composite programs through value and object edges; each program that passes execution and review yields an instruction and a completion check. Right: successful teacher rollouts form the SFT trajectories, and one-step teacher interventions in the policy’s action loops yield the recovery SFT data.

Bottom: MobileWeave composes each task as a program over a typed capability graph of app functions, verifies it by native execution, and only then turns it into an instruction with each dependency fixed by the program and enforced by its completion check. Right: success rates (%) of Qwen3-VL-8B and MobileWeave-8B.

papers.title: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents

papers.abstract: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Shreyans Jain, Apoorva Vashisth, Ankush Gupta, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the need to choose grasps that are both physically feasible and suitable for the downstream task.
Introduces a dataset with 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations across 100,911 image-task pairs and 17 object categories.
Generates task-independent grasp proposals, then uses a language-conditioned re-ranker to jointly evaluate them.
Outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points and is validated on real objects with a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LAGR. Given multimodal visual observations, a task-independent proposal generator extracts fused visual features and predicts physically plausible grasp candidates with associated confidence scores. A language-conditioned re-ranker combines proposal geometry, multi-scale visual features, and task instruction embeddings, then applies a proposal-context transformer to jointly evaluate candidate suitability. The final grasp is selected by combining task-compatibility predictions with physical confidence, without modifying the proposed grasp geometry.
Figure 2. Comparison of representative grasp annotations from existing datasets and LAGR.

Figure 1. Examples of LAGR generating distinct task-specific grasps for the same real-world objects. Functional tasks favor grasps that enable effective tool use, whereas handover tasks favor grasps that leave the handles accessible to the recipient.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison of task-conditioned grasp prediction and grasp stability. SR denotes grasp success rate, IoU denotes intersection-over-union with ground-truth grasp rectangles, and Angle Err. is grasp orientation error. GCR denotes grasp collision rate. † indicates the method was evaluated zero-shot.
Table 2. Ablation studies on the design components of our approach. Accuracy requires IoU ≥ 0.25 and angular error ≤ 30◦. Angle statistics use positive-overlap matches. Best mean results are bold.

Table 3. Real-world task-oriented grasping performance using a Franka Research 3 with a parallel-jaw gripper. Each object is evaluated on two tasks, with ten orientations per task. Results indicate successful grasps out of ten trials per object–task pair.

papers.selection_reason: Language-aware grasp re-ranking for task-oriented grasping; directly fits robot manipulation and vision-language-action.
papers.title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
papers.tldr: LAGR improves task-oriented robotic grasping by re-ranking physically feasible grasp proposals according to language-described task requirements.

papers.abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/
authors: Ghadi Nehme, Dahyun Nam, Akshay Govind Srinivasan, Faez Ahmed
bullets: Agents co-design robots from standard components plus a custom 3D-printed part, with simulated designs physically built and tested.
The benchmark includes 10 obstacles across three difficulty levels and evaluates four frontier coding agents.
Across 16,427 simulations and 135 physical robots, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and discover mechanisms beyond search baselines.
Only 66% of simulated passes transfer to the real world across all levels, and performance drops on harder tasks and universal-robot requirements.
Real-failure videos enable redesigns that sometimes correct the simulator and remove 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic robot co-design with real-world video feedback, directly relevant to embodied robot learning.
papers.title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
papers.tldr: RoboBuilder evaluates coding agents that jointly design robot hardware and software through simulation and real-world video feedback, revealing strong performance on easy tasks but persistent sim-to-real and generalization challenges.

papers.abstract: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.
authors: Jiakun Yan, Shiksha Patel, David Sidler, Gengyu Rao, Brandon Potter, Bradford Beckmann
bullets: Motivation: GPU-initiated communication is increasingly important, but reverse offload to host proxy threads is typically treated as a slower fallback to GPUDirect Async.
Method: KIWI provides a programmable GPU-to-CPU invocation layer and addresses shared-queue contention, polling overhead, and proxy load imbalance.
Contribution: KIWI-P2P offers SHMEM-like communication, while KIWI-EP redesigns mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine operations around workload-specific primitives.
Results: KIWI achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second.
Scope: Reported gains include up to 2.3× lower expert-parallel communication latency on AMD GPUs and up to 29% lower vLLM time per output token.

Fig. 2. Traditional reverse offload versus KIWI. (a) Traditional reverse offload hides the proxy and the NIC behind a fixed device API; all GPU threads share one queue, typically served by a single proxy thread. (b) KIWI exposes a single call, invoke, that runs user-defined callbacks on the CPU. Each wave owns its queue, several proxy threads poll the queues, and callbacks drive the NIC through any host library, such as LCI.

papers.selection_reason: Programmable GPU-to-CPU invocation layer reduces MoE communication latency and vLLM token latency, relevant to efficient AI inference.
papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.tldr: KIWI makes GPU-to-CPU reverse offload a fast, programmable first-class communication path, outperforming GPU-controlled alternatives for several communication and mixture-of-experts workloads.

papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.
authors: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang, Guanbin Li, Wanyi Chen, Weisheng Dong, Guangming Shi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints with static text-conditioned diffusion.
Uses hierarchical scene understanding to align structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence and interpret both object context and global semantics.
Distills MLLM feedback about candidate corrections into a lightweight reward predictor for efficient correction decisions.
Integrates selected object-level corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection during denoising.
On 3D-FRONT, improves functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive quality and diversity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReflectScene. ReflectScene integrates hierarchical scene understanding and MLLM-guided decisions into objectcentric diffusion. At each denoising step, intermediate clean estimates are assessed to select object-level actions, providing transient conditioning, while buffered non-STOP actions are executed every 50 steps to update a persistent correction state. This state is projected onto subsequent clean estimates before DDPM posterior sampling, with decision-effect consistency learning promoting target recovery and non-target preservation.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Across three room types, ReflectScene better preserves prompt-specified furniture arrangements and functional spatial relationships, producing more coherent layouts. Top: rendered scenes; bottom: 3D bounding-box visualizations.
