papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Apoorva Vashisth, Manav Kulshrestha, Damon Conover, Zachary Kingston, Aniket Bera
bullets: Targets performance degradation in long-horizon tasks involving interdependent manipulations.
Uses an execution-aware, VLA-agnostic framework that evaluates motion progress and revises future plans from observed outcomes.
Leaves the underlying VLA policy unchanged and requires no additional fine-tuning.
Improves success rates by 21.9% on RoboCasa365 and 10.4% on CALVIN over the next strongest baseline.
Also demonstrates real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RePlan-VLA. Given a long-horizon language instruction and visually grounded scene observations, the planner decomposes the task into executable short-horizon subtasks, which are sequentially executed by a frozen VLA policy. A separate progress estimator monitors execution at the manipulation-primitive level, detects deviations from the intended subtask, and generates naturallanguage failure feedback. Upon failure, the planner uses the updated scene observations and diagnostic feedback to revise the remaining subtask sequence. The bottom panel illustrates this closed-loop process: after successfully placing a croissant on the cutting board, the robot approaches an incorrect object while retrieving a jam jar. RePlan-VLA detects the mismatch and replans, enabling the robot to recover and complete the remaining manipulation.

Figure 3. Qualitative analysis of failure-conditioned recovery. Three representative manipulation failures and their corresponding recovery sequences. RePlan-VLA uses visual progress monitoring to identify discrepancies between intended and observed execution, generates diagnostic feedback, and revises the remaining plan. The examples illustrate recovery from an incorrect object grasp, restoration of a missing manipulation prerequisite, and completion of previously omitted actions. All three executions ultimately succeed.

Figure 1. RePlan-VLA: Execution-aware replanning for longhorizon robotic manipulation. Given a long-horizon language instruction and scene observations, RePlan-VLA decomposes the task into executable short-horizon subtasks, monitors the robot’s progress and detects discrepancies between intended and observed outcomes. In this real-world rollout, the robot initially fails to place the white block into the bowl. RePlan-VLA identifies the incomplete manipulation and replans to retry the failed subtask before proceeding with the remaining objectives.

papers.abstract: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.
authors: Bin Yin
bullets: The study tests whether continuing to learn state labels helps an agent adapt when interaction cues change their meaning.
A logistic state predictor with online updates was compared with an identical predictor frozen at transfer across ten conditions and six held-out environments.
Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates versus 64.63% when frozen; the adaptive predictor won in all six environments.
A direct policy reached 95.65%, while a contextual bandit reached 94.23% and higher cumulative utility by exploiting reward feedback that revealed the true state.
Development-history-based weights reduced cumulative utility relative to neutral weights, highlighting the effects of weighting and feedback information.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.
authors: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jatin Mitra
bullets: Targets draft models that inherit the large model’s hidden width, creating unnecessary compute and memory cost.
Applies width reduction to DFlash and EAGLE-3, evaluated with Qwen3-8B and GPT-OSS-20B.
For DFlash, the output adapter folds into the target’s vocabulary projection, preserving logits up to floating-point rounding.
End-to-end decoding accelerates by 1.06–1.12× on B200 and 1.13–1.44× on DGX Spark at batch size 1.
Speedups persist at larger batches, reaching up to 1.21× without narrow drafts becoming slower than full-width ones.

papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

papers.abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.
authors: Jiazhe Wang, Tianyi Yang, Ruihang Li, Fan Lu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Lei Yang

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.
authors: Jinbae Seo, Jungin Park, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jiyoung Lee, Kwanghoon Sohn
bullets: Addresses the challenge of expanding a trained agent’s tool space without disrupting previously learned tools.
Separates parameter directions for triggering tool calls from those selecting among tools.
Restricts each new tool’s adapter to calling directions, using orthogonal constraints to protect earlier tool choices.
Converts existing specialist-model annotations into verified multi-turn tool-use trajectories.
Experiments with two agents and three specialist tools improve performance across ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

papers.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.
authors: Yeongtak Oh, Donghyeok Lee, Joonhee Oh, Jaewon Jeong, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: PReMind-Bench evaluates memory access, visual grounding, abstention, hazard response, and their joint success across hazards and personal contexts.
The PReMind framework uses two-phase reinforcement learning with both on-demand and forced memory retrieval.
Existing models often handle personalization or safety in isolation but fail when both are required together.
At 4B, PReMind improves interdependency joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base and also improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention.
Gains persist under forced-call evaluation, a second LLM judge, multiple training seeds, and unseen hazard groups.

papers.abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.
authors: Yanchao Li, Ben Gao, Jiaqing Xie, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang, Yanbo Wang, Xiaohua Xu, Nanqing Dong, Tianfan Fu, Zhongyu Huang
bullets: SVG generation is slow because models require one forward pass per output token.
The authors find SVG speculative-decoding errors are rare and clustered, with accuracy remaining high deeper into drafts than in natural language.
Sightline uses a verification window as long as the drafter’s horizon and a draft tree wide enough to fill it.
Across text-to-SVG, image-to-SVG, compressed SVG, and Lottie JSON tasks, it is the fastest compared decoder in nearly all reported settings.
Longer windows recover rounds that shorter windows truncate; speculative decoding also speeds rendering-based sample selection.

papers.abstract: Tactile feedback helps visual manipulation policies respond to local contact, but changes in tactile observations do not always require corrective motion, and sustained corrections do not always require new tactile features. We introduce TacPilot, a tactile residual framework that separates representation updates from action intervention around a frozen visual policy. TacPilot uses a perception gate to determine when tactile features need refreshing and updates only affected regions while reusing unchanged features. A separate intervention gate determines whether bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals modify the nominal visual action. This separation allows tactile perception and action correction to follow different spatial and temporal demands during manipulation. In offline expert-trajectory replay, local feature reuse reduces encoded regions by 56.4% relative to periodic full encoding, with essentially unchanged action predictions. In an exploratory simulation evaluation spanning two cylinder sizes, TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%). We further validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 equipped with Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.
authors: Yunzhen Zhang, Yuxiao Zhu, Jie Yang, Yufeng Miao, Bing Luo
bullets: Avoids unnecessary tactile updates and corrective motions during contact-rich manipulation.
Uses a perception gate for selective local feature refresh and an intervention gate for bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals.
Reuses unchanged tactile features, reducing encoded regions by 56.4% with essentially unchanged action predictions in offline replay.
Achieves 26/30 successes (86.7%) in simulation across two cylinder sizes and is validated on OpenArm v2 across four manipulation tasks.
Scope: evaluations cover limited simulated object sizes and four real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
authors: Jinhao Zhang, Yushen Zuo, Ke Rui, Weitao Zhou, Haibao Yu, Honglong Tian, Xiaoheng Ma, Jie Mei, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li
bullets: Addresses WAMs’ limited open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning.
Uses a learnable embedding to exchange intent information between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images.
Introduces a two-stage training strategy for effective joint optimization and collaboration.
Reports leading performance across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro, and improved long-horizon planning on RoboCasa365.
Real-world experiments support the method’s practical effectiveness.

papers.abstract: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.
authors: Yang Li, Ziju Han, Aming WU, Zihao Zhang, Sijia Zhang, Yahong Han, Qinghua Hu
bullets: Targets efficient search for multiple objects in unseen environments without task-specific training.
Diagnoses failed searches, requests additional views when observations are insufficient, and generates targeted navigation revisions.
Links later search outcomes to the rules behind revisions, updating diagnosis, observation, and revision planning.
Carries accepted program updates and spatial memory across goals so experience improves future searches.
Benchmark and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate its effectiveness.

papers.abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
authors: Ahmad AliAhmad, Khemraj Shukla
bullets: Hessian eigenvalue magnitude alone does not reliably identify the directions used by optimization.
The dominant aligned subspace (DAS) selects Hessian eigendirections by their alignment with the gradient.
PINNs provide a challenging testbed because parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic operators create anisotropic, ill-conditioned losses.
Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers problems, DAS-restricted line-search training matches full-space training.
The analysis also examines Gauss–Newton structure within DAS and motivates subspace-aware optimizers.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Zhang, Bing Hu, Guangmin Song, Chenyi Zhang, Li Wang
bullets: Problem: KV-cache pruning lets growing reasoning tokens evict image tokens, causing larger accuracy losses in later conversational turns.
Method: Keep all visual entries in CPU memory and dynamically swap query-relevant visual entries into slots occupied by low-scoring text entries.
Training-free and compatible with existing retention policies, including DBTrimKV.
Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV improves DBTrimKV by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points when DBTrimKV has twice the memory.
It outperforms a fixed visual reserve in conversational settings without reducing standalone-question accuracy.

papers.abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.
authors: Jianhuan Mao, Mengxiao Zhu, Yue Pei, Lei Li, Haogang Zhu
bullets: Evaluates reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detection under controlled test-time adaptation.

Reduced reconstruction objectives do not consistently translate into better anomaly ranking.
The observed failure patterns persist across practical adaptation variants and modest label perturbations.

papers.abstract: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at https://2490o.github.io/CoCR.
authors: Zihao Zhang, Aming Wu, Yang Li, Yahong Han
bullets: 3D intent grounding must localize objects from abstract, non-descriptive language, which is harder than conventional visual grounding.
CoCR decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, forming an intent–function–object reasoning chain.
A functional dependency graph models requirement–attribute relationships, while causal-visual alignment connects functional reasoning with 3D geometric and semantic features.
Bidirectional verification links structured functional reasoning with visual evidence for more interpretable and robust localization.
Experiments on 3D intention and visual grounding show improved intent-aware object localization; the abstract gives no specific numerical results.

The graph is iteratively updated via causal–visual feature alignment and causal pruning. Finally, causal reasoning is conducted based on the updated graph to achieve object selection and localization.

papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.
authors: Rui Li, Liyang He, Zheng Zhang, Zhenya Huang, Qi Liu
bullets: Targets the high cost and latency of invoking a large System-2 model at every agent step.
Mines decision points from human-authored procedural skills rather than requiring workflow-specific hooks.
Trains a calibrated 4B pointer model on execution-grounded states, with System-2 fallback for low-confidence decisions.
Across three unseen benchmarks and multiple System-2 families, reduces episode cost by 75–91% and model-call time by 63–92%.
Supports zero-shot transfer of confidence thresholds while maintaining performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.
authors: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu, Jianguo Li, Yu Zhang
bullets: Replacement-only editing struggles with missing or extra tokens and errors spanning many positions.

On LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED improves average benchmark scores under confidence-guided and confidence-free decoding, and is more robust to large block sizes.
LED also achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, indicating greater generation diversity.

papers.abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning. We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.
authors: Chenxi Han, Ruby, Epoch, Orion, Luke, Bin, Dusk, Lyra, Cal, Alvin, Hubert, Alex, Jiahe Han, Tao Zhang, Hang Liu, Shoujie Li, Yizhe Li, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu, Guoping Pan, Yi Cheng

papers.abstract: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.
authors: Jinqian Chen, Jihua Zhu, Chang Liu
bullets: Problem: Leading-singular-value truncation can poorly preserve a client’s task-relevant responses, even at the same rank.
Method: RASA performs receiver-aware subspace adaptation using diagonal input second moments and uncentered PCA of weighted update responses.
Guarantee: Its rank-constrained readout is globally optimal for the receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric.
Additional technique: Spectral-reference aggregation removes personalized initialization offsets while retaining locally learned increments.

Results: Across DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI, RASA improves accuracy by 3.23 points with FlexLoRA and gains up to 8.33 ROUGE-L on seen and 4.37 on unseen SuperNI tasks, with modest overhead.

papers.abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.
authors: Gaoxiang Linghu, Haonan Zhou, Xuanhe Liu, Weili Xu, Kaiyue Zhou, Jun Xiao, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when updating 3D Gaussian fields with new observations.
Attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies to contributing Gaussians for primitive-level adaptation.
Uses per-Gaussian learning weights to balance current evidence with cross-state reliability.
The weights control both parameter updates and optimizer-memory refresh, renewing reliability over time.
Improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline across CL-Splats, WAT, and CL-3D; performs best on changed and unchanged views in CL-3D.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Framework of GAUSSLEARNER. Each Gaussian acts as a stateful continual learner with scene parameters and cross-state reliability. At each scene state, pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations are attributed to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a per-Gaussian learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both parameter adaptation and optimizer-memory refresh. Cross-state reliability is updated at state boundaries using resolved pressure and final support. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating continual learners.

Figure 2. Comparison of 3D Gaussian continual learning paradigms. (a) Existing methods treat Gaussians as update targets. Replay and regularization may retain obsolete content or hinder adaptation, while selective local optimization can propagate 2D detection errors into 3D updates. (b) GAUSSLEARNER instead views each Gaussian primitive as a continual learner equipped with a closed learning loop.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparisons on CL-3D. From top to bottom are ClubRoom, Fridge, OfficeHub, and StudyNook. GAUSSLEARNER adapts to revised content while preserving still-valid regions, with less forgetting and fewer reconstruction artifacts.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparisons on WAT and CL-Splats. From top to bottom are Grill, Car, Cupboard, and Desk. Red boxes and enlarged crops highlight how GAUSSLEARNER incorporates revised scene content while preserving surrounding content that remains valid.
Figure 7. Within-state self-regulation. Mean pressure P and learning weight W over normalized update progress. Shading denotes standard error.

papers.title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
authors: Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
bullets: Addresses unreliable decisions when policies must retrieve relevant information from long, redundant observation histories.
Uses Recall-Relocalization to connect episodic memories to the current view through a small number of recall slots.
Converts recall slots into Gaussian source components via Recall Anchors, guiding flow-policy generation toward intended actions.
The transport network completes actions from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.
Reports 80.4% average success on MIKASA-Robo, with gains of 20.3 and 18.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline on simulated and real-robot task suites, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RecallFlow. The present observation is encoded into tokens Zt. Recall–Relocalization lets Zt read the episodic memory bank and decodes K recall slots, each attending to the current view through a heatmap Hk. Recall Anchors turns each slot into a Gaussian anchor in action space; with a standard Gaussian, the anchors form the source p0. A transport network conditioned only on Zt carries x0 ∼ p0 to the action chunk, so memory reaches the action solely through the source.

Figure 3. Evaluation tasks in simulation. (a) RecallSuite consists of five memory-dependent tasks: the cue is seen only earlier in the episode, and the candidates look identical when the robot must decide. (b), (c) Tasks from MIKASA-Robo and RoboMimic.

Figure 6. Real-robot experiments. (a) We deploy the policies on an xArm 7 with a wrist camera and a third-person camera. (b) We design four tasks that differ in what must be remembered. (c) RecallFlow achieves the highest success rate on all four tasks. (d) The three behaviors observed on No Repeat: repeating one cup, touching one cup twice, and touching each cup once.

Figure 5. Memory decides where generation starts. (a) At a decision of a NOREPEAT episode, all thirty samples of RecallFlow head to the untouched container from the source on, whereas long-history DP starts from noise and commits only in its last generation steps. (b) Over 15 decisions, the source samples of RecallFlow are already at the target. (c) RecallFlow therefore keeps its success rate with a single generation step.

Figure 1. Start from what you remember. In memory-dependent manipulation, the evidence that decides which action to take (cue) disappears before the robot acts (now). (a) Feeding the memory to the policy as a condition still starts generation from uninformed noise. (b) RecallFlow starts generation from what it remembers: the episodic memory is the source, and the transport network sees only the present.

Figure 4. Effect of memory load, tasks without memory, and inference cost. (a) On RecallSuite, RecallFlow matches long-history DP when one item must be remembered and stays ahead of all baselines when several must be. (b) On RoboMimic, where memory is not needed, adding a long history lowers DP, whereas RecallFlow stays on par with its memoryless counterpart FM. (c) RecallFlow reaches the highest success rate on RecallSuite at nearly the inference cost of a memoryless policy. †Reported in [15].

Table 2. Comparison with published methods on MIKASARobo [8]. We report the success rate (%) on ShellGameTouch (SGT), InterceptMedium (IM), and RememberColor with 3, 5, and 9 colors (RC3–RC9). RecallFlow, averaged over three seeds, achieves the highest average (80.4 ± 1.1). ∗Available only on arXiv. ‡OpenVLA-OFT in [50].

papers.selection_reason: Episodic memory as source distribution for generative robot policies; combines manipulation learning with embodied memory.
papers.title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
papers.tldr: RecallFlow improves memory-dependent robot manipulation by using episodic memory to initialize action generation near remembered targets instead of starting from uninformed noise.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.
authors: Zecheng Hao, Zihan Huang, Shenghao Xie, Jiyuan Zhang, Zhaofei Yu, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant computation from fixed, uniform firing patterns in spiking vision transformers.
Uses attention-guided AdaE-IF routing to assign fine-grained firing to salient regions and coarse firing elsewhere.
Adds S-GSA and S-LGU for selective spike emission at token and channel granularity.
Trains routing and firing precision with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum.
On ImageNet-1k, reports 1.02–2.45 mJ per image and a 32×–72× accuracy-per-energy ratio.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Architecture of AdaS-ViT. Top: the macro pipeline stacks dual-mode AdaS-Blocks (S-GSA followed by S-LGU or S-FFN) over progressively downsampled token maps. Bottom: data flow of S-GSA, S-LGU and the parameterized S-FFN variants (I)(II) with convolution kernel size k and expansion ratio r.

Figure 4. Fine-grained energy breakdown of AdaS-ViT Large on ImageNet-1k. Module-level (a)–(c) and Operator-level (d)–(f) statistics of SOPs and average spike firing rates. For each block, Bar hues identify the module family, the total height of a bar denotes the theoretical SOPs Upper-bound while its dark lower segment denotes the actually incurred SOPs, the curve on the right axis reports the average firing rate.

Figure 1. AdaS-ViT establishes a compelling accuracy-energy frontier for spiking vision transformers. (a) Qualitative comparison of training paradigms over six axes covering training cost and inference behavior: prior paradigms trade these objectives against one another, whereas our test-time adaptive routing maintains a uniformly strong profile across all of them. (b) Quantitative comparison with prior SNN-based works on ImageNet-1k. The horizontal axis denotes top-1 accuracy and the vertical axis reports Ratio AE, i.e., the accuracy delivered per millijoule of inference energy. AdaS-ViT occupies the top-right region alone with the smallest bubble area, indicating markedly higher energy efficiency at a fraction of the parameters of prior art.

Figure 2. AdaE-IF: from uniform to adaptive and efficient spike firing. Top-left: the firing-rate curve of a vanilla IF/LIF neuron is ideally a uniform staircase, yet diverse input current patterns {Ilt} yield divergent firing rates F̃l 1:T for identical average input current Ĩl1:T , which accumulate across layers into conversion error and spatio-temporal gradient inconsistency. Bottom: AdaE-IF maps each spike firing pattern to its bit-granular equivalent, aligning training gradients and enabling precise regulation of Synaptic Operations (SOPs); guided by the attention score of the spiking feature map (Middle), it routes each token to a coarse-grained pattern that preserves energy efficiency, or a fine-grained pattern that enhances representation at only marginal extra cost; jointly scheduled under an ultra-low energy budget (Top-right), the two modes realize test-time adaptive firing precision.

Table 1. Comparison of representative SNN approaches across learning paradigms and network architectures on ImageNet-1k. Here T denotes the inference time-steps, Energy is the estimated inference energy per image, computed following the convention of [54]. Ratio AE quantifies the accuracy delivered per unit of energy cost, where a higher value indicates better energy efficiency.
Table 2. Generalization across data scales and modalities: comparison with prior SNN learning methods on static (CIFAR-10, CIFAR100) and neuromorphic (CIFAR10-DVS) benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time adaptive token routing in spiking vision transformers to suppress computational redundancy, fitting efficient AI and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: AdaS-ViT: Test-Time Adaptive Routing for Spiking Vision Transformers with Ultra-High Energy Efficiency
papers.tldr: AdaS-ViT adaptively routes spiking tokens across temporal, spatial, and channel dimensions to maintain competitive vision performance with very low inference energy.

papers.abstract: Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. GTA then populates the assembled environments with dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion are guided by the scene, yielding realized 4D worlds. Project page: https://zt-zeng-tao.github.io/GTA/
authors: Zeng Tao, Yunuo Chen, Xiang Feng, Yumeng He, Peihao Li, Nanxiang Jiang, Yaowei Guo, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Represents every unit in an adaptive scene hierarchy as a composable, self-contained holon.
Uses parallel agents for recursive top-down planning and bottom-up asset assembly and refinement.
Propagates scene-wide requirements through uniform interfaces to coordinate local construction.
Targets scalable world modeling under limited time and context budgets while maintaining structured layouts and fine-grained details.
Adds scene-guided human characters with coordinated appearance and motion to produce realized 4D worlds.

papers.abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.
authors: Abdiaziz Muse, Jiju Poovvancheri
bullets: The study probes 15 functional attributes across elements in 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings, holding out entire buildings for evaluation.
Models are compared using a shared linear readout, including hand-crafted descriptors, supervised point networks, frozen pretrained transformers, and random-weight controls.
From-scratch networks do not clearly beat descriptors, which reach 0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements.
Frozen Utonia reaches 0.732 mAP, with its gain over matched random-weight controls attributed to pretraining.
Pretrained features improve as labeled buildings increase; in tested settings, fine-tuning reduces their advantage.

Top: Google Street View (© Google), used to verify the labels; A has an opening sash. Bottom: the same windows in the LiDAR scan. (c) P (operable): the predicted probability that A (red) and B (blue) are operable, from a linear layer on each feature source.

papers.selection_reason: Probes whether 3D point representations and pretrained 3D models encode architectural function, relevant to 3D perception and foundation-model evaluation.
papers.title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
papers.tldr: Frozen self-supervised 3D point features encode architectural function better than hand-crafted descriptors or models trained from scratch, especially with limited labeled buildings.

papers.abstract: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs.
authors: Yangang Ren, Di Zeng, Jun Li, Zirui Li, Chengjiang Zhang, Xiaoqing Ye, Ji Tao, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses late or unnecessary human interventions that can make direct imitation unsafe or overly conservative.
Generates candidate trajectories by augmenting model plans and shifting human corrections earlier.
Uses a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer trained from expert demonstrations and unpaired takeover preferences to select better targets.
Distills selected targets into the existing driving model while preserving original targets during normal driving.
Closed-loop tests on reconstructed real-world scenarios show the highest overall success rate versus the deployed model, direct imitation, and trajectory post-optimization.

papers.abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing editable parameters and error signals for effective weight editing.

Evaluated on 22 scientific tasks with DeepSeek and Claude; reported gains include lower error on Burgers, DIODE, and other spatial prediction tasks.
Scope: improvements depend on the feedback-driven editing plans and the evaluated scientific tasks.

papers.abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.
authors: Sirisilp Kongsilp
bullets: Studies Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B models with nightly LoRA updates across long-running WebShop and τ²-bench tasks.
Compares oracle outcomes, user verdicts, and model judgments with separate feedback-sensing judges.
Self-judging initially improves performance but later decays; some feedback judges collapse quickly.
A discernment-based judge stayed near oracle performance for two weeks in most tested lives, then declined to self-judging levels by day 60.
Across 97 lives, the fraction of failed lessons strongly predicted outcomes (Spearman ρ = −0.81); user learning struggled when users could not see results.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.
authors: Keke Tang, Guolin Qiu, Tianyu Hao, Daizong Liu, Yikai Zhang, Peican Zhu, Zhihong Tian

Estimates low-executability directions from kinematic inefficiency and weak dynamic actuation.
Uses these directions to optimize an adversarial patch that degrades command realization and task completion.
Simulation across multiple VLA policies shows greater command–execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks.
Real-robot experiments validate execution degradation on physical platforms.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

bullets: Classifies edge hardware into mid-range GPU/NPU/TPU devices, embedded MPU/SoC processors, and microcontrollers.

Introduces a two-tier hardware-to-model mapping framework with Speed, Balanced, and Accuracy selection matrices.
Proposes design principles including peak-SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm–compiler co-design.
Identifies toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility as key challenges.

papers.abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.
authors: Jaehyun Kim, Wonseok Kang, Jeongmin Lee, Tae-Wan Kim
bullets: Compares eight learned 3D models with geometric estimation across five test sets, varying reference counts, pose components, and reference inputs.

With two references, geometric estimation plus one additional reference is more accurate at fine pose thresholds than every tested model on Cambridge and NAVER B1, and is never significantly worse as a fallback.
With three references, the better approach depends on the scene; translation magnitude helps most when references are spread out rather than top-ranked retrieved images.
At NAVER Gangnam Station, retrieval from multiple locations causes models to fail at different stages; robust alignment narrows Pi3X and MapAnything’s gap to adding references.
Controlled tests show alignment restores several models’ performance, but not Depth Anything 3; pose-conditioned Pi3X additionally requires masking distant poses during input-pose normalization.

papers.tldr: Geometric localization can outperform learned 3D models with fewer references, while learned pose cues help mainly when references are selected appropriately and model inputs are well aligned.

papers.abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.
authors: Dongkeun Lee, Wonjun Lee
bullets: Targets the memory and deployment challenges of sparsely activated MoE VLMs on edge devices.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficient on-device inference of MoE vision-language models via mixed-precision quantization and memory reduction.
papers.title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: MoMoVL compresses on-device MoE vision-language models by assigning expert bit-widths according to both expert activity and modality-specific sensitivity.

papers.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
authors: Johannes Mootz, Mani Amani, Reza Akhavian
bullets: Latent safety filters may reject many safe actions even when calibrated to accept unsafe actions only rarely.
The proposed overlap groups similar latents and actions into cells and measures the share of safe transitions in cells containing both safe and unsafe outcomes.
The overlap is proven to be the minimum fraction of safe transitions any cell-level filter must reject to accept no unsafe transitions in the data.
The framework applies to arbitrary latents and compares safety prediction via a classifier, the world model, or a separate encoder.
In visual navigation, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, rejects the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a conservatism measure for latent safety filters in world models and evaluates it in visual navigation, relevant to world models and embodied navigation safety.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
authors: Artur Kuramshin, Charlotte Cloutier, Michael Przystupa, Kirsty Ellis, Mohammad S. Akhter, Glen Berseth
bullets: Dexterous manipulation is difficult because most VLA training data targets parallel-jaw grippers, while multi-finger teleoperation data is scarce.
The study combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL) for adapting VLAs to a LEAP hand.
Across five fine-tuning recipes and two simulation tasks, SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-DSRL performance.
Freezing the VLM and tuning only the action expert yields the most steerable policy, including for out-of-distribution placements.
LoRA is reported as the least steerable adaptation approach.

papers.selection_reason: Studies fine-tuning recipes for Vision-Language-Action models on dexterous manipulation, directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
