papers.abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.
authors: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Praneeth Kacham, Rami Al-Rfou, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni
bullets: Builds a two-layer nonlinear memory by placing an activation between two delta-rule linear memories.
Uses chunk-level target propagation to provide hidden-layer targets while retaining efficient unmodified delta-rule kernels.
At matched sizes and training budgets, outperforms KDA across five model sizes on C4 and PG19; C4 perplexity matches or slightly improves on attention.
Its attention hybrid achieves the best perplexity among four tested hybrids, and its largest model reaches 51.84% mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks.
Maintains lower loss than KDA through 20K-token contexts and is substantially faster than tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a nonlinear memory architecture for LLMs using cascaded linear memories and target propagation, directly fitting LLM Memory.
papers.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
papers.tldr: Toaster creates a fast nonlinear recurrent memory by cascading two linear memories with target propagation, achieving stronger language-modeling and long-context results than comparable linear and deep-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: An anatomical pose provides interpretable joint structure, but no fixed set of physical landmarks can fully specify a person's movement. We introduce PRISM, a complementary representation that characterizes repetitive movement using tracked masks and dense optical flow. Torso-relative flow measures intensity, frame-wise mask variation measures spatial extent, signed-flow recurrence estimates frequency, and persistent sliding-window geometry describes the rhythmicity of the movement. Across 1,890 synthetic conditions, the measurements recover controlled speed, amplitude, and frequency while exposing observation limits. An idealized hand-motion experiment demonstrates variation omitted by identical exact COCO-17 trajectories; controlled corruption experiments separately examine measurement sensitivity. Audits of two pose methods on the same data cohort and 36,930 external skeleton clips document incomplete observation and dependence on processing choices. In 1,404 annotated complex stereotypical motor movement bouts from six autistic participants, total flow converges with pose motion, while matched-coordinate examples and repeated-session profiles show differences in intensity, extent, frequency, and rhythmicity within behavior labels. A separate VLM comparison evaluates quantitative frequency estimation, and a profile-conditioned decoder links the measurements to illustrative skeletal movements. PRISM connects numerical profiles to visible examples, providing an interpretable way to compare how the same behavior is expressed beyond its label or event count.
authors: Austin A. MBaye, Savik Kinger, Matthew S. Goodwin
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed anatomical landmarks and behavior labels for representing individual movement styles.
Combines torso-relative optical flow, mask variation, flow recurrence, and sliding-window geometry into quantitative movement profiles.
Synthetic and controlled experiments show the measures recover speed, amplitude, and frequency while revealing observation and processing limits.
Analyses of autistic participants show that people with the same movement label can differ in intensity, spatial extent, frequency, and rhythmicity.
Links numerical profiles to illustrative skeletal movements for interpretable comparison beyond pose trajectories or event counts.

papers.selection_reason: Profiling repetitive motion from video; fits video understanding.
papers.title: PRISM: Profiling and Representation of Individual Stereotypical Motion
papers.tldr: PRISM augments pose tracking with interpretable flow- and mask-based measures to capture how repetitive movements differ in intensity, extent, frequency, and rhythmicity.

papers.abstract: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
authors: Wei Liu, Abrar Anwar, Huihua Zhao, Soha Pouya, Yan Chang
bullets: World-action policies are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise useful for steering.
LoRN uses a small actor to choose directions in a fixed low-rank projection of high-dimensional noise.
A norm-controlled construction keeps steered noise near the typical scale of Gaussian samples.
Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy.
Simulation-trained steering transfers to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks without additional real-world training.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoRN enables low-rank noise steering of large generative robot policies. Existing noise steering methods improve frozen policies by steering the initial noise used to generate an action chunk. However, extending noise steering to the much higher-dimensional outputs of vision-language-action models and world-action models is challenging. Left: LoRN learns a small set of coefficients that selects a noise direction within a fixed low-rank subspace, keeping the actor’s output dimension small regardless of the full noise dimension. Middle: This formulation allows LoRN to steer either action noise or video noise in world-action models. We find that steering the video noise is surprisingly expressive for denoising actions, thus LoRN enables a new way to steer a world-action model’s actions. Right: Mean final success per policy family, averaged over its tasks, for the base policy, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN. Video-noise steering produces large gains on the evaluated world-action models; on action policies, LoRN achieves comparable final success to DSRL while generally improving early-training success (Table 11). The DSRL bars use the same variants as Figure 6, with its full-dimensional form on Cosmos3-Edge.

Figure 7: Action-noise steering across robot policies. Learning curves of LoRN (green), DSRL (gray dashed), and LP-DS (dark gray dash-dotted) on twelve tasks: the mean over five seeds with a band of one standard deviation across seeds. Dotted horizontal lines mark base-policy success. The 𝜋0 tasks use LIBERO and ALOHA, 𝜋0.5 uses YAM, and Diffusion Policy uses Robomimic. Horizontal axes show gradient updates for 𝜋0 and environment steps for the other policies, in millions; several panels end before the full training budgets of Table 4 to show the phase in which the methods separate, so training budgets should be compared within each task. The 𝜋0 and 𝜋0.5 curves are five-evaluation running means of 10- and 16-episode evaluations; the Robomimic curves are raw 200-episode evaluations. Diffusion Policy uses full-rank LoRN (𝑟 = 𝑁 = 28).

Figure 9: LoRN enables stronger steering while maintaining the noise norm. Steering-rule comparisons on Cosmos3-Edge using a rank-32 video projection. Bars show mean success with standard errors over three training seeds; dotted lines mark base-policy success. Increasing the steering strength 𝛼 improves LoRN’s performance, whereas additive steering increases the noise norm and loses task success. The LP-DS adaptation [24] and the PSS-related control [17] retain approximately the original noise norm but yield limited gains. Here, 𝛼 caps the steering strength while 𝛽 sets the LP-DS correction’s target norm limit √ 𝛽𝑁 . The relative noise norms are measured in units of √ 𝑁 . Both use our adaptations of the published steering rules within the shared setup, rather than reproductions of the complete methods.

Figure 6: Video-noise steering improves success across world-action models. Base-policy success, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN action- or video-noise steering on RoboLab and LIBERO. DSRL steers all 256 action-noise entries on Cosmos3-Edge, the stronger of its two forms there (Table 7); on DreamZero-14B it tiles a 32-dimensional latent over the chunk, and on DreamZero-5B it replaces the action noise with its latent. Bars show means; error bars show standard errors over three training seeds. Base-policy references have no training-seed error bars. Labels round means to whole percentages. Video steering achieves the highest mean on nine of ten model–task pairs; DSRL performs best on DreamZero-5B Moka pot. Evaluation protocols and retained training budgets differ across models and some configurations; see the appendix.

papers.selection_reason: Noise steering for generative robot policies; improves policy learning and transfer.
papers.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
papers.tldr: LoRN enables scalable reinforcement-learning-based noise steering for generative robot policies, substantially improving simulated and real-world task success without changing policy weights.

papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng, Alper Yilmaz
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen planners to notice when executed actions differ from commands.
Runs the world model in reverse to score hypothesized actuation shifts against actual observations.
The shift-specific score separates actuator shifts from the model’s intrinsic prediction error and supports locally optimal detection, estimation, and source identification.
Self-correction improves success on PushT and Cube tasks and reduces real-robot reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm.
Scope: evaluation covers simulated manipulation tasks and a real robotic arm with sealed or unknown action shifts.

papers.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
papers.tldr: A frozen visual world model can detect, estimate, and correct action-execution errors by comparing observed outcomes with shift-conditioned predictions.

papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.
authors: Shoma Yukawa, Meghna Roychowdhury, Arnab Sanyal, Chengwei Zhou, Shreyas Sen, Gourav Datta
bullets: Treats electrode count as a hardware variable using task-aware montage selection.
Generates only INT8 input regions needed by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization.
Uses halo reuse and memory-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory to reduce data movement.
On a Cortex-M7, achieves 11.38× lower peak SRAM, 2.57× lower latency, and 2.48× lower energy than baseline.
Retains 94–96% of full-montage accuracy using 19 rather than 62 electrodes.

papers.abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.
authors: Avinash Goutham Aluguvelly
bullets: A coding agent repaired rescaled projector rows and noisy vision-encoder weights in SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M without being told where the faults were.
It inferred scale factors, restored many or all affected weights exactly, and recovered accuracy near the original level; generated programs also repaired unseen checkpoints of the same model.
Repair relied on low-order bits preserved by 32-bit fault computation against 16-bit original weights, rather than solely on unchanged model behavior.
Rounding away those bits prevented exact repair, although value distributions and row norms still enabled repair when explicitly mentioned in the prompt.
Swapped rows or columns were not found unaided; the authors recommend reporting weight format and using rounded controls in repair studies.

figures.caption: Figure 1. What the agent reads. Eight weights from the SmolVLM projector, as 32-bit floats, one cell per bit. The two marked weights belong to rescaled rows. Clean weights take only bfloat16 values, so their low 16 bits are zero. A fault computed in float32 fills those bits, and rounding clears them while leaving the rows rescaled. The model gives the same answers to all test questions in both copies, but the agent repairs only the unrounded one (checkpoints A–C; clean accuracy 83.3%).
Figure 3. Fraction codes in one row of the SmolVLM projector (12,288 weights), before and after the row is multiplied by e0.5 and rounded to BF16. The rescaled row leaves 18 codes unused.

Figure 2. The repair task, shown for SmolVLM. A clean, adapted checkpoint is damaged by planted faults. The agent sees only the damaged checkpoint, a few labeled examples, and scores for candidate patches; its final patch is audited against the clean weights. papers.abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.
authors: Sara Amar
bullets: Four LLM agents manage companies in a rule-constrained serial supply chain with logged violations and a public message board.
The testbed jointly measures bullwhip effects, rule adherence, and attempts to collude under disruption and baseline conditions.
In the pilot, agents amplified variability substantially, often through batched ordering; rule violations and side-payment proposals were rare.
API failures were silently recorded as no-order actions, and identical seeds produced bullwhip differences of up to 17× across reruns.
The study recommends stronger reporting practices and provides public code, prompts, and decision logs.

papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.
authors: Yi-Cheng Lai, Hen-Hsen Huang
bullets: Uses timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes across 3,629 questions and six models.
The Verify prompt increases adoption of false answers on pre-cutoff events in all five tested models, often displacing previously correct answers.
On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini shows increased false-answer adoption; passage priority alone raises adoption, while adding checking lowers it.
Adversarial-Aware restores 82.5–98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with less than one percentage point change in true-passage accuracy.
The framework supports reproducible evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.
authors: Jebacyril Arockiaraj, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between incoming data rates and gradient-based training speed in online continual learning.
Accumulates feature statistics from every minibatch through a fast analytic path while a slow path periodically updates the backbone.
Adapts slow-path sample counts to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning.
Uses feature alignment to compensate for drift in accumulated classifier statistics.

Improves online accuracy by 9.67 percentage points on average over the strongest gradient-based baselines across four datasets and three budgets, with gains up to 4.00 points over analytic learning on CIFAR-C.

papers.abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.
authors: Maxx Richard Rahman, Wolfgang Maass
bullets: Addresses failures of transductive adaptation caused by independently estimating each class from sparse or absent samples.
Represents adapted prototypes as text anchors plus graph-pooled displacement fields with a Gaussian Markov random field prior.
Uses an explicit class-presence model and closed-form, gradient-free inference on cached features.
Absent-class prototypes become harmonic extensions of present classes; pooling strength is selected via empirical Bayes.
Improves over zero-shot models across eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, and outperforms anchor-based transduction when few classes are present.

papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
authors: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
bullets: Targets dynamic enterprise environments where models, workflows, and cost requirements change over time.
Uses self- or teacher-model failure attribution to create corrective micro-memories, consolidate them into macro rules, and retain updates only when held-out accuracy improves.
Evaluated across 14 SOP-Bench and τ²-Bench workflow domains with 5 models.
ARISE-Teacher improves baseline accuracy by 10.9 percentage points on SOP-Bench and 5.8 points on τ²-Bench; ARISE-Self gains 10.0 points on SOP-Bench.
ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost.

papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving memory architecture for LLM agents, directly relevant to LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.tldr: ARISE improves enterprise-agent accuracy and efficiency by turning failures into validated, retrievable memory and rules without changing model weights, tools, or workflows.

papers.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.
authors: Nidhi Parayil, Benjamin Greenland, Thierry Peynot, Chris Lehnert
bullets: Addresses contact-rich agricultural tasks where foliage blocks vision and contact observations are intermittent.
Uses a tactile-conditioned diffusion policy with tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback.
Supports passage through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around stems, and manipulation of blocking branches.
Achieved 95% branch-manoeuvring success and 87.5% zero-shot success on unseen tomato and lime plants across reported trials.
Outperformed tactile and reactive baselines and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned policy failed.

papers.abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.
authors: Pengju Liu, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Frozen DINO and V-JEPA feature distances poorly reflect object-to-goal distance, with rank correlation at most 0.11 versus 0.87 for object-mask centroids.
The learned representation reduces interference from background and robot-arm patches by separating object identity, spatial displacement, and dynamics.
DOCK uses forward kinematics from joint angles as annotation-free supervision for grasped-object motion.
In 21 simulated kitchen tasks, DOCK places the object in 15 tasks, matching an oracle using true object position and outperforming mask geometry (10) and frozen features (9).
Its task ranking transfers to unseen layouts, object instances, and categories, including scenes where an unseen robot arm is visible.

papers.abstract: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force ($R^2$ = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach $R^2$ = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.
authors: Md Rakibul Islam Prince, John Pelan, Zhiyuan Zhang, Adyaa Khera, Katherine Pesetski, Adeesh Desai, Akimizu Sugiyama, Minwoo Ki, Benjamin Alan Capelle, Temitope Ibrahim Amosa, Zijie Xu, Yihan Huang, Taehun Chung, Long Wang, Wei Li, Shaoting Lin, Yu She
bullets: Uses digital RGBC light sensors beneath interchangeable silicone gel cartridges to infer indentation and shear without cameras, magnets, or bump overlays.
The approximately 3.5-mm-thick array is flexible, scalable, and built from off-the-shelf components.
Normal-force sensing is highly linear, while per-taxel models estimate three-axis forces and shear direction across held-out sessions.
Adding LuxTac pressure sensing substantially improves peg-in-hole success for an Action Chunking Transformer over vision alone.
Design files, code, and videos are publicly available; results are demonstrated within the tested force range, cartridges, and robot-learning task.

papers.abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.
authors: Xinyang Li, Chih-Hsuan Yang, Xiaolong Ma, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Vikram Vasudevan, Rajeev Thakur, Feng Yan
bullets: The system skips a helper’s text or latent KV-cache message only when it certifies, with high probability, that no more than 5% of answers will change; otherwise it communicates.
Whether skipping is safe depends on how often and predictably a message changes answers—not on the helper’s accuracy.
On four settings where text messages helped, policies skipped 59–80% of messages while retaining an estimated 76–95% of the gain.
Prospective tests skipped 39.9% of verifier messages while retaining 12.55 of 12.80 points of gain, and skipped 68.4% of 32B-helper messages while retaining the full gain.
Safety and efficiency differ: text skipping saved hundreds of milliseconds per query at batch size one, whereas KV-cache savings were much smaller; certification extended to SQuAD but not GSM8K.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanisms for LLM agents to skip messages safely to reduce latency, a relevant optimization for agent efficiency.
papers.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
papers.tldr: A confidence-based finite-sample test lets LLM agents safely skip many helper messages, preserving most answer improvements while reducing latency when skipping is worthwhile.

papers.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $\Phi$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $\Phi$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $\Phi$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.
authors: Iv\'an L\'opez-Broce\~no, Maximilian St\"olzle, Daniel Feliu-Talegon, Daniela Rus, Cosimo Della Santina
bullets: Targets the limitation of deformation models that ignore dynamic and mechanical effects, especially for stiff, heavy, or fast-moving objects.
Combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network with a learned affine mapping from observed DLO positions to latent coordinates.
Its Lagrangian structure provides explicit energy expressions and supports a model-based PD controller with closed-loop stability and convergence guarantees.
Across simulated and real bimanual experiments, the approach improves prediction efficiency and substantially reduces endpoint regulation error versus model-free PD control.
The evaluation covers four simulated DLOs and one real robotic setup; broader conditions beyond these experiments are not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: VGGT reconstructs cameras and geometry from unposed images in one pass, but its global attention grows quadratically with the number of views. Training-free accelerators thin this attention and work well on redundant video, but lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry. This paper traces these losses to two kinds of cross-view information that a uniform sparse approximation can fail to preserve together: diffuse layers aggregate distributed context, whereas matching layers depend on query-specific interactions that carry little attention mass. A per-layer statistic measures the log-mass missed by a mean token. Its row-free proxy is the logit variance, and it selects the estimator for each layer. Diffuse layers use shared, importance-sampled hub keys, with log-weights that make the softmax numerator and denominator unbiased. Matching layers stay exact: every aggressive thinning tested cost accuracy. At equal cost, the selected layers outperform the four shifted windows tested. On 13 unseen low-redundancy scenes with 32 views, LMSA stays within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, compared with 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R; its difference from contemporaneous GPA-VGGT is not significant, and only its gains over AVGGT pass both scene-level tests. With 100 views, it stays within 1.9 AUC@5 while its aggregator runs $2.0\times$ faster. Used post hoc to choose the layers GPA-VGGT protects, the statistic improves it by 1.2 AUC@5 for 5% more FLOPs. Applied untuned to $\pi^3$, it beats AVGGT but remains further from dense accuracy.
authors: Sammam Mahdi, Fariha Binta Salim, K. M. Jubair Sami, Rakin Bin Rabbani
bullets: Uniform attention thinning can lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry.
A logit-variance statistic selects between shared importance-sampled hubs for diffuse layers and exact attention for matching layers.
On 13 unseen 32-view scenes, LMSA stayed within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, versus 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R.
With 100 views, it remained within 1.9 AUC@5 of dense attention while running 2.0× faster in aggregation.
The statistic also improved GPA-VGGT by 1.2 AUC@5 at 5% more FLOPs, but untuned transfer to π³ remained farther from dense accuracy.

papers.abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
authors: Guy Zyskind
bullets: Across 40 questions from newly accepted papers, models usually recognized that questions were unstudied but rarely stated this clearly in ordinary answers.
Six frontier systems had reporting gaps of 30–90 percentage points, with larger gaps among more capable models.
The failure was asymmetric: models more reliably identified studied questions when the relevant papers were supplied.
A fixed answer combining model judgments with separate citation checks raised clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95% for GPT-6-Astra and improved all six systems.
The method also predicted reviewers’ novelty grades competitively without requiring model weights or internal activations.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.
authors: Zelong Liu, Hamza Ahmed, Wynn Wingyi Lee, Mickael Torjman, Alexander Dimitrakakis, Jiahua Lu, Timothy Deyer, Bachir Taouli, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Finds substantial organ-level grounding and laterality failures across vision encoders and generative VLMs, including high-performing models.
Uses matched-patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations to test anatomical evidence dependence.
Aligns finding sentences with anatomy-aware image features and trains on edited scans to strengthen organ–text correspondence.
Achieves strong classification, laterality, visual question answering, and report-generation performance using only public data.
After organ removal, its generative VLM retracts 96–99% of target-organ findings, indicating improved evidence-dependent reporting.

papers.abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.
authors: Malak Gamal El-Din, Yasser Shoukry, Salma Elmalaki
bullets: Addresses accuracy and efficiency losses when compressing models or removing weight multiplications on microcontrollers.
Uses hardware-aware architecture search and knowledge distillation to find compact Bernstein-activation CNNs.
Projects weights into multiplication-free codes, then recovers accuracy with learnable activations and generates specialized kernels.
On human activity recognition, BeCNNs improve accuracy by 2.75 percentage points over same-architecture ReLU CNNs; projected models lose only 0.8 points while achieving 2.2× speedup on a Cortex-M4.

Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference, the unprojected model provides higher accuracy, 2.2× lower latency, and 6.4× lower flash; projected models remain within 1 point of reference accuracy and run 5.9× faster.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $\pi_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
authors: Amrit Lal Singh, Smarak Kanjilal
bullets: LIBERO-trained VLA policies often fail on LIBERO-PRO when objects move or instructions change.
The method augments demonstrations by relocating and rotating objects, transferring tasks across environments and surfaces, and paraphrasing instructions.
A perception module using frozen DINOv3 features provides object positions and gripper-state information alongside TinyCLIP image and instruction embeddings.
A from-scratch flow-matching diffusion transformer predicts actions from this decoupled representation.
RageVLA achieves 0.72 on LIBERO-PRO, compared with 0.53 for the best published model; performance remains strong under object displacement tests.

papers.abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Xiangyu Zhou, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Positive sink-aligned components increase attention to image and question tokens, while negative components decrease it; effects persist in later layers.
SHRINK partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation without training.
Across nine benchmarks, SHRINK raises mean accuracy by 5.1 points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and 2.7 points on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on two other models.
Rescaling sink-aligned key components can substitute for the attention operations in GIFT and ACG with comparable hallucination-benchmark accuracy.

papers.title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Sink-aligned key components act as a controllable reference for attention in VLMs, enabling the training-free SHRINK method to improve sampled-reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets the informationless BOS representation created by causal masking, which later tokens repeatedly attend to.
At one prefill layer, allows only the BOS query to attend to all visual and textual input tokens; all other causal attention remains unchanged.
Requires no training, added parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead.
Improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and recent sink-intervention methods across eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks.
Mechanistic analysis finds reduced BOS sink dominance and more attention allocated to content-bearing prompt tokens.

All other attention patterns, the architecture are unchanged.

papers.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.
authors: Bao Trung Truong, Dat Thanh Nguyen, Thinh T. Doan
bullets: Studies learning and control when two dynamical subsystems disturb each other.
Combines an actively tilted, steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning for the maze and model-free reinforcement learning for the pendulum.
Adding the pendulum sharply reduces maze success initially, but online adaptation restores pre-coupling performance within a few episodes.
Both independently trained policies successfully control their respective systems despite the coupling.

Camera images are processed locally into observations, sent to a remote server that runs DreamerV3 and updates the maze policy via a replay buffer, and returned as roll/pitch commands to the board. The two subsystems are physically coupled through the shared board, with the pendulum acting as a disturbance on the maze policy.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
authors: Xuanwei Liu, Guipu Cao, Zhongyi Luo, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Existing tokenizers concatenate both arms’ actions, leaving shared motions and cross-arm dependencies for the policy to learn implicitly.
BiCAT uses a shared motion representation, symmetric cross-arm attention, and a joint decoder to condition each arm on its partner.
It predicts each arm’s tokens in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it.
Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among compared tokenizers.
It improves simulated mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with 40.5 ms per action chunk; gains are largest for tightly coordinated tasks.

papers.abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.
authors: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Shengyu Chen, Jiaqi Gong, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu
bullets: Fixed-condition PDE models only partially follow within-trajectory changes, while simply adding condition inputs after pretraining has little effect.
PhysDial combines coefficients, condition fields, and equation text as conditioning for a pretrained video diffusion transformer across eight 2D PDE families.
Including intervention samples in Kolmogorov-flow training roughly halves errors after changes in forcing wavenumber or amplitude at matched compute.
A few trajectories at new amplitudes substantially reduce extrapolation error; without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models on two turbulent flows.
The approach suggests simulators learn to use conditions only when training data make them necessary for prediction.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).
authors: Anas Anwarul Haq Khan, Amrin Kareem, Muhammad Umer Sheikh, Biplab Banerjee, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Problem: 2D visual encoders and unreliable monocular depth struggle with long-range distances, altitude selection, and coordinating forward/downward views.
Method: Lift depth from both cameras into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame, while aligning visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training.
The two components address complementary failure modes: explicit 3D lifting reduces collisions, while implicit geometry alignment improves target completion.
GRID raises target-reaching from 61.5% to 69.5% and task completion after reaching the target from 57.7% to 61.4%, with reported statistical significance.
On TravelUAV, GRID achieves the best success rate across all splits, with relative gains of 9.5%–25.4% over the prior state of the art.

papers.abstract: Training 3D vision-language models (VLMs) on large medical imaging datasets collected across institutions is constrained by data quality. Vast, uncurated pools of image-report pairs are characterized by redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity. We address this challenge of data curation for improving 3D VLM pretraining by proposing an offline, training-free, reference-guided data curation recipe. Our approach leverages a small, high-quality reference set to independently extract quality signals for each modality of a large, uncurated pool and merges them through a rank-aggregation step into a single ranking that guides sample selection. We validate this method on datasets comprising 35k 3D abdominal CT volume-report pairs from two institutions and 58k 2D chest X-ray image-report pairs. On 3D CT, using our reference-guided data curation strategy, our curated model matches the zero-shot disease classification performance of a state-of-the-art baseline (Merlin) while using $3.3\times$ less training data and a reference set of 5k samples. On 2D chest X-rays, our method yields a curated model that matches or exceeds the zero-shot disease classification performance of a model trained on the full pool while using up to $10\times$ less training data and a reference set of only 74 samples. Ablations show that the selection is stable under resampling of the reference, that smaller reference sets still outperform random sampling, and that label rebalancing does not improve performance. To support reproducibility, we release our code.
authors: Faidra Patsatzi, Ashwin Kumar, Chong Wang, Curtis P. Langlotz, Reinhard Heckel, Akshay S. Chaudhari
bullets: Addresses redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity in large multi-institutional image-report pools.
Uses a small high-quality reference set to derive modality-specific quality signals and combines them via rank aggregation.
Validated on 3D abdominal CT and 2D chest X-ray image-report datasets.
Matches baseline performance on 3D CT with 3.3× less training data, and matches or exceeds full-pool performance on chest X-rays with up to 10× less data.
Selection remains stable across reference resampling; smaller references outperform random sampling, while label rebalancing provides no benefit.

papers.abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.
authors: Xi Ding, Jiawei Zhang
bullets: Targets slow sequential zoom-in reasoning in agentic MLLMs and the lack of answer reliability scores.
A small model drafts the next glimpse and re-answers; unchanged, confident answers terminate early.
The large model verifies or corrects uncertain glimpses, while unresolved cases receive a single tool-free agent pass.
The framework provides label-free reliability scores from the verification trace and avoids running the full loop.
On V*, HR-Bench, and POPE, SpecLook achieves 87.2%/86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7×/4.7× speedups; SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9×/6.3× speedups.

papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.
authors: Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Chen-Yu Lee
bullets: Targets regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat in editable AI-agent harnesses without weight updates or external graders.
Decomposes tasks into pre-execution self-checks and uses directional regret to distinguish new failures from unresolved problems.
Selects candidate edits with group-relative fitness and applies a Soft-HURT gate that accepts gains only when they outweigh regressions.
Scopes specialized fixes and protects gated behaviors from regression; deployment uses one frozen harness in a single pass.
Across memory, skill-evolution, continual-task, and domain-reasoning benchmarks, it improves performance while reducing forgetting, memory pollution, and deployment token usage.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.
authors: Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman, Ammar Mohanna
bullets: Early-step-weighted cross-step training improves acceptance by 15–24% over uniformly weighted detached training, while proxy cross-entropy does not reliably predict acceptance.
Under a fixed 256-node budget, confidence-guided candidate allocation raises speedup from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval and from 1.31× to 1.75× on MT-Bench.
Allocation gains also transfer to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify them.
Host-thread settings can nearly remove speedups without changing acceptance, highlighting the need for controlled end-to-end latency evaluation.
The study uses a lightweight feature-prediction drafter, a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target, and greedy decoding.
