papers.abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).
authors: Michael Schroeder
bullets: BiFPN alone does not beat a plain MBConv trunk, but adding stage attention raises accuracy to 73.15%.
Zero-gated residual attention adapters at P3–P5 achieve 74.02% standalone and a +0.954-point gain over a matched plain-B0 control.
Attention strength increases with semantic depth, from P3 through P5.
Naive kernel averaging and single-template tying substantially hurt accuracy.
Alternating two shared block templates reduces parameters by 10.9% and reaches 70.92% after one epoch, 1.84 points below the unshared control.

By epoch 80, learned branch update-to-input RMS rises monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 windowed MHSA → 45.4% at P4 global MHSA → 66.3% at P5 global MHSA). papers.selection_reason: Fits efficient AI through lightweight attention adapters and parameter-efficient weight sharing in vision backbones.
papers.title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones

papers.abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.
authors: Michael Schroeder
bullets: Quantization degradation is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers across ResNet and EfficientNet backbones.
A structured recovery analysis tests selective INT4/INT8 precision and floating-point scales.
Retaining less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of accuracy lost under aggressive sub-4-bit compression.
On ARM and x86 CPUs, software bit-unpacking causes reported execution slowdowns of 1.48×–21.5× depending on batch size.
The study highlights a trade-off between reduced model storage and practical edge throughput.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mechanisms of sub-4-bit quantization failure and the 5-step mixed-precision recovery waterfall on EfficientNet-B0. (A) Uniform 3-bit quantization fails due to three compounding effects: (1) each 3×3 depthwise spatial filter has only 9 weights per channel (unlike dense layers that average hundreds of inputs), so 7 signed levels ({−3..+3}) erase edge orientation in low-channel early stages; (2) a single outlier weight stretches the symmetric max-abs step size ∆ = max |w|/3, collapsing the inner 95% of weights into the zero bin (q = 0); and (3) coarse weight rounding shifts output channel means and variances, causing frozen FP32 BatchNorm statistics to mis-center activations and saturate ReLU6. (B) Protecting 0.34% of early weights (14 KB) at W8 rescues +42.92 pp when the rest of the model is W4 (65.95%). For a 3.55–3.56-bit mixed W8/W4/W3 model, combining per-channel MSE clipping (+9.00 pp), 1,000-image BatchNorm recalibration (+3.94 pp), 82-layer dynamic-programming bit allocation (+3.85 pp to 67.94% PTQ), and 1 epoch of QAT with post-QAT BN recalibration recovers top-1 accuracy from 0.30% to 68.98% across all 50,000 validation images.

Figure 3: The 82-layer mixed-precision allocation blueprint for EfficientNet-B0 (DP0.5, 3.56 mean bits, 2.35 MB). Top row: Architectural precision tiers showing Tier 0 (0.34% of weights, 13, 952 parameters in the stem and Stage 1–2 depthwise/pointwise layers protected at W8, which alone restores +42.92 pp on W4 while FP16 adds only +0.03 pp), Tier 1 (∼ 55.8% of weights in mid/deep 3× 3 and 5× 5 depthwise filters, Squeeze-and-Excitation bottlenecks, and the 1280× 1000 classifier head assigned to W4), and Tier 2 (∼ 43.9% of weights in wide Stage 5–7 1× 1 pointwise projections where high channel fan-in tolerates W3). Bottom row: The three post-selection calibration stages: per-output-channel MSE clipping (α∗ = argminα∈[0.5,1.0] ∥w−Qα(w)∥22), 1,000-image BatchNorm moment recalibration, and 82-layer dynamic-programming allocation followed by 1 epoch of QAT and post-QAT BN recalibration (68.98% top-1).

Figure 2: Uniform 4-bit (INT4) weight quantization on mature B0 and B1 checkpoints. Converged checkpoints suffer severe post-training accuracy drops (−49.82 pp on B0 and −24.39 pp on B1) across all 50,000 validation images, contrasting sharply with early-epoch pilots.

Figure 5: Measured LiteRT artifact size, full-validation accuracy, and CPU latency on mature EfficientNet-B0. Full-integer INT8 dominates FP32 on both size and speed with negligible accuracy loss (−0.058 pp). Mixed 4-bit (WI4) reduces storage further (−82.4%) but loses 9.60 points and increases median latency by 47.9% due to missing native sub-byte depthwise kernels.

Figure 4: The deployment gap between storage compression and execution speed on EfficientNetB0. Converting from 32-bit floats (20.43 MB, 9.81 ms) to full-integer INT8 (6.00 MB, 6.65 ms) simultaneously reduces file size by 70.7% and median CPU latency by 32.2% with negligible accuracy loss (−0.06 pp) because all 82 convolutional and dense layers execute on native 8-bit integer SIMD instructions. Below 8 bits, standard CPU runtimes lack native sub-byte depthwise kernels: LiteRT’s mixed 4-bit path (WI4, 66 INT4 + 16 FP32 depthwise operators) and custom packed 3-bit (INT3) bitstreams reduce storage to 3.59 MB (−82.4%) and 2.47 MB (−88.4%), but runtime bit-unpacking into floating-point buffers slows inference to 15.43 ms (+47.9%) and 376.8 ms (21.5× slower than FP32; 0.30% uniform INT3 accuracy in the packed CPU benchmark vs. *68.98% for the 3.56-bit DP0.5 + QAT recovery model).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes low-bit quantization collapse and mixed-precision recovery for efficient vision deployment, directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
papers.tldr: Sub-4-bit quantization collapses Vision CNN accuracy mainly in late pointwise and depthwise layers, while sparse 8-bit recovery can restore much of the loss but may incur substantial CPU unpacking overhead.

papers.abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.
authors: Abdul Qadir Ibrahim, Martin Burger, Abel Maviano Jonathan
bullets: Calibrated rules bound the probability of exceeding the error budget under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, abstaining when calibration is infeasible.
Mode selection reduces active Fourier support but not measurable latency because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate runtime.
Channel narrowing reduces Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection requires the dense prediction first.
An input-only width selector runs at 0.52–0.95× dense latency, yet often misses its 90% coverage target and is generally slower or less covered than matched static widths.
Adaptive methods should be evaluated by coverage and complete runtime against calibrated static baselines.

papers.abstract: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.
authors: Haisheng Fu, Gexin Huang, Haikai Zhao, Jie Liang, Zhenman Fang, Jingning Han, Xiaoxiao Li
bullets: Attention sinks make raw attention unreliable for visual localization.
Question-induced changes in attention amount and spatial focus separate; the spatial effect, measured in bits, identifies useful layers.
WhereBits combines this unlabeled layer prior with per-head contrastive scores.

Across eight VLMs, it matches box-tuned pointing accuracy on COCO and RefCOCO, generalizes to held-out models and higher resolutions, and reaches 0.72 COCO pointing accuracy versus 0.22 for mean attention.
Its training-free zoom-in crops improve V* forced-choice accuracy by 6.0 points.

papers.abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.
authors: Nischal Subedi, Cencheng Shen, Peng Zhao

It ranks best on average across 13 methods in few-shot BERT-base classification and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, despite a smaller initial input-factor norm.
Benefits shrink with more labeled data; extensions also report gains on 7B/8B Llama classification and GSM8K and StrategyQA.

papers.abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.
authors: Jinjun Peng, Wailiang Zhao, Baishakhi Ray, Zhou Yu, Jufeng Yang
bullets: Studies plasticity and stability at the module level across declarative memorization and procedural learning tasks.
QK and VO projections are most plastic for procedural tasks, while MLPs are most plastic for declarative memorization.
Stability does not mirror plasticity: updating QK preserves more stored declarative knowledge than updating MLPs or VO.
Reset-and-recovery experiments suggest plasticity reflects a module’s primary computation or storage role, whereas stability depends on all capabilities relying on that module.
Similar asymmetric dynamics appear in experiments with a realistic model and tasks.

papers.abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.
authors: Jensen (Jinghao), Zhou, Samuel Rota Bulo, Denis Rozumny, Duncan Zauss, Peter Hedman, Nikhil Keetha, Philip Torr, Christian Rupprecht, Andrea Vedaldi, Peter Kontschieder
bullets: Uses visual context for reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions.
Retrieves relevant input and generated views to maintain a bounded active context.
Fine-tunes a bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching, then trains a causal model on its rollouts.
Evaluated across camera and text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency.
The abstract reports adaptation across diverse input/output settings through a unified in-context interface.

papers.abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.
authors: Jiarui Cui, Boxun Yan
bullets: Introduces 10,000 simulated two-port planar RF layouts with editable geometry, raster images, occupancy grids, complex S-parameters, structural categories, and response labels.

Defines seven tasks covering layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator validation, diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification.
Benchmarks seven multimodal language models and finds systematic weaknesses in structurally valid generation and electromagnetically faithful response prediction.
RF-specific fine-tuning improves structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the within-2-dB response rate from 17.7% to 62.8%.
The benchmark supports evaluation of models that link RF design intent, layout representations, and physical behavior, but substantial challenges remain.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/
authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube
bullets: Studies LLM decision-making in iterative games with incomplete information.
Compares externalized reasoning traces with internal layer activations.
Finds that game representations are formed and revised throughout reasoning.
Shows that premature incorrect beliefs persist in both the trace and activations.
Provides an interactive visualizer for selected example traces.

papers.tldr: Mechanistic analysis shows that LLMs iteratively construct game representations during chain-of-thought, but rarely recover after committing to an incorrect belief.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.
authors: Hubert Strauss, Liam Fowl, Noam Razin
bullets: Sequence-level OPD has a future-agreement bias that token-level objectives avoid.
This bias can cause reverse learning: later positions are matched first, while earlier positions may favor teacher-improbable tokens.
Forward KL yields a well-behaved optimization landscape.
Other f-divergences, including reverse KL, can have vanishing gradients even when student and teacher distributions differ substantially.
The preferable OPD objective depends on the student, teacher, and post-training task.

figures.caption: Figure 13: Example of the user message given to gpt-5.6-terra for writing the programs in the code completion dataset (see Appendix E.3.1 for details on the dataset construction process). The model responded with a structured output containing one entry per program, whose fields are described in Appendix E.3.1.

Figure 5: RKL becomes more preferable to FKL as the capacity gap between the student and teacher grows. We trained Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base students using token-level OPD with the FKL and RKL divergences and Qwen3 teachers of varying sizes, on the MATH dataset. The left plot shows that the gap in accuracy between students trained with RKL and FKL grows with the size of the teacher (markers stand for means over three seeds, with error bars denoting standard deviation). The middle and right plots point to a potential cause: the tokens whose probability increases the most under RKL are typically already likely under the initial student, whereas under FKL they can have low initial probability, especially with the larger teacher, suggesting that FKL changes the student in ways that are less compatible with its initial capabilities. Specifically, for the 0.6B student with the 4B and 32B teachers, the middle and right plots show how the initial student probabilities are distributed for the tokens that increased the most in probability during training.

Figure 11: Sequence-level OPD can cause the student to refuse to answer even when its thinking block concludes that the request is safe. Shown is an output of the Qwen3-1.7B student for a benign training request, generated at training step 282 of a sequence-level OPD run in Figure 9. We show an output from this training step since, later in training, the thinking blocks of the student often become empty.

Figure 4: RKL and JS struggle to distill knowledge of new APIs in a code completion task. We trained a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Base student using token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B-Base teacher, on prompts requiring the use of Python APIs that were released after the student (see Section 4.2.1). Reported values are computed over training prompts for which the student initially assigns the first token of the correct API name a probability of at most 10−3, and averaged over three seeds (shaded areas mark standard deviation). In agreement with Theorem 2, FKL and its equal mixture with RKL quickly match the rate at which the teacher names the correct API, whereas RKL and JS are substantially slower to do so. Note that this slowdown is not due to insufficient sampling of unlikely tokens, since the divergences are computed over the full vocabulary and RKL and JS are slow to raise even the probability of the first token of the correct API name. Rather, it stems from their objective landscapes being flat along the logits of such tokens (as established in Section 4.1).

Figure 2: Future agreement bias prevents sequence-level OPD from efficiently solving the binary tree navigation task. We trained a randomly initialized Transformer student via sequence-level and tokenlevel OPD on the binary tree navigation task described in Section 3.2, using tree depth L = 15 and δ = 10−4. The left plot reports the probability that the student assigns to the correct pathy⋆ (i.e., success probability) and to the correct token at the root, throughout training. The middle and right plots report the RKL divergence between the student and teacher next-token distributions at each token position, across training steps of sequence-level and token-level OPD (averaged over 512 student-generated outputs and normalized by its initial value; error bars mark standard error). In line with our theory, sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root, correcting this mistake only after matching the teacher at later positions, whereas token-level OPD efficiently matches the teacher starting from the root. Figure 8 shows that token-level OPD with FKL and JS exhibits trends similar to those of token-level OPD with RKL.

Figure 3: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to cause over-refusal of benign requests. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using sequence-level and token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B teacher. The training prompts were taken from the WildJailbreak dataset and consist of an equal mixture of harmful and benign requests. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 17.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, sequence-level OPD lowers the safety accuracy of the student (i.e., the percentage of prompts for which it correctly refuses a harmful request or answers a benign one), whereas token-level OPD substantially improves it by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 1: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Section 3.2 (for depth L = 3). The student starts at the root, and its goal is to produce with high probability the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A), which reaches a fixed target leaf. The teacher assigns high probability to choosing the left child at the root and every node in its left subtree (δ = exp(−L)), but chooses uniformly among children if the initial token is incorrect.

Figure 7: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using a Qwen3-8B teacher via sequence-level OPD and token-level OPD with the RKL, FKL, and JS divergences on arithmetic problems, where each prompt instructs the model to either solve the problem directly or output a call to a calculator tool with an arithmetic expression. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator in only 7.2% of its outputs, sequencelevel OPD leads the student to call it for nearly all problems due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, the student attains near-perfect accuracy under sequence-level OPD, even surpassing the teacher. By contrast, token-level OPD leads the student to call the calculator less, and so its accuracy remains substantially lower than the accuracy achieved with sequence-level OPD.

Figure 12: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 7, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different system prompt (see Appendix E.2.2). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator tool in only 1.4% of its outputs, sequence-level OPD leads the student to call it for most problems. It therefore outperforms token-level OPD objectives, under which the student almost never uses the calculator and struggles to learn to solve the problems directly as accurately as the teacher.

Figure 8: Token-level OPD objectives exhibit similar trends in the binary tree navigation task since they all avoid the future agreement bias. This figure supplements Figure 2 by including experiments with token-level OPD using the FKL and JS divergences. The left plot is analogous to that of Figure 2 (for clarity, teacher probabilities are omitted). The middle and right plots are the same as those of Figure 2, but for token-level OPD with FKL and JS, respectively. Both objectives behave similarly to token-level OPD with RKL: they efficiently match the teacher starting from the root, whereas sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root.

Figure 6: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Appendix A.1 (for depth L = 3). The task and teacher are the same as in Figure 1, except that, alongside the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A) to the leftmost leaf, every path that starts with B is also correct. Thus, the task can be solved either by following y⋆, which the teacher strongly prefers (δ = exp(−L)), or by choosing B at the root and then any continuation.

Figure 10: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different prompt template (see Appendix E.2.1). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 12% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy. Token-level OPD, on the other hand, is able to improve the safety accuracy by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 9: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with thinking enabled). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that thinking is enabled. That is, instead of responding directly, the student and teacher first produce thinking tokens, enclosed in a dedicated block marked by <think> and </think> tokens. Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 7.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy, whereas token-level OPD keeps the refusal rate of the student on benign requests close to that of the teacher and improves its safety accuracy.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the time-consuming, model-specific redesign of post-training quantization recipes.
The agent iteratively builds and evaluates candidate recipes using output KL divergence on hidden reasoning traces, with long-generation checks for failures.
A compatible library of public PTQ methods speeds recipe construction across model architectures.
Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.
For GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy; checkpoints run on existing serving kernels without inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
authors: Stephen Chung, Wenyu Du
bullets: Separate per-layer n-gram tables are memory-intensive, while naïve sharing limits layer-specific preferences.
Chorus lets each layer adapt shared embeddings using a layer-specific projection and hidden-state-conditioned rescaling.
With 1.2B table parameters, Chorus outperforms FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram using 9.6B parameters.
It outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram across the compared table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters.
Combined with Ember, Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory by 99.2% versus AdamW without degrading training performance.

papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.
authors: Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Jaron Cui, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay
bullets: Introduces Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical rat body for embodied simulation.
Develops Rat NCAP, a mammalian spinal-circuit-inspired architecture with cell-type-specific connectivity and a flexor–extensor neuromechanical interface.
Uses GPU-accelerated simulation and training to optimize circuit parameters without imitation learning.
The model learns multiple locomotion speeds and gait transitions, with behavior, kinematics, and neural activity consistent with experiments.
Cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict responses to graded perturbations; interface design strongly affects trainability and gait quality.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.
authors: Zekai Chen, Yihan Sun, Xunkai Li, Xun Wu, Xinmo Jin, Yinlin Zhu, Haodong Lu, Xuaner Chen, Rong-Hua Li
bullets: Targets failures in agent interactions, message exchanges, and task dependencies that agent-level anomaly detection may miss.
Learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent states, messages, and dependencies.

Experiments across five MAS benchmarks show a 60.2% improvement in root-cause localization accuracy and consistent task-recovery gains over strong safeguards.

papers.abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.
authors: Mohammad Eslami, Mousa Moradi, Negin Ghamsarian, Nazlee Zebardast, Jennifer L Lindsey, Sophia Y. Wang, Lucia Sobrin, Rishi P Singh, Tobias Elze
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of searching large surgical video archives for similar operations, complications, and workflow events.
Combines eight public datasets spanning four surgical domains, six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips.
Provides Scene retrieval of operative states and Workflow retrieval of phase transitions or deviations, with safeguards against timing and labeling shortcuts.
Evaluates generic and surgical foundation models, retrieval methods, and benchmark-trained contrastive heads under within- and cross-dataset settings.
Frozen representations barely beat timing-only baselines, transition retrieval is near chance, and trained heads degrade substantially across datasets.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.
authors: Shing Wai Pun, Kai Wu, Pengfei Xia, Hui Zang, Wei Guo, Yong Liu
bullets: Targets GR inference with long prompts, wide beam search, and short fixed outputs.
Uses Tree Attention to share prompt-prefix computation and avoid redundant KV-cache accesses across beams.
Reduces overhead with pre-generated masks, static KV allocation, loop-unrolled dispatch, graph compilation, operator fusion, and constrained decoding.
Achieves latency comparable to a state-of-the-art custom-kernel solution.
Shows that end-to-end pipeline optimization can precede custom-kernel development.

papers.abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank
authors: Dmitry Ignatov
bullets: Represents each quality-resource frontier using effective active channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=s^2/\kappa$, versus remaining log-error depth.
Separates intrinsic frontier shape from the scale and origin of each resource axis, with bounds from complete monotonicity and divisibility.
For $N$ active resources, recommends operating where $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$ in delivered units.
Derives minimax prices $\lambda_i^\star=\alpha_i/(N+1)$ and worst-case regret $\ln(N+1)$ nats.
Evaluates the theory on 117 published frontiers and provides the open-source nn-rank package for pricing and ranking candidates.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The paper in one picture, and where each part is proved. The object is a Laplace transform of a task’s difficulty law evaluated at what the resource buys; the theory is the plane curve it traces; the two structural hypotheses are two differential inequalities on that curve, and the two walls that bound every frontier are those inequalities integrated from the floor. Everything in the dashed box is a consequence of the figure above it.

Figure 8: The rules actually in use, scored against the derived price on the same frontiers. (a) Regret of each selection rule, one point per frontier, bars at the median; the dashed line is the 0.05-nat band inside which the recommendation does not change. The canonical rule lies inside the band on almost every frontier, while the comparison quantifies the cost of alternative choices. (b) The bits gained against the extra resource spent past the canonical point: the median frontier buys 0.99 bits at 44× the cost, which is the price of not knowing where to operate. (c) The floor read from three models against the floor from a full fit. Detail in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

Figure 2: The theory as one curve. (a) The primitive is Neff against the depth still available, with Neff(0) = 0 at the floor. The axiom bounds its growth by ˙Neff ≤ Neff +1 and the hypothesis by ˙Neff ≤ 1; integrated from the same initial condition those two inequalities are the two charts, so the tangency at the origin is a property of one initial-value problem. The shaded wedge is the whole divisibility question, and the dotted rays represent the admissible constant-slope chart family. (b) The working statistic c3 ≥ 0 is ˙Neff ≤ 2: it cannot see the band between the two slopes, which D̂1 ≥ 0 closes at no extra measurement cost. (c) In the gaugefree coordinates of Proposition 6 the single-channel regret is − ln sinφ identically, the rule is the right angle, and the axiom states that φ is 1-Lipschitz with respect to arc length—whence L ≥ π over the complete sweep. (d) What the stronger rung is worth on clean charts at matched level; on this corpus both statistics stay at their nominal level.

Figure 3: The theory is one plane curve. (a) Channels remaining against depth remaining. The axiom confines every completely monotone frontier below e∆S −1 and the hypothesis below that curve’s own tangent at the origin, ∆S; the two bounding solutions are charts, the two-atom chart and the cure chart, and each is the unique frontier saturating its wall (Proposition 1(iii)). Every constant-σ chart is a ray whose slope is |σ| and whose intercept is the floor, so the admissible charts form a pencil (Corollary 4). The operating point is the height Neff = 1/t; where it meets a wall is the recommended depth, one bit on the axiom’s extremal against one nat on the hypothesis’s. (b) The gap between the walls closes quadratically at the origin, and the origin is the floor: a second-order test is powerless at the deep end by theorem, not by accident of this corpus. (c) The admissible arc is a functional of the same curve, so the walls bound it from below; with the covering law the right-hand axis reads the number of operating points a benchmark needs, and the hypothesis bound passes the axiom’s limiting value π at λ = π2/4. (d) The archive’s 117 frontiers, read with three accuracies per point and no bandwidth. The curve is noise-dominated: the median straightness is R2 = 0.22 and against a design-matched null no statistic read from it has power (Section 10).

(b) The mean regret (32) of an operating point placed uniformly in arc length: exactly one bit for a single reducible channel, rising to γ+ ln 2 and never beyond. This is the cost of not knowing where to operate, and it is bounded. (c) The microfoundation comparison: measured pairwise co-failure rates for the three mechanisms on the per-item panel of the technical report in the archive, § “What the item level says”.

Figure 6: The floor is not a parameter. (a) A two-atom fit to a frontier whose floor is exactly zero returns a floor that is a large fraction of the best observed error, monotone in the shape index, and the curve sweeps the whole of (0, 1) as the index does; the archive’s own median fitted share, 0.96 of the best observed error, is what a floorless frontier with β = 0.10 produces. (b) The shape index from three independent routes—a direct floorless fit, the bandwidth-free three-point chord arc, and the collapse coordinate ζ—on the frontiers where each is defined. (c) The arc predicted from β against the measured chord arc; the increasing-hazard frontiers, which have no arc at all, are the three distribution-shift evaluations. The three-parameter law plateaus well above the measurement noise (shaded); the whole completely monotone class, fitted nonparametrically, plateaus with it; the one shape parameter β of the stretched-exponential form removes most of the gap. (b) Agreement on the 2 025 pooled interior leave-one-out predictions. (c) The fitted β, with one point per frontier and a bar at the corpus median: corpus-specific and, on these windows, weakly identified. Details are provided in the Appendix, § “The empirical study”.

The shaded segment is the 0.05-nat band, the open circles are the five checkpoints of Theorem 15, and the inner curves are the 12 of the 18 archived ImageNet single-resource windows that have a measurable chord arc, median 0.39π, drawn on the same absolute scale and centered on the right angle so that their lengths can be compared—the chord returns a length and not a position, and the positions the jet does return sit deep, at a median Neff = 0.465 and hence φ = 1.20 < π/2. (b) Regret from the reference is minus the log sine of arc position, (29); the shaded cells are the five checkpoints’ covering neighborhoods. (c) Checkpoints the arc needs against Pareto points measured, one point per frontier; crosses are the six frontiers whose log-convexity defect is non-positive, on which the chord returns no arc and the law fails.

Table 3: Held-out prediction, scored per frontier. Interior is leave-one-out on each interior measurement; forward trains on the least expensive two-thirds and predicts the most expensive third; backward trains on the most expensive two-thirds and predicts the least expensive third. The error is | ln εpred − ln εobs|, summarized per frontier and then across frontiers, with intervals bootstrapped over the 117 frontiers—never over the 2 025 dependent prediction events. The lower panel is the paired comparison on the same frontiers. The law is better than the floorless power law on a majority of frontiers in all three regimes; it loses the interior to a model-free interpolator and wins the backward extrapolation against every baseline. Script 169, from script 68’s per-frontier output.

Table 5: Where each reported number comes from. The archive’s scripts are numbered and run in order; each writes a CSV under results/, so every figure below can be checked without typesetting a table. Three of the 163 scripts reach the network and none is needed to reproduce a number in this paper.

Table 1: What refutes the divisibility hypothesis, what it costs, and where it can be read. “Order” is the lowest derivative of S the test involves. In the derivatives of S alone the axiom and the hypothesis coincide at every order ≤ 2, so without a floor the discriminating content begins at order three; the order-2 rows buy their discrimination with a floor instead, which is the second of the two currencies named below.

Table 4: Selection rules on the 26 attainable single-resource frontiers of the archive, scored against the derived price. Regret is in nats; the tolerance is 0.05 nats inside which the recommendation does not change. Each rule is implemented directly on a discrete measured frontier. (2025), whose limitations are discussed by Dehghani et al. (2022); the knee is Das (1999); Satopää et al. (2011); the budget is the rule of Sun et al. (2026) at the geometric midpoint of each frontier’s own range. The fixed-exponent row is the soft objective of Tan et al. (2019), ACC · (LAT/T )w, whose target enters only through the constant T−w

papers.selection_reason: Develops a differential theory for quality-resource trade-offs in AI model selection, providing a framework for optimizing resource usage.
papers.title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price

papers.abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.
authors: Peng Xie, Amr Alanwar
bullets: Taylor reachability is limited by complex-plane singularities, especially in rational terms and sigmoid-like controller gates.

In closed-loop systems and MNIST classifiers, Chebyshev certificates remain valid in cases where Taylor certificates diverge or become unknown.
Measured width limits agree with theory to 89–94%, and certified claims passed Monte Carlo checks with zero observed violations.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a rigorous method (Chebyshev abstractions) for verifying the safety of learning-enabled controllers, which is critical for the deployment of safe robot learning and manipulation systems.
papers.title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
papers.tldr: Chebyshev polynomial zonotope abstractions provide wider and more reliable certified reachability bounds than Taylor expansions for learning-enabled nonlinear systems.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.
authors: Ayaan Qayyum, Bruce Yi Bu, Zicong Li, Jingfeng Zhou
bullets: Naive rate coding can produce inefficiently dense spike representations for vision tasks.
DoG and DVS-style delta modulation generate substantially sparser spike trains than rate coding.
Biologically inspired encoders provide the largest accuracy gains when model capacity is constrained.
K-FAC gives modest, consistent improvements over Adam, while Rouser thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13%.
Results are demonstrated on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST; broader generalization and hardware-level energy gains are not established here.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
authors: Guoqing Wang
Pin Tang
Xiangxuan Ren
Chao Ma
bullets: Pixel-level future generation contains many visually plausible but planning-irrelevant details.
The model represents each surrounding agent with discrete tokens encoding identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context.
Agent tokens are learned through geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning.
Open- and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios show stronger planning, better use of visual and dynamic information, and interpretable world states.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.
authors: Ibrahim Albool
Yasser Shoukry
bullets: Targets the difficulty of formally identifying safe initial states through scalable backward reachability analysis.
Refines an input-space cover by analyzing activation patterns and splitting where the relaxation gap is predicted to be largest.
Produces certified inner and outer approximations rather than relying on a single convex bound.
Evaluated on high-dimensional models, including a linearized Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein Transformer block.
Also examines how model-level reachability guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT systems.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

papers.abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. By reducing the computational cost, \textsc{cuPIQP} provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.
authors: Fenglong Song
Roland Schwan
Yuwen Chen
Yuning Jiang
Colin N. Jones
bullets: Targets the need to solve and differentiate through many QPs concurrently in robotics applications such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control.
Uses a proximal interior-point method with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage QPs.

In benchmarks with batches of up to 16,384 QPs, it achieves solve-time speedups of up to 18.8× over Moreau and 4.26× over eight-core PIQP.
Accelerates end-to-end learning by 4.6× over QPAX and 7.8× over Moreau.

papers.abstract: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

Vishnu Rao

papers.abstract: While velocity-commanded RL policies are effective for controlling quadrupeds, they are a limited interface for humanoids that need to perform complex whole-body motions. Furthermore, RL tracking policies for whole-body motions typically have limited information about the desired future motion, preventing them from performing controlled deviations to achieve long-term task success; such information is particularly relevant when a controller must prepare for transitions between behaviors. We address these challenges using concise motion representations that can be generated by a high-level controller, given a behavior label or text command. These representations can be fed directly into a tracking policy to provide a detailed motion reference. Our method exhibits a high degree of flexibility in performing real-world robot motions such as dancing, fighting, or walking based on conditional information. At matched capacity, our adopted stochastic motion tokenizer reconstructs motions from the Unitree G1 at a level that exceeds state-of-the-art approaches such as finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and the vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE). The resulting discrete interface conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions lasting 16.8 s each and a 35 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1.
authors: Michael Drolet
Oleg Arenz
Jan Peters
bullets: Velocity commands and short-horizon tracking references are insufficient for complex humanoid motions and behavior transitions.
The method tokenizes whole-body motion into concise discrete representations generated from behavior labels or text commands.
These tokens condition a tracking policy with detailed future motion information.
On a physical Unitree G1, the system executed 16.8-second dance, fight, and walk motions, plus a 35-second fight-to-dance sequence.
At matched capacity, motion reconstruction exceeded FSQ and VQ-VAE baselines.

papers.abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) enables fine-grained sensing of spatial relationships between wireless devices. The WiFi Sensor for Robotics (WSR) toolbox demonstrated that WiFi-CSI measurements collected during robot motion, combined with odometry, can be used to synthesize virtual antenna arrays, enabling motion-induced bearing estimation in multi-robot experiments. However, deploying the WSR approach has remained challenging due to its limited integration with standard robotics tools and reliance on deprecated WiFi-CSI acquisition hardware. This work presents an open-source simulation framework that integrates the WSR sensing pipeline within the robotic simulator Gazebo. The framework generates synthetic WiFi-CSI measurements with realistic physical signal properties and leverages realistic robot motion required for motion-induced sensing and downstream localization. It further supports processing both simulated and real WiFi-CSI data for direct comparison and validation. Our aim is to make WSR-style sensing accessible as a modular sensing modality for robotic research. We validate our framework by comparing simulated and real-world experiments using TurtleBot3 robots, and demonstrate its use for bearing estimation and robot localization. This work lowers the barrier to entry for WiFi-CSI-based sensing in multi-robot systems and provides a foundation for integrating WiFi-CSI sensing with multi-modal perception for localization and coordination. All code and experimental details are publicly available at https://github.com/baharhaghighat/DARS_2026_Dijkstra_et_al
authors: Brendan Dijkstra
Ninad Jadhav
Maurice Stoffijn
Stephanie Gil

bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using WSR sensing due to limited robotics-tool integration and deprecated CSI hardware.

Validated with TurtleBot3 experiments for bearing estimation and robot localization.
Provides a modular foundation for WiFi-CSI-based multi-robot perception, localization, and coordination.

Our simulation framework operates fully independently from the WSR toolbox software package as we directly implement its methods within MATLAB.
